entities.search_text: Senior factor and matriarch of the Havrana-Jenga House at Tavakh-Qarat, the Basin's largest warehouse-port. She is in her early sixties and heads a four-generation commercial line of Oravan-Ndjadi blended descent: her mother was Halanimoa-Oravan of the diaspora-commercial line, and her father a Mbu-tier Ndjadi whose house she has never publicly named. She is the only senior factor at the seat who reads Wazahaki tier-prefix notarization without a translator's hand, the prefixed marks that fix which clerk of which tier certified a rate and under whose authority it stands; she learned them at her father's knee before the abacus, and that reading is the personal fact on which her institutional standing actually rests. Her instrument is the terms of warehouse-credit, and her discipline is to set them. She is the one who decides whose word the house's credit will carry next, and for six years she has decided not to decide. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. A successor. The house is four generations old and is owed its fifth matriarch; the senior cohort, the Khazadari rate-setters who watch the seat, and the two claimant coalitions beneath…

Junior underwriter of the Havrana-Pulino workshop on the Halanimoa offshore cove. She is in her thirties and carries the workshop's compound lineage name as her own: a Tarano-tier artisan-underwriter whose institutional standing is the binder she can issue under the Concord's parallel pricing circular, and the craft is in knowing which rate instrument holds where. Her workshop is Concord-aligned by the maritime-registry fact that distinguishes it from the Covenant's receipt-book houses; she is not neutral between the two systems. The binder she tendered for the Tin-Aghīz-Lam-Chen partnership's cyclone-season cargo was issued at the circular's rate because that is the rate the workshop signs for. The suspension that arrives three days after the determination is the rate dispute she has been underwriting around for the length of her career, arrived at her specific binder. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. A cleared binder, and the cargo that cannot move without it. Twenty-one loads of grade-certified clove and seven loads of obsidian-blade consignment waiting at the Halanimoa cove; Amori Lam-Chen Phyi's signature on the binder is a…

Fourth-year Tongue-Guild apprentice. Father's line: Ndjadi ka-tier scribal, Kibwana house. Mother's line: Oravan Teirun harbor matrilineage. Age approximately nineteen. The mixed-heritage multi-register competence is the canonical motif that gives an apprentice of this heritage institutional standing across all three Harbor-Oath-War jurisdictional claimants — and the institutional vulnerability that the arc turns on. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. An apprentice bond, four years old, nearly paid: forty-two khatti credit remaining of the original hundred-and-ten. The count is tracked in the Tongue-Guild's ledger at the Tavakh-Qarat basin-port seat. Each certified sealing reduces it. An uncertified sealing reduces nothing. The bond line is the count that carries tension across all five scenes of the harbor-oath-war arc. Built. Four years of register competence across the three major commercial-oath registers: Wazahaki (father's register, the ka-tier scribal tongue), Tavamala (Oravan hull-and-cargo witness protocol), and the Ṣāliqūn-prefix Qalīb form the Frankincense Syndics use for oath-binding. Multi-register competence at this…

A consecration-mark assayer, Gold-Sodality-formed on the plateau, now in commercial service at the cinchona-cataract ports of the Aethelian Basin. Age in her middle thirties. She learned to read a guild mark by hand-pressure pattern the way every Sodality apprentice does, in the first year, before she ever struck one herself; she left the plateau for the Basin, where the same forensic eye that authenticated regalia for the Sodality now authenticates cargo for merchant houses that pay better and ask fewer questions. The competence that made her valuable on the plateau is the competence that makes her dangerous to her Basin employers, and the Metal Interdict is the crisis that sets the two against each other. She is Ngaru-Bon by formation, not by the Basin's accounting. The Basin registers her as a commercial assayer of no civ; the plateau registers her as a Sodality-trained hand who left. Both registers are correct, and the arc turns on the gap between them. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. Her standing in the Basin commercial assay register, which is worth exactly as much as it has never been bought. An assayer's seal certifies that…

Concordant of the Ancestor-Register, the Ñawpa-Khipu Hatun, at Wawa-Kocha. He is late forties and slight-framed, of a lineage descended from the cliff-road observatory's third-generation cohort but trained from the start in the long-form genealogical cords rather than the solstitial computation of the senior almanac. He is the Register's current Concordant: the officer authorized to read the long-form genealogies aloud in ratification proceedings and to issue the genealogical seal that validates an altitude-tier promotion on its own ground, independently of which calendar is reckoned above it. The Register's holding-vault sits on the Wawa-Kocha middle terrace, two altitude-bands below the senior calendar-keeper's observatory and above the Cinchona Sodality's grove-access archive, a position that states the institution's standing in stone: allied to the Alto on the calendar-side, independent on the genealogical-side. The independence is the load-bearing part. As long as the Register appears to stand on its own, the genealogical record can be treated as settled ground while every calendrical question above it stays in dispute, and that appearance is commercially load-bearing for…

> Known in the Basin as Perry. His true name is Peiric, of the merchant House Castaigne, carried > from his homeland across the western ocean. The Tongue-Guild clipped it to the sound its own tongues > could hold, and "Perry" is what came back; he answers to it. A Tongue-Guild translator in the Aethelian Basin, twenty-seven years old, and one of the few in the crossroads who looks the way he does. He is six foot one, with light brown hair, blue eyes, and light skin, pale among the dark-eyed, brown-skinned peoples of the six civilizations. He is rare here, but not alone in it: the young western route lands a thin, shifting handful of his own coast's sailors at the port where it berths, and he is among the few who stayed. The blue eyes are his rarer mark, uncommon even among his own people and seldom seen in the Basin, though he is not the first to carry them here. He came young. His father was a merchant of Vaucresne, an island land across the western open ocean, who left his elder son home to keep their mother and the House name and took Perry across for his hands; the two of them sailed over together when Perry was fifteen or sixteen, on a trade route still young enough that…

Senior administrator of the Floodwatch Augmented Bureaucracy, the Ndjadi bureau that reads the river and times the dams. She is mid-career and holds the senior ra-tier post at the central cataract observatory, where she takes the crest gauge at dawn, certifies the season's flood-record the Flood-Yield Registry classifies from, and sets the order in which the upstream and downstream gates are let down. The Court of the Three Mouths seated her in the ra-tier over the House of Kagbende's objection, by a special-ceremony certification under its appellate authority; her training had not included the upper-college fire-vigil sequence the tier normally requires, and the Kagbende ratified under a protest they have never withdrawn. She has kept her record immaculate ever since, because the record is the only standing a contested appointment leaves a person. She is the one who decides when the water comes down. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. The season's certified flood-record, due to the Flood-Yield Registry before the levy-schedule publication. The Registry classifies the season ordinary or heavy from what she certifies, and the levy every…

Reservoir-engineer of the Wa-Kande building guild, the Ndjadi guild that raises stone reservoirs in soft delta mud and reads wet ground the way a scribe reads a ledger. She is mid-career and ka-tier, the grammatical tier the guild's women carry by default, and she has spent thirty years making the delta's water do what water does not want to do. The Wa-Ngo-Mkuu's ordnance establishment pulled her off the barays in the dry season and gave her two things to make work: the artificial niter beds that would let the delta grow its own fire, and the fire-devices the Irrah caravan had carried up the Southern Thread, which had to be kept dry and serviceable in a country that is never dry for long. She took the work as the proof of her standing. She is the one who is supposed to make the delta able to make powder. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. A serviceable powder supply, due to the ordnance establishment before the rains close the savanna and end the campaign window. The host can only move on the hard ground of the dry season; the window is the one stretch of the year the cavalry and the river-column can act together against the wet…

Calendar-keeper of the Alto Concordance's technical tier, retained by the Pacha-Urco Merchant House as a contract examiner at Ki-Mbuhari. He is approximately fifty-five at the time of the arc. He trained in the Alto observation network as a young man and has kept Alto dates for thirty years, the last twelve of them as the examiner the Pacha-Urco desk calls when a certificate is questioned and the house wants a finding it can stand behind. He is not a lineage head and not a delegate. He is the man who reads the cord. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. A single examiner's finding, commissioned by the Pacha-Urco Ki-Mbuhari desk and due before the Triple-Seal Court's sitting on the disputed cinchona contract. The retainer is half paid against delivery of the finding. The count that carries tension across all five scenes: five days to the hearing at arc start, the hearing itself by the close. What the house has bought is an authentication it can put before the Court: whether the intercalation certificate on the contract was issued on the date it claims. Built. Thirty years of Alto date-keeping and twelve of contract examination, producing a…

Double-Keepers Technical Secretary. Father's family: Alto Concordance lineage (adoptee). Mother's family: Upriver Confederation observation network, Sapa Mayu sub-cluster. Age approximately twenty-six at the Wawa-Kocha Session arc. She refused lineage affiliation at sixteen and took work with Pacha-Urco Runa-Yaq's Double-Keepers operation the following week. The name Upriver-Alto is her own coinage: the two factions joined in a single personal name, which is also a refusal of both. Owed, Built, Loved Three facts, established before they are threatened. Owed. Seven technical-reconciliation briefs commissioned by Runa-Yaq for the Wawa-Kocha Almanac Synchronization Session — one per disputed intercalation date in the current cool-season window. She owes her employer a complete, professionally defensible brief package attested and delivered before the session's technical docket opens. The count that carries tension across all five scenes: seven briefs outstanding at arc start, zero by session day. Built. Nine years of calendar-competence work since her refusal at sixteen, producing a specific capability that exists nowhere else in the Double-Keepers' operation: full working fluency…

Lead of the Imajīn Caravan Council, the Majlis al-Imajīn, at Tin-Aghīz. She is in her mid-fifties and matrilineal head of one of the three wealthiest Imajīn houses, and her name is a claim before it is an identity: the historical Zanūba ult Wahab attempted a confederation-to-empire that was crushed five or six generations ago, a defeat that scattered the original Tin-Aghīz drum and left the modern Council with its procedural temperament of consensus rather than command. She is the inheritor of that ancestor's commercial-political position and not, by the Namesake-is-not-Identity precedent the Irrah themselves observe, the ancestor returned. What she leads is a body whose very form is the scar of the project her dossier records her quietly rebuilding. She also holds a second seat far from the drum. At Halani-Tamu she is first chair of the Tin-Aghīz-Lam-Chen Corresponding Partnership, the consolidation-phase Basin trading house that the Khazadari rate-setters have begun to favor and the Havrana-Jenga incumbent refuses to credit at parity. In that seat she is one of two principals and the political weight on the Irrah-trade side of the book, not a matriarch whose word is the…

How to Read This Index This index lists every named individual person in the canon, with affiliation, a one-phrase role gloss, and pointers to the files where they are documented. It is a pointer apparatus under ADR-0024 D3: it asserts no new lore, and where a gloss disagrees with a home file, the home file wins. Persons appear once, under the civilization that holds their primary affiliation; Basin residents and operators of trans-civ institutions appear in the Basin section regardless of origin. The first path in each row's last column is the person's fullest treatment. Fourteen figures carry full dossiers (identity, institutional role, documented moral compromise) in the files; one Basin matriarch carries hers in . Maintenance discipline: a session that names a new person in canon adds a row here in the same PR, and every new row is grep-verified against the corpus before it lands. Standalone entities are created only under the ADR-0024 D2 earn-it rule; this index is the default home for a name. Stripped by quill-cutting — longitudinal incisions, peeled and rolled to dry into concave quills. Period note: Indigenous febrifuge use is pre-Columbian. Quinine-specific antimalarial application is post-1630 and anachronistic — use as generic fever-bark in-setting only. Coca Erythroxylum coca on warm valleys at 600-2,000 m. Leaves plucked 3-4x/year, sun-dried, chewed with lime ash (llipta) to release alkaloids against hunger, cold, and altitude hypoxia. State-tribute commodity. Precious Metals Highland polymetallic veins yield both silver and tin. Qollari is a secondary silver source (Irrah is primary). Tin feeds bronze production continent-wide. Anthrax: painless raised black eschar on forearms of felt-makers (cutaneous); pulmonary form from inhaled spore-dust…

The Caravan Physician's World A physician crossing Veydria in 1300 carries: a humoral or energetic framework for balance, a small travelling case of dried simples and distilled oils, a lancet, a cautery iron, a cupping horn, and bandages. What changes from region to region is not her craft but her eyes: the sign-clusters she recognises, the plants within a day's walk, and the ailments she has been taught to name. Design philosophy: Ecology is real; magic does not touch it. No germ theory, no microscope, no anaesthesia beyond opium/mandrake/hemp/henbane/alcohol, no surgical asepsis beyond wine/vinegar/honey. Childhood mortality is high because it was; chronic illness is common because it was; occupational disease is a moral fact of ordinary work. Four-Pillar Signature by Biome | Biome | Occupational Disease | Dramatic Fever | Chronic Wasting | Acute Trauma | |-------|---------------------|----------------|-----------------|--------------| | Oravan | Beri-beri in rice-fed sailors | Dengue "bone-break fever" | Yaws with late gummata | Ciguatera / reef envenomation | | Ndjadi | Schistosomiasis in paddy-labourers | Falciparum malaria | Guinea worm and river blindness | Hippo and…

Endemic Diseases | Local Name | Real-World Basis | Pattern | Key Treatment | |---|---|---|---| | q'ayma-sunqu | Acute mountain sickness | Any ascent >3000 paces, within hours | Coca leaf; chachacoma; muna | | p'uka-uya | Chronic mountain sickness (Monge's) | Long-term altitude dwellers | Palliative; bloodletting | | qhaqha-sinka | Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis | Yungas cloud-forest, year-round | No cure; supportive | | llakiy-sunqu | Chagas disease | Lower valleys, thatched houses | Palliative | | q'ita-nawi | Snow-blindness (UV keratitis) | High snowfields, spring-summer | Darkness; coca leaf on lids | | q'arachukchu | Shivering fevers (incl. bartonellosis) | Specific river valleys | Cinchona bark decoction | Soroche (q'ayma-sunqu, "the heart gone thin") strikes within hours above 3,000 paces: pressing headache, nausea, staggering gait. Chagas (llakiy-sunqu, "the sorrowful heart") from triatomine bug bite at night in thatched houses: Romana's sign (painless one-sided eyelid swelling) in childhood, then decades later an enlarged failing heart or grossly dilated…

The Rahab and Arwat rahab (Camelus dromedarius, dromedary pack camel; plural ruhub) and arwat (aristocratic riding breed). Names preserved verbatim — no alteration, no alternative proposed. Co-Evolutionary History The Irrah interior is hyper-arid and forbids any economy that cannot walk from oasis to oasis. The camel's physiology is the solution: oval red blood cells that circulate through dehydrated blood without clumping; selective brain-cooling via the carotid rete; tolerance of 30-40% body-weight water loss; the ability to drink 140 liters in a single session; a fat hump decoupled from water storage; nasal passages that recover exhaled moisture. Two functionally distinct lines from the same species: - rahab — stocky, broad-chested, carrying 150-250 kg at caravan pace for weeks between wells - arwat — light-skeletoned, deep-girthed, "greyhound-bellied," bred for speed and endurance under a single rider The two lines interbreed but the distinction is maintained by ownership lineage. One does not load a known arwat with trade goods; one does not ride a rahab to one's own wedding. Cultural Role The rahab moves desert commerce — salt, dates, textiles, glass, copper — along…

The Tokhan Horse Tokhan (Equus ferus caballus, Mongolian-type landrace). Back-harmony vowels o and a, aspirate kh, final nasal n typical of Kheshkai animate nouns. Plural: tokhat (collective suffix). Phonological note: Revised from original "Turghan" proposal (which contained forbidden /r/). Tokhan uses back-harmony /o/ + /a/ with no liquid consonants. Co-Evolutionary History The Kheshkai steppe swings from -40 C winter to +40 C summer, and the tokhan survives the full swing without shelter. Small (12-14 hands), stocky, thick-coated, hard-hooved, it paws through snow for winter grass, tolerates dehydration, and needs no shoeing. Selection for hardiness, foraging self-sufficiency, and endurance over speed — mediocre sprinter, extraordinary distance animal (60-80 miles/day when remounted). The composite recurve bow is usable from the saddle only because the tokhan is trainable to respond to knee pressure. Conversely, the bow made the tokhan the state's strategic asset. Each fighting man keeps 3-5 remounts on campaign, with preference for lactating mares (airag-analog dairy always at hand). The five-snout herding package (tokhan, cattle, sheep, goat, camel) is ecologically…

The Ndowu Buffalo Ndowu (Bubalus bubalis, water buffalo — swamp type). Prenasalized nd- onset, round back vowel o, open u final. Tone: low-high (ndo-wu). Plural: bandowu by class-prefix. Co-Evolutionary History The Ndjadi delta alternates deep-flood and cracked-clay drawdown, and the ndowu is the only bovid that thrives across the full cycle. Splayed hooves and flexible pasterns let it plow belly-deep mud where any cow would founder; sparse sweat glands make wallowing obligate. Centuries of selection for draft power over dairy yield produced a stocky swamp-type animal — smaller than upland river-type dairy buffalo, but tractable, surefooted in paddy, and long-lived. The ndowu's true agronomic gift is puddling: repeated passes under yoke churn flooded topsoil into a compacted plow-pan that seals the field against percolation, multiplying the value of every unit of irrigation water. Without the ndowu, the delta's wet-rice economy does not run at scale. A pair is the practical minimum for a tenant household; a team of four marks a landed family. Cultural Role The ndowu is the Ndjadi's working partner. The first ndowu yoked to turn a new paddy is garlanded and named; its horns are…

The Longa Cattle Longa (Bos taurus africanus, Sanga-type cattle of the Nguni lineage). The everyday stock-name takes plain pulmonic onsets; the lateral fricative and click that an earlier draft stacked into the word (hl-, nq-) belong to the Gyamsgra sacred forge-register and do not surface in common cattle-names. Noun-class plural: iziLonga (many cattle), uLonga (a single named beast). Co-Evolutionary History Descended from ancient Sanga hybridization of taurine and humped stocks. Characteristic cervico-thoracic hump (muscular, set forward), lyre-shaped horns, short glossy coat in hundreds of named patterns, and tolerance for tick-borne disease, heat, and drought no imported breed matches. Selection primarily for hardiness and coat-pattern beauty rather than raw milk yield or carcass weight — a herd is read as a living textile. The mixed woodland-savanna ecology rewards a browsing-tolerant grazer that moves between grass and scrub and survives seasonal drought on body reserves. Longa's central economic role: the interest-bearing capital of the lineage — they reproduce, move, and bind families through transfer. Cultural Role Longa are bride-wealth made animate. Marriage…

The Naluma Tree Naluma (Artocarpus altilis, breadfruit). Strict open-syllable CV-CV-CV, low back vowel a with rounded u break, liquid l. No consonant clusters, no closed syllables. A cultivar is a naluma; a grove or lineage-orchard is a nalumarai. Co-Evolutionary History Austronesian colonists carried breadfruit along every leg of the archipelagic expansion because a single adult tree can feed a household for fifty years on almost no labor once established. Clonal propagation from root suckers let founders move selected varieties onto new volcanic islands within a generation of landfall. Centuries of selection produced scores of cultivars distinguished by fruit season, flesh texture, seed-bearing vs. seedless, and trunk straightness and latex yield. The tree solved four problems at once: staple starch, canoe timber, caulking gum, and bast fiber for cordage and tapa-analog cloth. No other Oravan cultivar is simultaneously food, hull, and glue. The volcanic archipelago's thin young soils, rapid leaching, and frequent cyclones favored a deep-rooted, wind-flexible, fast-regenerating tree over cereal agriculture. Cultural Role Naluma groves are inherited matrilineally and mark the…

Design Principles 1. Keystone status chosen for ecological indispensability, not cultural prestige alone. The water buffalo is named for the Ndjadi because puddling wet-rice paddy is non-substitutable work. 2. One civilization gets a tree rather than an animal — Oravan's Austronesian maritime economy pivots on a single multi-use cultivar (breadfruit). 3. Irrah terminology preserved verbatim — rahab, ruhub, arwat, Qeturin. No new name proposed for that slot. 4. All names built from stated phoneme palettes rather than borrowed whole from real analog languages. 5. Tech ceiling 1200-1450 CE — no closed-shed dairy, no herdbooks, no artificial insemination, no shoed horses where analog went unshod. The Q'awa Camelid Q'awa (Lama glama, llama). Initial ejective uvular /q'/ — the Qollari signature sound. Back low vowel a, open CV final. Plural by reduplication: q'awaq'awa for a drove, q'awakuna with plural suffix. Co-Evolutionary History The Qollari altiplano is too high for the horse, too cold for the ox, and too steep for the wheeled cart. The q'awa resolves all three problems. Bred from the wild guanaco over four to five millennia, it evolved for cloud-forest and puna pastoralism at 3,500-4,500 m. Its soft two-toed pad puts negligible pressure on fragile ichu-grass soils; high-affinity hemoglobin lets it work above 5,000 m; low water demand matches a glacial-stream landscape. Selection pressure has been for pack endurance over speed: carries 25-30% of body weight 15-20 km/day across passes no mule could cross. Two parallel lineages bred alongside: a finer-boned fiber variant (alpaca analog) and a state-protected wild fiber giver (vicuna analog). Cultural Role The q'awa is the state's logistical spine and religious offering of first choice. Royal white herds maintained at the highest shrines for ritual sacrifice at accessions, imperial illness, and consecration of new…

Six Nations at One Quay — A Week in the Basin Day One — Dawn at the harbor. You come in on a galley overnight, riding the last of the land-breeze. The harbor takes shape before the sun does. First the bell of the northern merchants' fondaco tolling Prime, then — almost answering from the minaret opposite the Customs Mole — the muezzin-analog's long vowel flattening across the water. Overnight rain has steamed off limestone quays; the smell is tar, wet stone, and the sharper reek of garos — fermented fish sauce the dockside taverns ladle by the thimble. Rigging creaks; a caulker's mallet starts in on a hauled-out galley. Gulls (Larus spp.) quarrel over the night's fish-gutter. The mattanza boats come in heavy with bluefin (Thunnus thynnus) still-bleeding; women sort sardines (Sardina pilchardus), octopus (Octopus vulgaris), flathead mullet (Mugil cephalus). A European shag (Phalacrocorax aristotelis) dries its wings on a bollard. Midday at the Funduq of the Six Nations. The sun has whitened the walls until the eye refuses them. The central piazza is the polyglot bazaar: the dogana weigh-beam clanks; a money-changer's hammer rings on the touchstone. In one corner: bales of Ndjadi…

Three Non-Negotiable Rhythms Dawn-Midday-Night Triptych Every biome has a distinct triptych: - First sound (hornbill duet, fish-eagle yelp, muezzin-analog, rooster across a lagoon) - Peak-sun hazard (heat shimmer, reef glare, altitude UV, reg-gravel that eats shoe-leather) - Night-presence (wolves, leopards, karakurt, horned viper, corsair-galleys, malarial quays) Drop one and the biome reads generic. Waystations Are Contracts A waystation is always a three-part protocol (greeting, exchange, reciprocation) and the protocol is never purely symbolic — something tangible moves: - A tambo issues rations by quipu count - A dzimbahwe smith relights his bloomery at dawn; iron hoes are the unit of reciprocity - A rahab-caravan buys water-rights at the foggara outlet in rock-salt and silver - A Kheshkai yam inspects the paiza before rotating horses - A Basin caravanserai shares one courtyard wall between mosque, chapel, and shrine Seasonal Doubling Every region must read as two places. Designers should have two encounter-table skins per region and swap whole rows by season: - Dry-season Ndjadi (cracked mud, cattle-in-riverbed) vs flood-season Ndjadi (villages-as-islands) - Summer…

A Crossing of the Irrah — Seven Days on the Salt Road Before the muezzin-analog has finished the dawn call from the mud-brick minaret of the oasis, the Qeturin is already out past the last date palms (Phoenix dactylifera), crouched on the reg, letting a handful of gravel sift through his fingers into the wind. He is reading the grain-drift — the faint striae that every wind-reader knows. He tastes the air for the metallic dryness that foretells qibli, the harmattan-analog dust wind. Today: cold, clean, dry. A winter crossing. Good. In the staging-yard the ruhub groan as the packers heave salt-slabs — each roughly the size of a tombstone, two to a rahab — and lash them with plaited palm-rope. Breath steams. Saddle-leather creaks. An arwat, the lord's riding camel, stands apart, haughty, breathing plumes. The last stars fade over the foggara mouths — the tunnel-shafts pocking the gravel in a dotted line back toward the fossil aquifer — and the merchant counts his goatskins of water one final time. By mid-morning the oasis is a green smear behind. By noon it is nothing. The caravan crosses hammada — black gravel reg that "eats shoes" — the stones ticking and cracking underfoot as…

A Seven-Day Crossing of the Kheshkai The first light over the Kheshkai Steppe is not light but cold — a blue, breath-stinging cold that bites even in the Grass Moon of high summer. You wake inside the felt tent to the bitter sweetness of dung smoke — argal, dried sheep and horse pats layered into the central iron stove — and the sour-milk damp of the airag skin swinging from the door-frame, punched by every passer-by to keep it churning. The felt walls, bone-white with chalk on the outside, are warm as a lung within. You step out right-footed — never onto the threshold, which steppe custom calls the neck of the house, and which it is ruinous to tread. Horses are already nosing a seep where dark water wells through Carex sedge and pale rye-grass (Leymus), and the men water them in turns, whistling low; somewhere a Siberian marmot (Marmota sibirica) whistles its own sharp alarm from a burrow-mound crowned in silvery wormwood (Artemisia frigida). Before riding out, the three-bowl protocol: milk-tea, then aaruul (dried curd), then fermented mare's milk. You take it with the right hand, left hand cupping the right elbow. You flick three drops — sky, wind, earth — before you drink.…

Upriver Through the Ndjadi — A Seven-Day Passage Day One — Tidal delta. The dhow leaves saltwater on the ebb, its lateen sail slack in the dead air before dawn. Mist lifts from the brown water in sheets, and the first cry of a fish eagle (Haliaeetus vocifer) — that rising, yelping whistle, thrown back and forth between perches — announces the sun. The smell is wet silt, rotting mangrove, woodsmoke from fishing hamlets where women split catfish (Clarias gariepinus) on split-palm racks. Pied kingfishers hover; a Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus) slides from a mudbank like poured oil. Pirogues arrow out from the reed screens, offering smoked bonga and green oysters knotted on vine. By midday the papyrus (Cyperus papyrus) stands so tall the boat vanishes between green walls. Day Two — First market town. A river port built on a tell of older mud-brick. A caravanserai-on-stilts leans over the landing, its floor three cubits above flood-mark, smelling of sun-cracked palm thatch and drying indigo. Guest-right is simple: a handful of kola-analog nuts pressed into the traveller's palm at the gangplank, and a drum-line across the water announces new arrivals. Papyrus-makers work on the…

The Ngaru-Bon Crossing — A Foot-Caravan Traveller's Account Dawn on the second day out finds the caravan already moving. The plateau air is cold and mist hangs blue in the shadow-pools beneath the kopjes, those piled granite whalebacks. A pair of southern ground hornbills (Bucorvus leadbeateri) is booming in duet somewhere east, the deep ooomph... ooomph... oo-oo carrying four or five kilometres over the wet grass, answered by a Swainson's francolin (Pternistis swainsonii) going kek-kek-KEK from the kraal thorn. Wood-smoke, cattle-dung smoke, and the rust-blood smell of the smith's lean-to — the waystation's bloomery was relit an hour before sun, and the hammer-ring on anvil is already beating like a slow heart against stone. Iron hoes, axe-heads and spear-blanks lie cooling in sand; they are this waystation's second currency, after cattle-count. The waystation itself is a low dzimbahwe in the southern style: courses of hand-fitted granite laid without mortar. A cattle kraal at the centre; a grain-bin on stilts, mudded against weevils; the chief's hut set behind the inner wall; the smith's forge apart, as the old rite requires — Iron Age plateau smelting being treated as a kind…

Passage Through the Archipelago The first watch of a dry-monsoon morning breaks grey over the anchorage. Before the sun lifts above the palms, the lagoon is a sheet of pewter; you hear the village before you see it — the thump-thump-thump of an outrigger paddle on a hollow hull as a fisherman scares baitfish, the wet slap of a net cast, a rooster on the beach answering another across the channel, and from somewhere in the coconut grove (Cocos nucifera), the ratcheting call of hornbills and the argument of lorikeets in a flowering Syzygium. The wind carries damp palm thatch, wood smoke, the green-iron smell of mangrove mud where the aerial roots of Rhizophora apiculata bristle at low tide, and the sweet-resinous breath of Pandanus tectorius drying on a rack. A great fruit-bat (Pteropus vampyrus) straggles home across the sky, late from its feeding. In the shallows a water monitor (Varanus salvator) swims with only its nostrils showing. We weigh anchor on the ebb. The jurumudi at the steering oar calls the approach through the reef the old way — reading the swell-refraction, where the pattern of a wave bending around an unseen head is as legible as the height of the Pole Star. By…

A Llama Caravan on the Qhapaq Nan — Five Days Vertical Day One — Yungas. You set out before dawn from the cloud-forest tambo where the paved road begins its climb out of the valley. The air is warm and wet, black with the smell of wet moss. Fog drips from tree-fern fronds; Masdevallia orchids cling to the bark; a sparkling violetear hummingbird (Colibri coruscans) hums at a red cinchona (Cinchona pubescens) blossom. The arriero warns you to shake your sandals: in this band alone the pit viper (Bothrops atrox) hunts among the leaf-litter. Thirty llamas (Lama glama), their packs balanced in pairs, grumble and hum their low nasal complaints as they step onto the stone-cut steps. Somewhere below, a waterfall roars white through the tree-line. Day Two — Kichwa. By dawn we have climbed above the cloud. The world is suddenly hard blue. Thin sun burns the back of the neck even as breath steams. Terraces stepped like the ribs of a giant — Andean potatoes of thirty colours, quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa) beginning to redden at the tassel. Women in alpaca-wool (Vicugna pacos) skirts dyed cochineal-red pause to watch us pass. At the tambo the quipucamayuq records on coloured cords our number,…

A grounded reference for a late-medieval, pre-gunpowder setting (~1200-1450 CE tech ceiling). No fantasy biota, no magic ecosystems. All species are real; all processes and numbers are drawn from historical metallurgy, archaeobotany, and economic history. Directory Map Design Rails 1. No fantasy biota. Every species is real, identified by binomial nomenclature. Vernacular names conform to each culture's phoneme palette, validated against the palettes (see Name Resolution below). 2. Tech ceiling: 1200-1450 CE. Where a real-world fact is anachronistic (e.g., Dutch clove monopoly, European quinine extraction), the pre-1450 analog is substituted. Anachronisms are flagged explicitly. 3. Ecology drives trade. Resource chains exist because of ecological constraints, not arbitrary worldbuilding decisions. The three master constraints: - Irrah's timber absence forces permanent dependence on Ngaru-Bon iron (no wood = no charcoal = no smelting) - The tsetse barrier gives Ngaru-Bon metallurgical apex with no cavalry - Point-source biota (clove on 5 islands, nutmeg on 1 archipelago, vicuna above 3,800 m) create fragile monopoly rents 4. Real analogs cited. Every claim traces to a historical…

The Three Master Constraints Three ecological constraints do most of the work in driving continental trade: 1. Irrah's timber absence is the continent's single largest trade driver. No wood means no charcoal means no primary iron, forcing the desert into permanent dependence on Ngaru-Bon bloomeries and making the iron-north/salt-south axis of trans-desert caravan trade structurally inevitable. This is the Saharan reality, not a worldbuilding flourish. 2. The tsetse barrier silently shapes Ngaru-Bon's military and logistical profile. A metallurgical apex with no cavalry and severe pack-transport limits exports gold and iron but cannot project force, pushing its trade outward through the Swahili-coast analog rather than overland. 3. Point-source biota — clove on five islands, nutmeg on one archipelago, vicuna above 3,800 m, frankincense on specific fog-fed escarpments — create monopoly rents that fund entire civilizations. These monopolies are inherently fragile; a single bad volcanic year in Oravan or a failed monsoon on Dhofar would reshape continental politics. Secondary Constraints Llama load ceilings (25-30 kg) mean Qollari's metallurgical and textile wealth moves through…

What the Basin Produces The Basin produces almost no commodity and governs the movement of nearly all of them. Its economy is institutional arbitrage, the sale of services that turn a stateless delta into the continent's single clearing house, and enumerates five. The warehouse-keeper guilds hold goods through their seasons, storing grain eighteen months, cotton three years, and spices indefinitely, and they are paid in the commodity stored, accumulating diversified portfolios without ever trading. The khazadari money-changer guild sets the daily cross-rates between salt-weight, iron-weight, cotton-weight, grain-measure, and silver-by-weight. The triple-seal panels arbitrate contracts. The tithe-operators sell insurance. The investor dynasties structure partnerships. What the Basin sells is not a thing but a guarantee: that a good can be aged and released against monsoon timing, that an oath will be enforced, that a loss at sea or in the desert will be made good. The five guilds hold mixed, multi-civ membership, which is the mechanism that keeps the clearing house neutral, because any visible bias would trigger defection by the disadvantaged civilization. What the Basin Cannot…

What Irrah Produces Irrah holds the continent's rock-salt monopoly, and the monopoly is the load-bearing fact of its economy. The sabkha slabs cut from its salt-flats, the Taghaza and Taoudenni analog of Veydria, are the most universally accepted inland commodity money on the continent, and the salt itself is the northern anchor of the continental spine against Ndjadi grain. Around the salt, the drylands yield natron, dates, lode silver from Jabali-analog deposits, impact-silica glass, and medicinal gums from the Sahel-margin thorn-savanna. A second export cluster sits on the southeastern coast: frankincense and myrrh from a Dhofar-analog shore, the resin trade that gives Irrah a maritime outlet entirely independent of the Basin. Irrah also breeds the camel stock the desert trade runs on, rahab pack-animals and arwat riding-camels, and it sells the crossing itself. The caravan is the product as much as the cargo, and Qalībin escort and certification are billed services in their own right. What Irrah Cannot Make Irrah has no timber, and timber is the dependency that organizes its weaknesses. Without wood there is no charcoal, and without charcoal there is no sustained bloomery,…

What Kheshkai Produces Kheshkai sells two things the continent cannot do without and a third that is the trade itself. The first is warhorses and remounts, the only cavalry-grade source at scale on the continent, an export that confers military capability no settled neighbor can manufacture. The second is tin, drawn from a Zeravshan-analog source so geologically rare that two or three nodes supply the whole continent, and tin is half of bronze. Because Ngaru-Bon copper cannot become bronze without it, Kheshkai tin underwrites the steppe's political autonomy as surely as its horses underwrite its raids. Around these the steppe exports felt and wool, furs, amber, hides and sinew, and livestock on the hoof. The third product is protection: the rent a caravan pays for safe passage, the steppe selling the absence of its own predation. Horse, tin, and protection are the levers, and each one binds a settled civilization that would rather not need the steppe at all. What Kheshkai Cannot Make The steppe cannot grow grain. Rainfall below three hundred millimeters cannot support plow agriculture at the population scales a nomad confederation reaches, and herds give dairy and meat but no…

What Ndjadi Produces Ndjadi is the breadbasket of Veydria, and that single fact organizes everything else about its economy. The floodplain produces a continental staple surplus in wheat, barley, millet, and rice, the only bulk-carbohydrate output on the continent large enough to feed populations that cannot feed themselves. The surplus exists because the river floods on a predictable cycle and deposits new alluvium each season, a renewable fertility that needs no fallow and no manure. Around the grain sits a second tier of floodplain products: cotton cloth and raw cotton from the irrigated margins, a papyrus-analog for the scribal trade, dried river-fish, indigo, flax and linen, natron, and ceramics fired from delta clay. Ndjadi also exports copper drawn from upstream-margin deposits on the Sinai-analog edge of its territory, and that copper is the primary feed for the Ngaru-Bon bronze trade along the Copper-for-Steel Road. None of these are point-source monopolies in the way Oravan obsidian or Irrah salt are. Ndjadi's leverage is bulk and reliability: it sells the one commodity four other civilizations must buy or starve. What Ndjadi Cannot Make The delta is rich in soil and…

What Ngaru-Bon Produces Ngaru-Bon is the metallurgical apex of the continent. Its bloomeries produce iron bars of a quality no other civilization can match, its crucibles produce steel ingots that exist nowhere else at scale, and its smiths turn out finished work that the whole continent buys: chainmail, curved blades, architectural supports. The plateau also exports copper from Katanga-analog deposits, ivory, and gold, though gold occupies a category of its own. What makes Ngaru-Bon's position singular is not the volume of its metal but the absence of competitors. Iron and steel are existential to most settled civilizations and critical to all of them, and the plateau is the source. Where Ndjadi sells a bulk commodity that four neighbors need to eat, Ngaru-Bon sells a finished good that the same neighbors need to farm, fight, and build, and it sells it without any second supplier to discipline its terms. What Ngaru-Bon Cannot Make The plateau cannot keep a horse. The tsetse belt that surrounds its approach corridors causes nagana in any draft or cavalry animal that tries to cross, which means the continent's greatest forge has no force-projection capability whatsoever. records…

What Oravan Produces Oravan trades in things that grow nowhere else. The volcanic archipelago holds two point-source monopolies: obsidian, the sharpest cutting edge available to civilizations without universal iron access, drawn from five islands, and the deep-sea spices, clove and nutmeg and mace, endemic to a handful of islands and a single archipelago cluster. To these the islands add pumice, coral-stone blocks for architecture, cured fish, teak and belian hardwoods, pearl, tortoiseshell, and sandalwood. The spice and obsidian trades are what give Oravan its weight on the continent, because both are genuinely irreplaceable: there is no second source of clove, and obsidian's precision edge is needed even by Ngaru-Bon, whose iron is too soft for the finest work. Oravan's wealth is the wealth of a monopoly holder. It is also the wealth of a monopoly holder whose entire stock can be destroyed by a single bad season. What Oravan Cannot Make Oravan has no iron and no bog ore. The andesitic and basaltic volcanics of the archipelago are ore-poor, so every nail, every fish-hook, and every ship-anchor is imported, and names iron as the irreplaceable dependency. The dependency is…

What Qollari Produces Qollari sells altitude. Its highland exports are high in value and low in bulk: medicinal bark, the cinchona-analog fever-bark that no lowland can grow, rare dyestuffs of the cochineal kind, and the fine camelid fiber, vicuna-analog above 3,800 meters, that constitutes a wool monopoly the lowlands cannot touch. To these the cloud-states add structural timber from the wetter slopes, silver, gold, processed tin-bronze worked from imported Kheshkai tin, and freeze-dried chuno that keeps for years. The economy is built around goods whose worth per kilogram is high enough to justify carriage by an animal that refuses to be overloaded. Qollari does not compete in bulk staples; it competes in the irreplaceable and the rare, the fever-bark a dying merchant will pay anything for, the dye a priestess-queen's robe requires, the fiber that no flock below the snow-line can produce. What Qollari Cannot Make Qollari cannot feed itself. The terraces raise tubers and a quinoa-analog, but they cannot produce bulk carbohydrates at altitude in the quantities a population needs, and names grain as the irreplaceable dependency. The Continental Spine Revisited The whole Veydrian order bends around two axes that ecology made inevitable. The first is Grain against Salt. Ndjadi alluvium floods and refertilizes itself each season and produces the only bulk-carbohydrate surplus on the continent, while it raises neither salt, nor metal, nor stone, nor timber. Irrah sabkha yields the only continental rock-salt and stands on a desert with no tree from which to draw charcoal. Four civilizations cannot feed themselves without Ndjadi grain, and the same four and their herds cannot survive without Irrah salt. Neither the breadbasket nor the salt-pan can ever supply what the other holds, and so the two ends of the continent are locked into a dependence that no innovation will dissolve. The second axis is metallurgical: bronze requires Kheshkai tin from two or three rare nodes joined to Ngaru-Bon copper, and iron and steel come from the Ngaru-Bon plateau alone. The spine is not a trade pattern that happened to form. It is the shape the continent must take given where the salt, the grain, the tin, and the ore actually lie, and every other flow bends around it. The Complementary-Asymmetry Principle The Veydrian economy rests on a single structural fact: no civilization can supply itself, and every civilization holds at least one thing that no other civilization can substitute. The six settled powers and the Aethelian Basin do not trade because trade is profitable at the margin. They trade because the alternative is collapse. Ndjadi grows grain on an alluvium that yields no metal, no salt, no stone, and no timber. Irrah holds the only continental rock-salt monopoly while owning not a single tree from which to make the charcoal its forges would require. Ngaru-Bon stands at the metallurgical apex of the continent and cannot keep a horse alive past the tsetse belt that walls its approaches. The dependencies are not soft preferences; they are listed in as irreplaceable, civilization by civilization, and each one binds its holder to a named supplier whose leverage is structural rather than negotiable. Value in this system is created at borders, not at sources. Institutional Substrate Kheshkai is "Non-institutional" in the typology of magic/06, the only Veydrian civ at this position on the Schism Axis. There are no colleges, no guilds, no lineages in the formal sense; master-shamans take one to three apprentices over a five-to-ten-year horseback apprenticeship; identification is by the hearing-gift, a phonological capacity detectable in childhood. Orthodoxy does not survive a master's death unmediated. Every shaman is a potential single point of failure, and every harmonic pattern is one bad transmission from extinction. Reform is structurally unproducible — there is no institution to reform, and no institution from which to reform. The factions named below sit on this absence rather than on an institutional structure; they are arrangements of personal authority, marriage politics, and apprentice-placement networks rather than guild bodies. The consequence is fragility. A faction whose strength depends on a single master's continuing competence is one bad winter from collapse; a faction whose authority is the marriage-network of a single qaghan loses coherence at his death. Institutional Substrate Ndjadi is "Institutionalized with reform" in the typology of magic/06, and its position on the Schism Axis is the Open and active one — the Vernacular-Habal Movement is named, organized, currently publishing, and recognized as a faction even by the elder colleges that condemn it. The literate scribal infrastructure of the imperial colleges, the habal copy-service traditions in the delta trading ports, and the river-court tribunal apparatus all share a single institutional skeleton across hundreds of leagues of Ngandim floodplain. That skeleton has carried three readings of the tier-prefix system — conservative, progressive, and naturalist — for several generations without fracturing. Reform pressure is absorbed into tribunal procedure rather than expelled from it; what would be schism in a non-literate tradition is, in Ndjadi, a documented disagreement that competing parties cite when it suits them. The factions named below all sit on this absorbing structure. They do not produce it; they exploit it. Institutional Substrate Ngaru-Bon is "Monolithic" in the typology of magic/06, the only Veydrian civ at this position on the Schism Axis. A single guild — the ancestor-smith federation of click-and-lateral-trained lineages — controls every household that addresses infants in Gyamsgra click-speech, every forge that produces consecrated metal, every shrine that certifies the genealogical binding of consecrated weapons to their lineages. Reform from outside is structurally impossible: the click-and-lateral phonology must be acquired in infancy, the developmental window closes at five to seven years, and no external critic can acquire the register to critique it from inside. Reform from inside is rare and expensive: an internal critic who departs the guild loses the phonology's social infrastructure, and the guild has within living memory used violence twice to enforce the consequence. The factions named below all sit on this monolith. They are not external rivals; they are internal fault lines within a single institution that has historically presented unity to outsiders. Relationship Summary The Ngaru-Bon plateau and the Qollari highlands share a single documented direct coupling: a doctrinal correspondence between the Monastery-Citadel Concordat and the Alto Concordance on ritual calendar-keeping. No Ngaru-Bon gold-work reaches Qollari markets through any documented channel; no Qollari cinchona reaches Ngaru-Bon Dzong-circuits through any documented route. The two civs' commercial orbits are entirely separate, and their doctrinal intersection is limited to equinoctial observance commentary and calendrical-cosmological edge-case arbitration. Relationship Summary The Oravan archipelago and the Irrah drylands maintain two documented channels of cross-civ contact, neither of which constitutes a political or commercial alliance. The two civs do not share a border, a military objective, a theological tradition, or a linguistic substrate. Their exchange is routed through Basin port zones and through Tongue-Guild translation; the channels that exist are negative-space alignments — they are defined by what they oppose rather than by what they affirm. Relationship Summary The Oravan archipelago and the Ndjadi river delta share no border, no direct commodity exchange route, and no linguistic substrate. The two civs are separated by the Aethelian Basin's full maritime width, by the absence of any traditional overland corridor, and by the incompatibility of their institutional forms — Oravan's matrilineal harbor guilds and Ndjadi's river-lord house system have no shared procedural language, no overlapping certification regime, and no historical treaty relationship. What exists instead is a single narrow mediated channel: the Oravan Harbor Covenant and the Ndjadi Court of the Three Mouths do not deal with each other directly, but both deal with the same three Ki-Mbuhari-based intermediaries, and the intermediaries' rate coordination produces a shadow alignment that neither civ acknowledges and neither can control. The sparse-matrix entry for this civ pair is therefore unusually narrow. The relationship exists almost entirely in the negative space of triangulated commercial dependence, and the few positive connections are procedural handoffs rather than political alignments. Relationship Summary The Oravan archipelago and the Qollari plateau share no documented direct political coupling, no commercial exchange route, and no institutional contact of any kind. The two civs are separated by the Aethelian Basin's full width, by the incompatibility of their transport modes — Oravan's maritime spice routes and Qollari's overland cinchona caravans have no physical intersection — and by the complete absence of any traditional correspondence between their respective institutional ecologies. What exists instead is a documented structural fact: both civs export through Basin intermediaries, both denominate their export volumes in Khazadari terms at Basin ports, and both rely on the Triple-Seal Arbitration Court for contract enforcement. These are structural residues, not bilateral ties. The absence of direct coupling is not an oversight; it is the defining characteristic of the Oravan-Qollari relationship. Relationship Summary The Qollari-Basin relationship is the continent's most calendrically complex commercial nexus. Qollari produces cinchona bark — the primary high-altitude pharmacological export — and the Basin's four port zones consume, trans-ship, and reinsure virtually the entire Qollari export volume. No other civ depends on the Basin so completely for market access, and no other civ imposes on the Basin so thoroughly the problem of how to date contracts that cross a disputed intercalation window. The relationship is not civ-to-place in the Oravan sense; the Qollari highlands are a fixed geographical fact, and the Basin's institutional ecology has adapted to that fact by developing calendar-arbitration services that exist nowhere else in continental commerce. Commercial Layer The Pacha-Urco Merchant House (Pacha-Urco Yaqucha-Tamu, factions/02transciv/basinmerchantdynasties.md) is the load-bearing institutional fact of the Qollari-Basin commercial relationship. Relationship Summary The Qollari-Ndjadi relationship is the thinnest documented cross-civ connection in the Veydrian corpus. The two civs share no border, no direct commodity exchange, no linguistic substrate, and no historical conflict. Their geographical separation — the Qollari high-altitude cliff-roads and the Ndjadi Ngandim floodplain are separated by the Aethelian Basin and several thousand leagues of intervening territory — precludes the kind of overland caravan commerce that binds Kheshkai to Irrah or Oravan to the Basin. What exists instead is a pamphlet correspondence: two working-class literacy movements on opposite sides of the continent have discovered that they share a structural grievance, and they circulate each other's arguments through Tongue-Guild translation without ever meeting. Fracture Substrate The Ngaru-Bon calendar is held not in months or years but in the names of the smiths who hold tier-credentials. The ancestor-smith tiers — Nokul (initiate), Amori (master), Lapam (ancestor) — are temporal coordinates. A tier promotion closes one generation and opens another; the date is inscribed in the forge-temple's click-register ledger, the only written calendar the Ngaru-Bon maintain. The Outside-Forge Network uses the same tier names but refuses the Inner Council's promotion authority. The Network's "Amori Phyi-Ma" may be the same mortal who held the name twenty years ago, or a successor who inherited the name, or a fiction the Network maintains for contractual continuity. Neither the Inner Council nor outsiders can determine which without disrupting the institutional position. The ambiguity is the point. The fracture is whether a tier-name without verifiable mortal continuity is valid temporal accounting or institutional forgery. The Network holds that the name carries the credential and that credential continuity is what matters for contract clearance. The Council holds that a name without verifiable mortal continuity is a void claim to ancestor-tier…

Fracture Substrate The Kheshkai political economy is built on Varkosh oaths underwritten by herd wealth. Every pasture-rotation assignment, marriage-alliance commitment, and protection-rent obligation assumes that the animals producing the wool, the felt, the horse-geldings, and the meat will survive the winter. The Oral-Memory Council's doctrine acknowledges one exception: a dzud — the summer-drought-plus-deep-snow winter that kills herds in place — voids the oaths that the herds underwrite. "It can only be voided by a subsequent Council ruling or by ecological force-majeure — a dzud that kills the herds underwriting the oath." The doctrine is clear for a single oath. It is silent for a thousand. A dzud that arrives before the autumn slaughter is complete does not merely kill animals. It destroys the material substrate of the confederation's political economy before the Oral-Memory Council's autumn hearing can ratify emergency rotation assignments or adjust marriage-alliance reciprocities. The slaughter-and-dry is the load-bearing season: felt-making requires warm water, caravan departures carry Council-certified goods, and the winter tebenevka assumes stored meat and culled…

Fracture Substrate The Irrah calendar's distributed architecture — many parallel Azmara? star-readings, each valid through its own isnad-chain — assumes that astronomical observation is the authoritative substrate for commercial time. The Unnamed-Water School's gauge-data methodology challenges this substrate at its root: if hydrological measurement can produce drought classifications without star-readings, then the calendar's agricultural and commercial decisions can be made without isnad-chain certification. The Qeturin sub-register — the wind-readers whose pharyngeal register determines caravan route-timing — is the directly threatened guild. If the Water-Allocation Court adopts gauge-data as sole authority, the Qeturin become secular meteorologists. Their oaths lose Varkosh-class binding weight. Their route-timing declarations become engineering opinions. The isnad-chain architecture does not collapse; it is bypassed. The Dormant State The fracture is partially engaged but not yet decisive. The Water-Allocation Court has adopted gauge-data methodology for drought classification in the northern district. The Northern Qalībin has responded by commissioning independent…

Fracture Substrate Tegu Bokh's doctrine is simple: ONE sky = ONE correct liturgy. This would collapse the polyvocal seasonal-oath practice — in which different clans, different master-shamans, and different herder-mothers may observe slightly different festival timings based on local grass conditions — into a fixed calendar of correct liturgical moments. It would be the first written-and-codified Kheshkai calendar. The Oral-Memory Council's entire authority rests on polyvocality. The Council does not consult archives when two speakers disagree on what was ruled in a given year. It hears both recitations and rules which version carries weight. A written calendar would make this oral archive obsolete. The Council would transform from a living body of witnesses into a custodian of documents. Kheshkai time would become legible to Basin merchants without Tongue-Guild translation overhead. The gate — access to the oral corpus — would cease to exist. The Dormant State The Heresy is monitored but not suppressed. The Bokh Heresy Watchers distribute early-warning intelligence about bad-grass conditions and track apprentice-curious populations for Heresy-sympathetic tendencies. The…

Fracture Substrate The Basin's composite reckoning depends on translation. Six civilizations bring six calendars to four ports, and no contract can reference more than one calendar without a Tongue-Guild calendar-translator rendering the dates legible across registers. The Guild's basin-port seat at Ki-Mbuhari maintains parallel correspondence in six languages and employs apprentices who spend their first two cycles in Tabbaq ult Halu's procedural-instruction rotation before advancing to translation work. The Guild's standing threat — that it could teach the Filer's Hand cadence to a non-Basin coalition — is the load-bearing pressure on the water-court institutions. The non-exercise is itself the institutional fact that shapes every negotiation between the Guild, the water-courts, and the merchant dynasties. Fracture Substrate The Oravan calendar is performed, not computed. Each priestess-queen declares the monsoon-window opening from her own polity's cyclone-shoulder observation, and no central council resolves inter-island disputes. Workshop pluralism — three to seven senior workshops per polity, each with divergent phonetic and observational traditions — means that two priestess-queens on different islands may observe the same cyclone shoulder two weeks apart and produce incompatible calendars. Both observations are theologically valid. Both priestess-queens are in their dual-aspect register. The calendars they declare are each valid for their own polity and commercially hazardous for the other's convoys. Catalog Substrate A dormant faction is one whose institutional preconditions exist, whose grievances are already articulable, and whose membership pool is already identifiable, but whose activation-trigger has not yet fired. Dormants are not merely hypothetical organizations: they are political-organizational potentials held below the coalescence threshold by the structural interests of every faction that would otherwise oppose them, by the absence of the specific trigger their organizing principle requires, or by both at once. A suppressed faction has identifiable enemies acting against it; a dormant faction is held below the coalescence threshold without active suppression, because the coalescence has not yet been provoked. This catalog records 20 dormants distributed across the six civilizations and one trans-civ dormant — the first non-civ-specific dormant in the corpus. The Core Question Every ongoing Veydrian dispute is in fact a contest among at least five positions, not two. Behind every "reformer" stands an apostate who was a reformer in the previous generation and now accepts patronage from the establishment; behind every "conservative" there are moderates who privately agree with the reforms but cannot afford to be seen agreeing; and around both there are opportunists who service whichever side currently pays better — and who provide the information flows that make the conflict legible to outsiders. The factions layer names the organizations, leaders, funding bases, and tactical repertoires that make these contests politically concrete. Where and give the theological spine of the disputes, and gives the institutional-type substrate, the factions layer gives the named actors — the specific lineages, councils, pamphlet networks, and merchant dynasties on either side of each contest. Why Binary Opposition Is Insufficient The Qalībin Naturalist Schism is not "hydrologists vs. traditionalists." Institutional Substrate The Irrah scrublands produce frankincense (luban-harra, the resin of Boswellia sacra) from limestone-slope groves in the Dhofar-analog highland zone, salt from the sabkha flat-mine complexes at the scrubland's lower margins, and silver from mid-slope outcrop veins. The continent's iron-timber deficit — Irrah lacks both bloomery-grade iron and sufficient charcoal hardwood for sustained metallurgy — makes it critically dependent on Ngaru-Bon iron imports and produces the continent's defining structural bottleneck: the civilization with the highest trade-volume frankincense and the most sophisticated water-management systems cannot produce its own metal tools without external supply. The frankincense economy runs across two parallel institutional governance tracks. The first track — Boswellia tree access and resin-harvest certification — is governed by the Ḥārrā Tappers' League, whose tapper-lineage network holds hereditary grove-access rights over the limestone-slope production zones. The Tappers' League is categorically distinct from the existing Frankincense Syndics (Ṣāliqūn al-Lubān) documented in factions/01civfactions/irrah.md: the Syndics are…

Institutional Substrate The Kheshkai steppe produces two primary trade goods: compressed felt from the undercoat of winter-grazed sheep and goats, and horses bred from semi-feral herd lines managed through multi-generation stud-book oral records maintained by herder-mother lineages. Felt is a bulk commodity; horses are a premium strategic resource whose price is set by Basin buyers and Aethelian military procurement. Together they constitute the Kheshkai's continental commercial footprint, denominated in Khazadari rate-schedule terms by the Basin-facing commercial factors the Khazadari guild trains. The two goods require institutionally distinct governance. Felt quality depends on seasonal grazing management, fiber-blend technique, and compression protocols — knowledge held by the Felt-Fold Council's senior elders, who witness and ratify quality-grade oaths in Varkosh back-vowel harmony before Basin buyers accept shipment. Horse quality depends on genealogical integrity: a horse whose lineage is certified by the Stud-Registry Herder-Mothers commands three to five times the price of an unregistered horse, and the certification is backed by a Varkosh breeding-oath whose social…

Institutional Substrate The Ndjadi floodplains produce sorghum, millet, and wet-season rice under a flood-pulse agricultural cycle whose timing and yield are determined by the Ngandim river system's seasonal surge. Grain surplus is the Ndjadi's primary export commodity and the foundation of the Ki-Mbuhari Basin trading hub's provisioning economy: every overland caravan that winters in the Basin depends on Ndjadi grain at Khazadari-denominated levy rates. The flood-grain economy runs across two institutional tiers. The first tier — flood-allocation and levy assessment — sits upstream with the Flood-Yield Registry, the bureaucratic institution that monitors gauge-readings, assigns field-water allocations across competing upstream and downstream polities, and sets the seasonal levy schedule that determines how much of each harvest the state takes in tribute before surplus reaches the market. The second tier — commercial assembly and Basin export — sits at the Ki-Mbuhari confluence, where the Basin-Grain Syndicate aggregates regional surpluses from independent factor-houses, denominates export contracts in Khazadari rate-schedule terms, and negotiates the prefix-notarized shipping…

Institutional Substrate Ngaru-Bon produces placer gold from river-terrace alluvial deposits, bloomery iron smelted using miombo and mopane hardwood charcoal during the dry-cool smelting season, and copper from hillside surface outcroppings. Gold is the continental luxury currency; bloomery iron is the continent's critical strategic input for tools, weapons, and agricultural implements; charcoal-grade hardwood is the bottleneck fuel that determines whether the continent's metallurgy operates at capacity or at shortage. All three commodities are exported through the Halani-Tamu Basin interchange via the Tin-Aghīz-Lam-Chen dynasty's cross-continental trading operations. The metallurgy economy runs across two institutional tiers, both of which operate in direct tension with the Inner Council of Ancestor-Smiths (Gyalpo Pho-lha) — the prestige governance institution of Ngaru-Bon's metallurgical culture documented in factions/01civfactions/ngarubon.md. The first tier — export-grade metal production and Basin-bound metal trade — is governed by the Outside-Forge Network (Phyi-yi Gar-Ba), the uncertified-steel and export-arbitrage faction whose relationship to the Ancestor-Smith Guild is…

Institutional Substrate Oravan produces cloves and nutmeg from five volcanic island concentrations in the southern archipelago — the continent's only source of both spices — plus volcanic obsidian, teak and belian timber for deep-sea vessel construction, and sea-salt from the evaporation pools maintained across the larger volcanic island platforms. Cloves and nutmeg are the luxury commodities; obsidian and ship timber are the strategic materials; sea-salt is the secondary production that Oravan's island geography enables at low marginal cost and that sustains the archipelago's own preservation economy. The spice economy runs across two institutional tiers. The first tier — island-access certification and spice-grade authentication — is governed by the Harbor-Spice Consortium, whose certification authority over the five volcanic island production zones gives it the ability to set which cove-masters may sell spice in certified-grade Basin contracts. The second tier — inter-island and Basin-bound maritime transport — is governed by the Spice-Route Convoy Guild, whose deep-sea convoy operations connect the volcanic island production zones to the Tavakh-Qarat Basin interchange and…

Institutional Substrate The Qollari highlands between 1,500 and 2,700 meters produce cinchona bark (Qillqa-panqa in the highland register), harvested by quill-cutting — a seasonal technique that strips bark in spiral cuts without killing the host tree. The bark's pharmacological properties (fever suppression, pulse regulation) make it the Qollari's principal export to Aethelian and Basin markets; its advance-purchase contracts are the primary mechanism by which Qollari calendar-dates enter Basin commercial circulation. The bark economy runs across two institutional tiers. The first tier — extraction and certification — sits at altitude: the Cinchona Sodality controls grove-access rights, grades the seasonal yield, and issues the certification stamps that Basin buyers require for contract validity. The second tier — processing and bundle-preparation — sits at mid-altitude terrace stations: the Terrace Compounders receive bulk-certified bark, prepare it for long-haul transport, and negotiate loading contracts with Imajīn caravans and Chaski-Run courier-arbitrators. The two tiers are structurally complementary but politically rival. Each holds that the other captures rent it does…

Purpose The ecology layer () documents what each civilization produces, harvests, and exports: cinchona bark in the Qollari highlands, flood-grain surplus across the Ndjadi floodplains, felt and horses on the Kheshkai steppe, gold and metallurgy from Ngaru-Bon, sea-spice from the Oravan volcanic archipelago, and frankincense alongside water-rights in the Irrah scrublands. The ecology layer is substrate — it describes the physical and seasonal facts of resource production without naming the institutions that govern, tax, certify, monopolize, or dispute those resources. This directory closes that gap. Every primary resource identified in now has at least two named governance factions: one representing the extraction or first-production interest, one representing the processing, certification, or secondary-market interest. The central distinction this layer enforces: Resources without governance are substrate; resources with governance are leverage. The ecology layer tells you what exists. This layer tells you who holds the institutional claim over it, who challenges that claim, and what the claim is worth in a continental market. The layer instantiates Design Rail 9 of the…

Institutional Substrate The Aethelian Basin's four major commercial ports — Tavakh-Qarat at the eastern Irrah-Ndjadi interface, Halani-Tamu at the upriver-cataract gate, Ki-Mbuhari at the central confluence, Dzong-Tamu at the highland-descent shelf — are each currently dominated by a single Basin merchant dynasty whose continental commercial reach exceeds any civ-internal noble lineage's. The four houses are not allied; they compete for one another's port volume on margin and only occasionally share a common interest sufficient to warrant correspondence. Each is, by every test that matters, a continental-scale commercial actor — but each is also contingent. The Basin economy maintains four dynasty-seats, not four hereditary kingdoms. When the fracture-pressure that the late-institutionalization phase invariably produces becomes terminal at any port, a junior house at that port replaces the incumbent within roughly half a generation. This has happened twice within living memory at Halani-Tamu and once at Tavakh-Qarat; both Ki-Mbuhari and Dzong-Tamu have not yet experienced it but have entered the early-fracture phase the historical pattern predicts. In colloquial Basin commerce…

Institutional Substrate The Khazadari guild — formally the Northern Khazadari Money-Changer Guild, colloquially "the Khazadari" without modifier when context permits — is the continental clearing-house for cross-civ commercial credit. Its rate-setting determines the terms on which Oravan wave-tithe insurance, Ndjadi prefix-notarized contracts, Qollari calendrical-cinchona instruments, Kheshkai pastoral-product underwriting, Ngaru-Bon metallurgical-export receipts, and Irrah caravan-tithe pools all clear at the Aethelian Basin. There is no Basin economic instrument of consequence whose pricing does not pass, at some stage, through the Khazadari rate-schedule. The guild is not a state. It holds no charter, has no royal patron, and is not formally recognized by any civ's legal apparatus. It operates as a hereditary professional association of twenty-two senior changer families, all resident in Ki-Mbuhari and the Halani-Tamu satellite seat, organized into the Rate-Setters' Inner Circle as the apex body. Below the Inner Circle sit the Junior Clerks' Association, the formally-organized apprentice-stratum body whose hereditary-apprenticeship grievances against the Inner Circle have…

Institutional Substrate The Three-Tithe Pool — Taxatikh Tripartite in the Triple-Seal-court formal register, the Pool in colloquial Basin commerce — is a cross-collateralized continental insurance arrangement that pools three civ-internal tithes into a single actuarial fund: Oravan maritime wave-tithe, Irrah overland caravan-tithe, and Ngaru-Bon metallurgical stone-tithe. The Pool's payouts subsidize across the three tranches: a sunk fleet in the Halanimoa archipelago is paid by a successful caravan in the deep desert, a forge-strike in Nokul-Gar is paid by a successful Wave Council reinsurance cycle, a frankincense-caravan loss in the Tabbaq oases is paid by a successful Halani-Tamu metallurgical-export season. The actuarial discipline is denominated in Khazadari rate-schedule terms; the Pool's continental volume is the largest single insurance instrument in Basin commerce. The Pool is not a state apparatus. It holds no charter from any civ and is not formally recognized in any civ's legal apparatus — except indirectly, through nominal supervision by the Triple-Seal Arbitration Court whose own jurisdiction is itself trans-civ and whose rulings are enforceable only through the…

Institutional Substrate The Tongue-Guild — Vakhi-Asakh in the mixed-register etymology its members prefer, vakhi a Wazahaki nominal stem for what passes between and asakh a Qalīb term whose etymology is contested (Guild practitioners link it to the oath-binding root √s-l-q established at religion/04sacredregisters/qalib.md, though Basin linguists propose a separate root, possibly √s-k-h, related to witnessing or plain speech) — is the continental syndicate of certified cross-register translators.
