None of these…

Warfare: The Basin has no army, no native ethnicity, and no military authority; its wars are fought by merchant dynasties, dock-brokers, oath-courts, and confraternities through embargo, blacklist, and forum-shopping, capped by total grain-import dependency. Who Fights No one fights in arms. The contestants are merchant dynasties, dock-brokers, oath-courts, confraternities, and the factors of upstream powers. They fight through the institutions of a clearing-house port, and the only blood spilled is metaphorical until it is not. How War Is Waged War is embargo and the blockaded river; forum-shopping between jurisdictions; the dock-broker blacklist; the honor-debt that can ruin a name; smuggling and counter-smuggling; and the rare quiet assassination. The three active crises, the harboroathwar, the metalinterdict, and the calendarschism, are the worked examples; they are linked here and not restated. A factor who loses a jurisdictional appeal may simply reopen the case in a competing oath-court, and the merchant who can forum-shop longest can outlast a rival who has right on his side. The Limit The Basin grows nothing and makes nothing; it is total grain-import dependency. Its…

Warfare: A desert warrior-nobility over vassal herders and the enslaved raids caravans, while irrigated-plain citizen levies and mercenaries weaponize canals; both are capped by water and the well. Who Fights Two systems fight under one name. In the desert, a hereditary warrior-nobility commands vassal herders and the enslaved who work the oasis gardens. On the irrigated plain, organized citizen levies and mercenaries fight under the city. The Ḥarrāb, the caravan-company that crosses the wastes, is both target and sometimes ally. The enslaved who tend the oasis gardens are sometimes armed in emergencies and placed in the front rank; their freedom, if they survive, is promised and rarely granted. How War Is Waged In the desert, war is the mobile hit-and-run caravan raid; the warband strikes a Darb, seizes what it can carry, and vanishes into the gravel before relief arrives. On the plain, war is siege and the deliberate weaponization of hydraulic engineering: canals are cut, diverted, or breached to flood a field, erase a border, or wash away an enemy's harvest. The Rubāṭ, the fortified way-station, is the pivot between the two worlds. It stores grain, water, and fodder along…

Warfare: A universal mounted-archer levy in which society is the army, fighting through feigned retreat, ambush, and the encircling drive, supreme on grass and helpless off it, ending in a protection-racket equilibrium with settled neighbors. Who Fights There is no standing army separate from the people. Every household sends its men with their own mounts and provisions, so the levy is the herding economy in another season. The Tzin-Taka, the warlord who can hold a coalition, rises by success in raid and gift, from birth or from merit depending on what the season rewards. A household that cannot mount a son falls into debt to a richer cousin, and the loan is often repaid in daughters, grazing rights, or a season of unpaid herding. How War Is Waged The host fights as mobile horse-archery: feigned retreat, ambush from a dry fold, and the great encircling drive that turns an enemy against itself. At the sub-imperial scale, a punitive cattle-raid is regulated by the Oral-Memory Council as a tool of redress and redistribution; it looks like low-intensity war because that is the face it wears. The great encircling drive can take days to close, and the council records the boundaries…

Warfare: A warrior cavalry aristocracy ruling free levies and bound slave-soldiers, with a hereditary riverboat corps, wins battles on the dry savanna and the river but cannot cross the fly-belt to hold the wet lowland. Who Fights A warrior cavalry aristocracy sits at the top of the host, with shock horsemen drawn from families that keep imported horses at the expense of households and client lineages. Beneath them march free levies raised by district obligation and bound slave-soldiers stripped of lineage. A hereditary riverboat corps supplies the river-navy, giving the empire reach along the great river that is its spine. The bound soldiers are drawn from captives taken in earlier raids or pawned by indebted kin; they fight without lineage and are buried without song. How War Is Waged On the dry savanna, massed shock cavalry breaks an enemy line. On the river, war-canoes and troop-boats move upstream and down, seizing trade-towns and cutting supply. The real objective is rarely the battlefield; it is control of the wealthy entrepôts where goods are taxed both ways. The Wa-Ngo-Mkuu, the military general, coordinates the two arms, while the Court of the Three Mouths settles…

Warfare: A small standing core, mass corvée peasant levies, and monastic soldier-fraternities housed in fortress-monasteries, defending passes and besieging strongholds, blocked by altitude and malaria in both directions. Who Fights The host is a small standing core swollen by mass corvée peasant levies. Beside them stand the monastic soldier-fraternities housed in the great Dzong and Khar, the fortress-monasteries that are also economic and political hubs. The monk-soldier is a kinsman of the plateau who has taken a different oath from the lay levy. The monastic fraternities are funded by butter, grain, and metal donated by lay households, and in return they man the walls when the pass bells ring. How War Is Waged War is defense of passes and siege of fortress-strongholds, not sweeping maneuver. Men fight brutal close work in freezing, funneled terrain, and the Drak-Khar, the cliff citadel, is both refuge and trap. A Drak-Khar cannot be stormed from below; it is starved, undermined, or betrayed, and its fall usually means the massacre of every adult male inside. Internal monastic-political brawling over succession and economic interest is as much a part of conflict as any…

Warfare: A stratified society under hereditary chiefs raises a mass levy of nearly all men, stiffened by veteran-warriors, to raid by sea and siege hill-forts, but the ocean limits occupation to a seasonal tributary network. Who Fights Oravan is a stratified society under hereditary chiefs. The war-party is a mass levy of nearly all able-bodied men, stiffened by a respected veteran-warrior class. War is a societal and religious obligation, not a standing profession, and the chief who cannot raise a war-party loses the prestige that holds his line. A chief's power is measured by the number of canoes he can fill, and a young man who refuses the call is shamed through silence and the withholding of marriage alliances. How War Is Waged War is the naval raid, the amphibious landing, and the protracted siege of the engineered hill-fort. Combat is intensely personal hand-to-hand work; there is no bow. Siege is by starvation and by elaborate deception when the fort cannot be stormed. The hill-fort is built with terraced earthworks and hidden sally-ports, and a war-party that does not know the ground can be led into an ambush by a single false path. The Da, the spear, and the Kelada,…

Each of the seven civilizations fights in a different way, and each tells a different story about what its wars mean. This sub-layer documents war itself: who fought, how war was waged, the terrain and logistics that capped it, why it so rarely decided anything, what it cost, and the gap between the heroic account the warrior elite told and the ground-level reality the commoner lived. It does not restate the cold conflicts already in canon. The three active crises and the window-war () are the worked instances of conflict-by-other-means; the warfare files link to them and add the per-civ military texture those files assume. The Cold-War Thesis Veydrian conflict is structurally cold. Its normal mode is commercial, legal, and theological: embargo, forum-shopping between jurisdictions, blacklist, tribute, requisition, the withholding of grain or water or metal, and the occasional assassination. Hot war exists, but it is rare, heavily terrain-gated, and self-limiting. When force reaches the operational limit its geography, disease, and logistics allow, it cools back into raiding, siege-stalemate, negotiated tribute, or slow administrative absorption. Durable conquest by decisive…

Warfare: A mass corvée infantry levy raised by rotational labor-draft and anchored by a small royal guard, projecting power along a road-and-storehouse network until altitude and the absence of heavy pack animals force conquest to be finished by demographic resettlement. Who Fights War is one turn of the labor obligation that also builds roads and works mines. The host is a mass, ethnically mixed levy raised by rotational draft and commanded in decimal units, with a small pure-blood royal guard at its core. The waqcha and the kinless poor fill the ranks because they have the least leverage to refuse a draft that the state records as reciprocal service. How War Is Waged Coercive diplomacy comes first: gifts, retained rank, and the promise of shelter for those who submit. If submission fails, the levy besieges hilltop forts with ramps, fire, and starvation, using percussive and projectile arms but no siege engines. Alongside these campaigns runs a ritualized, contained proxy-fight over water and grazing rights, fought at appointed places so that a larger war does not have to be fought. The Chaski-Run carries the terms of submission ahead of the host, so that a fort may surrender…

Pacha-Urco desk, Ki-Mbuhari confluence-warehouse, five days before the deferred hearing --- The Pacha-Urco desk kept its certificates in a cedar press on the landward wall, where the river damp reached last. Wata-Niy had asked for that wall the first season the house retained him, twelve years ago, and the desk had given it to him without argument, because a khipu cord that swells with damp reads as if its knots have shifted when they have not, and a finding the house paid for could not rest on a cord that lied because it was wet. He stood at the press now with his coat still on. He had come down from the highland in four days on the cliff-road and the river-stage, and the grain-port heat was in the room the way it was in every room at Ki-Mbuhari, thick and low and smelling of drying fish and hot papyrus. He was a highland calendar-keeper in a Ndjadi grain-door, and the copy-houses had graded him on the way in. He had paid the highland surety the classification set and waited the half-day it cost a man of his coloring to be read, and he had done both without remark, because the friction was older than his retainer and would outlast it. The Pacha-Urco standing carried him the…

A copy-house reading-room, Ki-Mbuhari, four days before the hearing --- The copy-house rented reading-rooms by the half-day to factors who needed to study a contract before they signed it, and the rooms were the only quiet at Ki-Mbuhari that a man could buy. Wata-Niy took one on the upper floor, away from the street, with a north window for steady light and a board he could clear. He set the certificate cord along the board and laid the published dates beside it: the Alto Concordance's almanac extract for the disputed window, in cliff-road observational notation, and the Upriver Confederation's observation tally for the same season, in cord-copy. The house had obtained both. A finding the Court could read had to show its work against what both lineages had published, or it was one man's word against a cord. He began the way he began every cord, with his thumb on the intercalation knot and his eyes on the window. The Old Upriver intercalation knot was a three-course working: the observation course on top, the count course in the middle, the date-tally pendant below. A keeper reading it by eye read the courses in order and trusted the cord. A keeper reading it by hand read the…

The confluence-warehouse record-room, Ki-Mbuhari, three days before the hearing --- A certificate did not stand on its own. It was struck from the season's observation tally, and the contract chain carried a certified copy of that tally, knotted by the observing station and registered with the contract before any window was drawn from it. The Confederation's own master khipu stayed at the observing station; what the Ki-Mbuhari confluence-warehouse held in its record-room, with the rest of the chain, was the contract's certified counterpart. The warehouse was the Kagbende-Khazadari House's, and the Pacha-Urco standing got Wata-Niy into the room on the house's correspondence with it. A warehouse clerk brought the certified tally to a side-table, watched while he worked, and entered in the room-log that the examiner had handled it. Nothing left the room. That was the regime, and it was the regime that made the room worth coming to: a registered cord kept under the warehouse's own hand could not be quietly swapped for a friendlier one. He read the certified tally first, alone, before he set the certificate beside it. A finding that the certificate had been shifted was worth nothing…

The reading-room and the wharf, Ki-Mbuhari, two days before the hearing --- The Alto delegate came to the reading-room without sending word ahead, which a senior man of the Concordance did not do unless he wanted the meeting unrecorded. Wata-Niy knew his rank by the cliff-road braid on his coat before he knew his face. The delegate did not sit. He asked, in plain Alto speech, whether the examiner had reached a count, and Wata-Niy, who had kept Alto dates for thirty years and did not lie to the Concordance, said that he had. Nine days. The middle course cut and re-tied. The delegate said that the Concordance already knew. The practice had run two cycles, and the Concordance had come by its own proof of it. Then he said the rest of it, which Wata-Niy had not known and did not want. To publish a finding of backdating against the Upriver keeper would open a restitution proceeding, and a restitution proceeding would put the Concordance's own records into the Court, and in those records was a second house, an Alto-aligned trade family, that shifted its own certificates the same way, at its own seasons, and that the Concordance permitted to do so because the permission was a leash.…

The Triple-Seal Court's Ki-Mbuhari sitting, the hearing day --- The Court sat in a notarial hall the copy-houses kept for it, the prefix-grammar of a hundred cleared contracts stamped into the registers along the walls. Wata-Niy sat in the examiner's place to the side, where a man who had filed an instrument waited in case the bench wanted him, and was not called. The house had submitted his leaf the evening before, as part of its demand. The clerk had taken it under the deferred matter and read its two measurements into the day's record without adopting them. A finding became, at that moment, a thing other men used. The Pacha-Urco factor used it first. He stood with the house's grievance and read the examiner's leaf aloud to the bench, the count course cut and re-tied, the window short of the certified tally by nine days, and he let the two measurements stand as what they were and then named them what the house needed them to be. An Upriver-aligned keeper had falsified a certificate to rob an Alto-aligned house of a season's bark, and here was the count, sworn by a keeper of thirty years, and the house demanded restitution from the Upriver Confederation. Wata-Niy listened to…

The knotting style was pre-schism: the three-cord base with the supplementary quipu running perpendicular to the primary, the configuration her mother's family had been using for household accounts since her grandmother's time, before anyone had found a reason to argue about which observatory's…

Wawa-Kocha compound, the working area and outer chamber, second day of session --- Three paths. She named them on the walk from the archive room back to the Double-Keepers' working area, because naming them was how she worked through problems she had not been trained to solve. Brief five would document the eleven-day discrepancy between the Upriver cord-record and the Alto almanac extract, cite the Confederation's primary-evidence bundle as the computation basis, and characterize the discrepancy in the category of competing-observatory-jurisdiction disagreements. The eleven-day gap was the Schism; both lineages had argued it for three cycles and would argue it for three more. The four-day gap was different. The cord's calculation sat four days below the Sapa Mayu observatory's own historical record, and a…

Wawa-Kocha compound, the working area and plenary chamber, final day of session --- The chair's response arrived in the Double-Keepers' correspondence tray on the third morning: a single page in Mbu-Bwana ra-Kilomba's hand, addressed to the Double-Keepers' Technical Secretary. Tavakh-Qarat, the Tongue-Guild's moral-correspondence overflow room, third day after the triple-seal hold --- The surge work was not regular contract translation. Regular contract translation was Halu-Tabbaq's domain: commercial-oath rendering, witness-clause nuance, the precision work the Guild priced at the top of its schedule. Surge work was what the Senior Council assigned when the moral-correspondence circuit overflowed, and the circuit had been overflowing since the Vernacular-Habal pamphlets started moving at volume. Ki-Vita had been assigned to the overflow room at the third hour.
