Institutional Substrate Banditry is the overland counterpart of the maritime predation documented at law.underworld.piracy. The institution preys on the caravan routes that connect the seven civilizations across desert, gorge, steppe, and forge-route, and it survives because no civilization's writ runs reliably beyond the reach of its own escort. A bandit who robs an Irrah caravan and is caught on the desert track by Irrah riders is an Irrah criminal under the qaṭʿ al-ṭarīq category at law.civ.irrah; the same bandit becomes an underworld figure at the moment he flees across a frontier that the pursuing civilization's institutions do not cross, at which point his survival depends on whether the receiving civilization's institutions accept him, ignore him, or negotiate his return. The institution is an exploitation institution in the taxonomy of law.underworld.overview. The bandit does not contest the legitimate order's claim to define the lawful, in the way that the heresy undergrounds at law.underworld.heresyundergrounds do; he profits because the legitimate order has produced the caravan-route economy and cannot police every length of it. Institutional Substrate Counterfeiting is the underworld institution that attacks the evidentiary primitives themselves. Every other underworld offense, in the taxonomy of law.underworld.overview, parasitizes a particular trade, route, or commodity; counterfeiting parasitizes the legal-certification mechanism on which the trade in question depends. The pirate takes the cargo, but the forger produces the seal that allows the cargo to be resold as legitimate. The smuggler moves the obsidian past the interdiction, but the forger produces the consecration mark that allows the obsidian to clear at a Basin warehouse. The institution lives, in this sense, one layer beneath every other underworld trade, and the cargo of the other trades is only as valuable as the forgeries that attend it. Each of the seven civilizations of Veydria certifies legal acts through a distinct evidentiary primitive. The Basin clears a contract by the rotating-chair-recognized Triple-Seal panel and the Filer's Hand cadence. Irrah certifies a binding act by the isnād-chain of named witnesses verified through jarḥ wa-taʿdīl scrutiny. Ndjadi certifies by the Kagbende-ordained prefix-tier notarization in Wazahaki…

Institutional Substrate The heresy undergrounds are the underworld's canonical opposition institutions, prosecuted by each civilization not for what they steal but for what they reject. Where the smuggler at law.underworld.smuggling and the counterfeiter at law.underworld.counterfeiting parasitize the legitimate order's sanctions and certifications without contesting their authority, the heresy underground rejects the authority itself. The smuggler does not deny that the Metal Interdict is law; the heretic denies that the institution producing the law is competent to make it. The opposition is the structural fact, and it determines the punitive instruments brought against the institution at every level. Three named heresies form the principal undergrounds documented in current canon. The Single-Sky Heresy reduces the Kheshkai shamanic-pantheon multiplicity to a single sky-deity reading, rejecting the Four-Sky Hearing Circle's canonical five-layer harmony in favor of a single back-vowel cycle; it is documented at religion.reform.kheshkaisinglesky. Institutional Substrate Marronage is the underworld institution of escape from unfree labor, and it is, with the heresy undergrounds at law.underworld.heresyundergrounds, one of the two canonical opposition institutions in the taxonomy of law.underworld.overview. The smuggler at law.underworld.smuggling parasitizes the legitimate order's sanctions; the maroon rejects the standing-architecture on which several civilizations' law rests. The runaway's act is, in the strict reading, the reclamation of the body as a thing that cannot be owned, and several of Veydria's seven legal architectures hold this reclamation to be precisely the kind of offense the order cannot accommodate without unmaking itself. The Irrah Ghūlām who deserts his caravan-guard service, the Ndjadi corvée laborer who flees the river-lord house, the Oravan indentured cove-laborer who reaches a sanctuary cove, the Ngaru-Bon Slag-Road corvée runaway who arrives at a dzong gate are, in each home civilization's reading, persons who have taken from the order what the order claims to own. What the Underworld Layer Documents The seven civilizations of Veydria each prosecute their own internal crime, and the record of that prosecution lives in the per-civilization files of law.civ.basin and its companions. Each of those files carries a Crime Catalog: the offenses a civilization names, the court that hears them, the punitive instrument applied, and the evidentiary primitive by which guilt is established. A theft in an Irrah caravan is an Irrah matter, weighed on the isnād chain before an Irrah panel and answered with an Irrah penalty. A breach of a Wazahaki prefix-notarized contract is a Ndjadi matter, brought before the Court of the Three Mouths and resolved through jelis-mediated palaver. The civ-internal Crime Catalog is the law of a place applied to the people of that place. The underworld is what survives in the spaces between those places. This layer documents the institutions that persist across civilizational borders by operating in the seams that the seven legal architectures leave open. Veydria has no continental sovereign, no court whose writ runs across all seven civilizations, and no shared register in which a cross-border offense could be certified as…

Institutional Substrate Piracy is the underworld institution of continental shipping predation, and the institution is shaped, in the first instance, by the absence of any continental naval authority capable of suppressing it. Each of the contributing civilizations of Veydria handles its own coastal waters under its own legal architecture: Oravan binds its archipelago's waters within the tapu and rāhui complex documented at law.civ.oravan, Basin port-zones maintain harbor-patrols whose writ ends at the breakwater, and the riverine approaches to Ki-Mbuhari are governed by the Court of the Three Mouths' twelve-house assembly. None of these institutions runs into another's waters by right. The stretches of open sea between them, particularly the Halkar narrows that connect the Oravan archipelago to the Basin ports, are the unpoliced spaces in which piracy lives. The institution exists on both axes of the opposition-exploitation taxonomy described at law.underworld.overview. The taking of an Oravan keel in the Halkar narrows is exploitation of the commercial route that no continental authority protects and, in the same act, opposition to the maritime authority-claim that the Oravan…

Institutional Substrate There is no single Veydrian institution of sex-labor, and the absence is the first fact this file documents. What exists is seven legal architectures that each name, license, tax, prohibit, or ignore the sale of sexual labor according to the same evidentiary primitive and the same standing-gradations that govern the rest of a civilization's law. The Irrah weigh it on the isnād chain and answer it with the Mālikī penalty for zina. The Ndjadi bring it before the Court of the Three Mouths and resolve it through jelis-mediated palaver under the slave-body protection that the twelve-house assembly enforces. The Oravan bind it, like every other use of the body, within the tapu and rāhui complex. The Basin, which has no internal code, neither names it nor forbids it, and treats the contracts that surround it as the commercial instruments they are. To speak of sex-labor in Veydria is to speak of seven different things that share a continental commerce. That shared commerce is what makes sex-labor an underworld matter rather than a purely civ-internal one. Where a free woman of Irrah sells her own labor in an Irrah town, the question is entirely an Irrah…

Institutional Substrate Smuggling is the underworld institution that moves goods the legitimate order has sanctioned, restricted, or required certification for. It is the canonical exploitation institution in the taxonomy of law.underworld.overview; the smuggler does not contest the legitimacy of the sanction or the certification regime, he profits because the sanction creates the margin and the certification creates the gate at which the margin can be captured. A goods-market without sanctioned-and-restricted categories produces no smuggling; a market in which every cross-civ instrument requires Tongue-Guild certification and every Ngaru-Bon metal sale requires Inner Council consecration produces an underworld economy whose volume is roughly proportional to the strictness of the certification regime. Three primary categories define the institution. The first is the obsidian-and-metal trade under the active Metal Interdict at factions.crisis.metalinterdict; the Inner Council of Ancestor-Smiths' forge-strike against the Altan-Ordu Qaghan's Vanguard has produced a continental-scale sanction that has, since onset, generated a parallel uncertified-metal economy operating through…

If institutional facts are sustained by collective intentionality — the frame a Veydrian jurist would recognize from real-world social ontology — what happens when collective intentionality attenuates? The question crystallizes in three forms, each currently live within a specific tradition. None is resolved. Each tradition's answer is internally contested, and each tradition's unresolved dispute is load-bearing for the tradition's political structure. Form 1: The Ndjadi Cross-Border Oath Does a Ndjadi ra-prefix oath bind a Kheshkai who refuses to accept Ndjadi cosmology? Three positions: - Conservative Ndjadi scribes hold that the prefix operates on the cosmos, not on the speaker's beliefs. The oath binds regardless of what the Kheshkai thinks about Ndjadi cosmology. - Vernacular-Habal reformers hold that the prefix operates through institutional recognition. A Kheshkai outside the institution is outside the binding. - Basin practice, ambiguously, treats the Kheshkai as bound in Ndjadi courts and not bound elsewhere — a jurisdictional compromise that pleases neither party but stabilizes trade. The Kheshkai themselves have no stake in the dispute: they consider all Ndjadi…

The Question Does accumulated practitioner wear increase, decrease, or stay neutral to the binding authority of a sacred register? Every Veydrian tradition pays a physical price for its register — laryngeal damage, muteness, silicosis, daylight blindness, burn-scarring, spinal compression, forearm strain, altitude wear, repetitive-strain hoarseness, sterility-by-vow. The practitioner is visibly spent. The question of what that spending means for the authority of their subsequent utterances is not settled anywhere on the continent. This document synthesizes the position each tradition takes, identifies the patterns that emerge when the six civs are compared, and flags the scenarios where cost-efficacy readings become decision-theoretic rather than theological. One: aged matriarch purest. Two: only full-vigor binds. Three: age irrelevant. | Fragmented (3-7 workshop-lineages per island) | | Ndjadi | Wazahaki | Kinship-severance…

The Question What happens when a sacred register is produced incorrectly? Every Veydrian tradition has a failure curve — a gradient from trivial consequence (a drifted reduplication corrected in real time) to catastrophic backlash (an institution fractures, a lineage dies, a practitioner's breath fails mid-utterance). The curves are not parallel across civilizations. Each tradition's failure-mode gradient reflects its institutional structure, its physical register demands, and its political embedding. This document maps the six failure gradients side by side, identifies the patterns that emerge, and locates where the gradients intersect dangerously (e.g., when a Basin cross-register contract routes failure through two incompatible punishment-ecologies). The Master Gradient (5-Step Canonical Frame) Across traditions, failure severity can be ordered on a five-step gradient: 1. Social correction — error caught and repaired in real time by peers or seniors; no lasting consequence 2. Liturgical void — the specific utterance is null; ritual must be restarted or abandoned; no personal consequence beyond time lost 3. Commercial/reputational death — the practitioner's professional…

The Question How does each tradition organize its practitioners, and what structural consequences follow for doctrine, schism tolerance, single-point-of-failure risk, and the shape of political leverage available to outsiders? The six Veydrian sacred-register traditions are not merely six different phonologies. Each is also a distinct institutional design — a mechanism for identifying, training, licensing, disciplining, and sometimes reforming practitioners. The institutional shape is not arbitrary. It is produced by the interaction of three forces: the phonological demands of the register (what kind of body and training can produce it), the transmission mechanism available in the culture (literate/non-literate, settled/itinerant, caste-bound/open), and the political context in which the register operates (monopolistic/competitive, centralized/distributed). This document maps the four institutional types that emerge from those interactions, identifies where the Schism Axis falls for each civ, and analyzes how institutional asymmetry becomes political leverage at the Basin. A Ngaru-Bon smith's click-blessing and a Kheshkai shaman's harmony-oath meet at a bride-price exchange. The smith cannot evaluate the harmony; the shaman cannot evaluate the click. Neither register binds across the gap. Tavas-Kaj pidgin — the Basin's continental lingua franca — cannot bind by any standard. It has no sacred register, no institutional authority, no isnād, no calendar, no harmony, no click, no tier-prefix. It is a commercial tool and nothing more. The Basin's Architectural Answer The Basin's institutional architecture is the answer to this problem. The triple-seal contract is a workaround: parties sign under three separate traditions simultaneously, so each party is bound under the tradition they recognize, and enforcement is distributed across jurisdictions that do not need to be mutually intelligible so long as they are jointly available. The architecture is expensive — three witnesses, three physical costs, three audit chains — but it is the only continental mechanism that has scaled. The Implication: Permanent Pluralism No unified continental law is possible because no register can evaluate another. A Kheshkai bound under Varkosh who enters a Ndjadi…

When three religious jurisdictions witness a Basin oath — a triple-seal contract — and the oath is breached, which jurisdiction's ecology enforces the consequence? Four readings circulate in the Basin's port cities, each with partisans among the dragomans and factors whose livelihoods depend on having an answer. No tribunal has ruled across all three cases in a way that would discriminate between them. The Basin's pluralism is load-bearing: each reading produces the same contract-behavior most of the time, and the rare cases that would discriminate are settled before reaching a ruling. The question is not settled. Reading 1: Additive Each jurisdiction enforces independently. A breach triggers three separate excommunication processes, each operating within its own tradition's ontology: - The Ṣāliqūn withdraw the isnād - The Ndjadi college voids the ra- or ka- tier prefix attached to the breaching party's name - The Ngaru-Bon guild imposes an Interdict on the party's metal-work Consequences compound. Most merchants behave as though this reading is correct, because it produces the most conservative contract-behavior. The additive reading is the unofficial operational default — the…

The Ontological Frame What outsiders call "magic" in Veydria is better described by what Veydrians themselves, when pressed, tend to call it: correct speech under correct authority. The six civilizations that rim the Aethelian Basin share no term for what the word "magic" covers. Each has a distinct taxonomy — tavamala (craft-voice), wazahaki (craft of truth), willkaqallu (sacred tongue), varkosh (oath-wind), gyamsgra (forge-voice), qalīb (the mould) — and each taxonomy rejects the premise that the others describe the same phenomenon. Two observations organize the magic layer. First, every Veydrian sacred register is a narrow, institutionally-governed speech practice. The phonology is specific (sacred vowel-length, tier-prefixes, calendrically-bound ejectives, vowel-harmony patterns, clicks and laterals, pharyngealization) and, in all cases, non-trivially difficult to produce. The grammatical feat of producing the register correctly is, across traditions, insufficient. The registers are also gated by institutions — workshop-lineages, scribal colleges, calendar-keeper houses, master-shaman apprenticeship, ancestor-smith guilds, isnād-chains — that independently certify who is…

Setup Prince Yaqucha is invested at Pacha-Urco on a day the Alto-Lineage identifies as solstitial and the Upriver-Lineage places outside the licit window. Both calendar-keeper lineages are present. Both sign the rite. The Prince is formally invested. The rite required heavily aspirated breathy phonology, the register's most taxing form and the one reserved for direct address to Karuwel; the officiating calendarist, an Alto woman of advanced years named Sumaq Urpi whose laryngeal wear had already cost her the lower aspirations, produced it once and did not speak again that day. The Alto-Lineage places the solstice on the ninety-fourth day of the cycle and the Upriver-Lineage on the ninety-third, a single day's divergence that has stood unreconciled for three cycles and that no living calendarist expects to see closed. Both lineages attended because a contested investiture witnessed by only one is worth less than no investiture at all, and both signed because to withhold the signature would have been to concede the other's reckoning. The divergence is not error but method. The Alto khipu reckons the solstice from a sequence of dawn-shadow observations at the high terraces above…

Under Upriver reckoning, it falls outside it. The elder subscribed to Alto; the Upriver reckoning is, by her…

Setup A young woman raised in a Basin port by a Qeturīn father and a Kheshkai mother produces both the whistled surrogate-language and back-vowel harmony natively. She seeks institutional legitimation from one or both: - The Qalībin refuse without isnād - The Kheshkai master-shamans refuse without a lineage sponsor, which she cannot obtain Her name is Imna, and she was born at Ki-Mbuhari to a Qeturīn wind-reader who had taken Basin work after his guild-service and a Kheshkai woman of a horse-clan that wintered at the Basin's edge. She learned the whistled surrogate-language from her father and the back-vowel harmony from her mother before she learned to read a tally, and by adolescence she could produce both phonologies in a manner any hearing-gifted Kheshkai or any Qeturīn would recognize as native. What she cannot produce is a lineage. The Qeturīn whistle-register is gated by an isnād she does not hold; the Varkosh harmony is gated by a master-shaman's sponsorship she cannot obtain, since no steppe lineage will sponsor a child raised in a port to a mother who left the migration. She is, in both traditions, perfectly capable and perfectly illegitimate. She has worked the…

Setup An aged Ṣāliqūn, silent for eleven years, is called to witness a triple-seal contract at the Basin's eastern port of Halani-Tamu. The commissioning merchant's rival has privately retained a junior Ṣāliqūn who will argue, in the inland tribunal if the contract is breached, that the mute witness is void under a minority reading of the isnād-chain. The mute witness is named Tāhirah bint Ṣaliq, and she is among the most senior oath-binders the Qalībin still seat: laryngeally spent at fifty-nine, mute these eleven years, her isnād traced through four teachers to a Ṣāliqūn of the Five Waters generation whose name still carries weight in inland tribunals. The commissioning merchant retained her precisely for that pedigree, on the principle that the strongest possible witness forecloses dispute. The principle has failed him. Setup A mid-tier Basin merchant, impatient with triple-seal expense, executes a high-value contract in Tavas-Kaj pidgin alone, with signatures but no sacred-register witness. The counterparty breaches. The merchant is named Habbu, a mid-tier factor of Halani-Tamu whose margins have never been wide enough to absorb three witnesses on every consignment, and the contract is the largest he has ever attempted: a forward purchase of Qollari worked-silver against Ndjadi grain, executed in Tavas-Kaj with signatures, a notarized tally, and no sacred-register witness of any kind. He had reasons beyond thrift. The season was short, the silver was moving, and a rival factor was circling the same Qollari supplier; assembling three witnesses would have cost him days he believed he did not have, and the counterparty, eager to close, encouraged the shortcut in terms Habbu only later understood as the first move of the breach he is now litigating. He calculated that the counterparty's commercial reputation was security enough. He calculated wrong. Setup A junior Ndjadi scribe publishes a vernacular-glossed edition of the tier-prefixes, accessible to literate non-scribes. The Elder Scribes of the senior college convene to decide whether to suppress the edition, discredit the scribe, or issue a counter-gloss that re-encodes the cosmological work. The scribe is named Wa-Sukuma, a ka-tier notary three colleges down from the senior houses, and the edition is a slim thing: the three tier-prefixes set beside vernacular Ndjadi glosses, with worked examples drawn from common river-court matters, copied at a price a literate grain-factor could meet. He published it under his own name, which the Elder Scribes read as either courage or provocation and cannot decide which. The senior college that convenes to answer him is the Ramwen house, oldest of the ra-tier colleges, whose authority over cross-tribunal notarization is precisely the authority the edition threatens to make unnecessary. He is not the first to gloss the prefixes, only the first to do it for sale and under his own name. A vernacular key has surfaced perhaps three times in the colleges' memory — once as a dying scribe's private bequest to a son outside the order, once…

Etymology: from the triliteral root √q-l-b ("to turn, to pour"). "The mould" — the base sacred register of the Qalībin order, with three institutionally-distinct sub-registers: Ṣāliqūn (oath-binders), Qeturīn (wind-readers), and Azmarāʔ (star-readers). The structural analogy to real-world Tuareg religious-linguistic orders is close enough that Basin scholars cite it; the Qalībin themselves trace the order to the Five Waters and reject the comparison. Shared Phonological Character (All Three Sub-Registers) - Exaggerated pharyngealization — every consonant bearing secondary pharyngeal constriction - Graded vowel elongation — one to six mora depending on liturgical weight - Ritual nasalized vowel /ɑ̃ː/ — absent from vernacular Irrah; its presence alone signals a binding context - Qalqala-style percussive release on final unvoiced stops - Mandatory one-breath delivery — a mispronounced Qalīb utterance is actively dangerous: the one-breath requirement combined with maximal pharyngealization means breath-failure mid-utterance is a physical event as well as a liturgical one Authority: The Isnād-Chain Authority in all three sub-registers is gated by isnād — the teacher-to-student…

Etymology: var (oath, promise) + kosh (wind). "Oath-wind" — the sacred register of the Kheshkai steppe-peoples. Phonological Character Alone among the six, Varkosh has no institution. There are no colleges, no guilds, no lineages in the formal sense. Master-shamans take one to three apprentices; apprenticeship runs five to ten years on horseback during seasonal migration. Identification is by "hearing-gift" — a phonological capacity often associated with perfect-pitch individuals — detectable in children aged eight to twelve. The phonology is strict: - Back-vowel harmony in /a, o/ governs binding oaths, investiture, and war. The canonical pattern is a-o-a, preserved in the name Qarughan and transmitted through the Qarughan investiture-cycle. - Front-vowel harmony in /i/ governs domestic blessings, horse-consecrations, and well-namings. - Broken harmony is unmarked everyday speech — non-binding. - Harmonic completeness is absolute: a single disharmonic syllable voids the utterance. - Rising terminal intonation and glottal-onset emphatic stress are characteristic; the register is designed to project upward, under open sky. The Practitioner's Account Varkosh is heard by the sky.…

Etymology: waza (skill) + haki (truth, justice). "Craft of truth" — the sacred register of the Ndjadi scribal colleges. Phonological Character Wazahaki's defining feature is a three-tier cosmological prefix system: ra- (sky, primordial, above), ka- (river, mortal-ordered, middle), and nga- (deep, chthonic, beneath). Per ADR-0005, the tier-prefixes operate on a separate axis from the vernacular Ndjadi noun-classes (Mbu-, Wa-, Ki-) and can co-occur with them: - — "primordial reservoir" - — "a mortal working man" - — "settlement-ruins of the chthonic" The tier-prefixes are found only in Wazahaki. Vernacular Ndjadi noun-class morphology is structurally analogous to Bantu systems familiar to comparative linguists, but the tier-axis is an additional register-specific layer that no vernacular context licenses. Other features: - Tonal contours vary by speech-act (narrative level-mid, juridical rising-falling, devotional sustained) - Prenasalized agreement markers (mba-, nda-, ŋga-) track the tier - Final-vowel lengthening to two or three mora marks phrase ends - Tier-prefix stops take obligatory implosive voicing [ɓ, ɗ] Vernacular Ndjadi is non-tonal, which makes the register's…

Etymology: gyam (forge) + sgra (sound, voice). "Forge-voice" — the ancestor-smith guild's sacred register, and the most institutionally monolithic register on the continent. Phonological Character Gyamsgra's defining feature is the three-tier ancestral sub-register structure: - Nokul-tier with dental click [ǀ] — cattle-origin blessings - Amori-tier with lateral click [ǁ] — inventory and resource-counting - Lapam-tier with lateral fricative [ɬ] — metal consecration and weapon-genealogy The shift from click to non-click encodes, in the phonology itself, the civilizational transition from pastoral to industrial — a compression of historical narrative into articulatory gesture. The structural echo of real-world Tibetan Bon's click-and-lateral liturgical inventories is, scholars note, suggestive rather than genetic; the guild rejects the comparison. The critical constraint is developmental. The click-and-lateral phonology must be acquired in infancy; guild families address infants in click-speech from the first day of life. The phonological window closes at five to seven years. Adults cannot acquire the articulatory gestures; the attempt produces characteristic…

Etymology: tava (voice) + mala (craft). "Craft-voice" — the sacred register of the Oravan palace-priestesshood. Phonological Character Vernacular Oravan is a non-tonal, open-syllable language whose vowel-length distinction is allophonic. In Tavamala, the distinction becomes phonemic and obligatorily carries a high-falling [˥˩] contour on lengthened vowels. Ritual reduplication — taa-ma taa-ma with sacred lengthening, against the vernacular emphatic tama tama — produces a characteristic sing-song recognizable across a harbor. The register's defining feature, however, is kinetic rather than acoustic: Tavamala syllable-timing locks 1:1 to concurrent craft-labor — the loom-beat, the chisel-strike, the paddle-stroke. Invocation without accompanying labor is, by universal agreement, inert. The Practitioner's Account When Tavamala is correctly produced during craft-labor, the artifact is consecrated. A loom-blessed cloth does not unravel under the weight of generations. A hull sung over the adze during carving does not split at the Aethelian crossings. A chisel-line haft carries a specific workshop-lineage's signature, detectable by priestesses of that lineage centuries later. The…

Etymology: willka (sacred, sun-related) + qallu (throat, passage, from kullku). "Sacred tongue" — the calendrically-gated register of the Qollari. Phonological Character Willkaqallu's characteristic feature is not phonological exclusivity but temporal licensing: the ejectives [p', t', k', q'] and the uvulars [q͡χ], [q] are producible by most Qollari speakers, but they are liturgically valid only on specific calendar-days, computed from khipu by lineages of calendar-keepers. An ejective on the wrong day is not a malformed speech-act; it is, in the practitioners' account, the right sound in the wrong cosmological moment. The aspiration hierarchy marks the weight of the binding: - Unaspirated — ordinary - Moderately aspirated — ancestral - Heavily aspirated with breathiness — direct address to Karuwel Khipu-rhythm governs syllabification; the tempo is the knot-count made audible. The Practitioner's Account The Qollari cosmos runs on solstitial, processional, and seasonal rhythms, each encoded in khipu by a distinct calendar-keeper lineage. When a calendar-correct ejective is produced, and the speaker is a recognized member of the appropriate altitude-tier institution, the…

Kitabu cha Safari ya Mbu-Kibwana ka-Pamba, kwa Watu wa Mazi Watatu. The Book of Mbu-Kibwana ka-Pamba's Journeys, for the People of the Three Mouths. Dictated to Mbu-Ulinzi ka-Vita, junior scribe of the Ki-Pamba house, in the three cycles following the writer's return. --- Book One — The Basin Passage Frontispiece I write this for the men of my house and for the boys who will be sent out as I was sent out, and for the river-courts of the Three Mouths who will be asked to certify what I have written. I am Mbu-Kibwana ka-Pamba, son of Mbu-Pamba ka-Lisala by my mother Mbu-Kilonzo wa-Pamba, junior scribe of the Ki-Pamba line by my mother's brother's patronage, trained in the prefix-notary tradition at the Mbu-Lisala river-court for six years, sent across to the Basin in the year my mother was deeded the third-floodfield, returned in the year my father's brother was buried. What I write is not what I saw, exactly. What I saw was confused, and a man who tries to write what he saw on the day he saw it writes a record of his own confusion. I have waited three full cycles since my return. The men who heard me speak in the year of my return remember me saying things I do not now remember…

Book Two: The Long Road Home and the Court's Tongue. --- Book Two — The Long Road Home and the Court's Tongue Preface to Book Two The first book is of the going-out. This second book is of the coming-back, which is the harder writing. A man going out is twenty and sees the world for the first time and writes what he sees. A man coming back is twenty-three and sees the world for the second time and writes what he had not been able to see the first time, including some of what he had seen and not understood and now thinks he understands and may still be wrong about. This is my third crossing of the western water. I have come back through the Halkar narrows, and the two arrivals are not the same harbor. The first was late dry season: the pilot on the second afternoon, a fair tide, the anchorage by dark. This crossing is the monsoon. The westerlies carry rain off the open water, and the passage holds more sea than I remembered it holding. The pilot said nothing about the conditions that I could hear above the noise of it. The hull cleared the narrows on the last of the tide and we lay at anchor in the rain. --- The clearing-station is the same stone building on the Halanimoa arm. The clearing-officer worked through my lading-declaration as she had before: spice, the small metal, cloth, each by column, each at its rate. When she reached the paper she entered the weight in the separate column that paper requires. Paper pays at the Covenant's seasonal rate. It did on the first crossing; it did on this one. I paid and the hull passed into the inner anchorage. --- The Havrana-Pulino workshop sits where I left it, the loggia canvas down against the rain. This was at the Basin port in the western season again, a year on from the season I set down the one water, with the hulls of my own coast in and their men ashore for the short while the winds allow. A hand I knew a little, of a hull newly berthed, came to me with a thing to place. He had carried it on his own account, a small venture folded in among the House paper, and he came to me because I am the man of our coast who knows the Basin's buyers and can speak the price in the Basin's own tongue. It was fire-flowers. I knew it before he had the wrapping off. We have them at home for the turning of the year, the powder packed in a paper tube that throws colored fire when it is lit, and the children stand for it in the cold and the old hands sell it from a tray. It comes to us from further out than our own coast, from somewhere east of east that our masters do not name and I have never been told, and it is dear at home for the distance it has travelled. I took it for what it has always been to me, a bright trifle of the holidays, and I reckoned the Basin would pay well for a thing it had not seen, the Basin paying always for the new. I wrote that evening that I had been brought…

I set down on an earlier leaf how a petition came against my seal, how it was answered, and what the answering cost me. I did not set down whose petition it was. That season I had no room to ask. This leaf is what I have since learned of the house that moved against me, and what the learning has made of me. --- The petition was sealed under the Wa-Kilomba house, an old house of the quarter that has kept its counting-room off the Arcade for as long as the quarter remembers and has never once been counted among the great. It stood nearer to mattering two generations back than it stands now. Its warehouse trade has thinned to a few certified lines it holds by long custom, and its sons take places in other men's houses where their grandfathers gave places to other men's sons. The man who set the seal to it is Wa-Kilomba Ndzabu, the eldest factor of the house, near sixty, who came up in the trade back when his house was still one the quarter reckoned with. I have had him shown to me since, at the Arcade. He is spare and straight and dresses a shade finer than his trade now carries, and he did not turn his head to me, though he knew me. He does not look at what he means to have shut…

It has been six days, and this is the first I can hold the pen. My father died in the night, in the room above the cordage-yard where we have kept our account since the year we came over. The medego had named it tisi a month gone, and the cough said it plainer. At the end he offered what mercy he had. My father took the opio for the cough and refused the spongia, for he meant to keep his head to the last. When the medego had nothing more, he said the thing they all say here, that nature can do no more, and went down to the yard to leave us the room. He was clear to the last hour, and he set the house in order the way a man goes over a lading-bill. The trade is my brother's now, as it was meant to be from the morning he left him on the quay at home to keep our mother and the name, and took me along for his hands. I am to hold the Veydria end, the tongues and the seals and the houses, and to send word and silver home by every hull I trust. He did not weep, and he did not let me. He said I was to write to my mother in my own hand and tell her he had not been afraid, which was near enough true to be set down. He had crossed knowing the water might keep him, and he provided for…

The hull came through the narrows on a fair tide in the late dry season of my twenty-seventh year, on the afternoon of our second day at the western anchorage. The pilot is an Oravan. The Halkar pilot-houses are Oravan, the fees are Oravan, and the rates are Oravan, because the strait is half a march wide at its narrowest and a keel that does not know the passage will not find the thread of it on its own, and the Oravan keep the knowing. He came aboard at the anchorage on the second afternoon, looked at the mouth of the passage for a time that seemed long to me and short to him, and said we would go on the afternoon tide. The ship's master asked the fee. The pilot named it. No one spoke again about the fee. I will say here to any who cross the western water and come to the Halkar passage for the first time: pay the pilot. What you pay is what you would spend across a season regretting the alternative, which three captains in the last cycle tried, preferring the open ocean and the monsoon to the pilot-house and the fee, and who have not been heard from since. We came through on the afternoon tide and were at the harbor-mouth anchorage by dark. --- The wave-tithe is collected at…

This was at the Basin port in the western season, when the hulls of my own coast were in and the men of them ashore between the wind that brings them and the wind that takes them home. I keep that company while it is here. It is the only company of my own tongue the Basin gives me, and a man hears the news of his own coast in no other place. One of them, newly come across, carried a thing the older hands had carried before him, a story off the Vaucresne shore from the season past. I set it down here because I am the only man in this place who is fit to set it down, and because it is not a thing to be set down in any place but this one. --- A hull had come ashore on the home coast in the dead of the turning season, on the cold rock north of the roads, when no keel of ours is at sea. It was not one of ours. The build was wrong for our yards and right for some other, and the men who broke it up for the timber knew the make of it for what it was. It was an Oravan hull, of the kind that pilots the enclosed sea a long water away to the east, that has no trade on our coast and no road to it that any master of ours has ever kept. There was a man alive in it. One. The cold had been at…

This season my business took me to Tavakh-Qarat, the old quarter on the north shore. The Khazadari keep the Arcade of Scales here. Each morning they call the day's cross-rate, salt-weight against iron-weight against grain-measure against silver. The Triple-Seal Courts sit under the one arcade, three jurisdictions ruling together on a single contract. It is the most mixed of the Basin's faces. A man of my coloring is one strange blood among many here, and less remarked for it than anywhere else I go, which is a thing I have come to value and to use. My business this time was not a cargo. I came to be entered. I have carried the House paper through the Basin these eleven years on my Guild certification and on the standing the firm has held here since my father's first account, and the Triple-Seal has certified my paper as an outland good crossing in. But the certification was of the cargo and not of me. In the Basin's own registry I have held no standing in my own name. I have sealed under the firm and witnessed under another's seal, and where the courts of this place keep the list of the men whose word is good in them, my name has not been on it. I came to put it there. On the…

This is my fourth crossing of the western water. I came through the Halkar narrows in the dry season, the pilot and the passage as they have always been, and I was at the Halanimoa anchorage by mid-afternoon of the second day. I walked the arm to the Havrana-Pulino workshop that same afternoon. I had not come on my own purpose on my first arrival, when I came as a stranger, and on the third the binder matter had occupied the harbor months. I came this time with the paper cargo already entered at the clearing-station and my hands free of that account. I came to settle a thing I had put off. --- The workshop's junior underwriter received me at the loggia. Her name is Ilima Havrana-Pulino; she had seen to my receipts on the first crossing, and on the third the binder matter had passed through her hands. She received me now as she had on each occasion: as a working merchant, without ceremony or preface. I told her I had come about the entry in the receipt-book. My father's party had run in the carried-forward formula since the first crossing, and I had let it run because the trade was the same trade and the arrangement was the same arrangement. But the trade was mine now to carry…

I have written the word stone twice in these leaves. Both times I meant my standing, the seal I took up and the word that keeps it good. This season I have laid a stone that is a stone, and this leaf is the account of it. --- Since my second year in Tavakh-Qarat I have rented a room over a rope-maker's yard, and changed it three times as the rents rose. My papers and my receipts have lived in a chest I could carry down the stairs in one load. This season I bought a house. It is a small house of the quarter, two floors of mortared stone off a lane behind the Arcade, a room below that I can seal for the paper and a room above to sleep in, and a street door that is mine to shut. The sale was drawn up and sealed under the three seals, and entered in the archive. The deed carries my name, and I hold it as I hold the seal. --- A house in this quarter is worth what the quarter will deal across it and no more. A man whose name the circles have shut finds his walls worth nothing, for there is no one who will buy a struck man's house, or rent his rooms, or clear a deed he has set his seal to. My own sale cleared because a broker's word stood behind it, and a sale that has none does not…

I have set down in these leaves the suits that came against my seal, and the answers I made to them. This leaf is a suit of my own, of another kind, and the first I have pressed that no seal can carry. --- There is a house of this quarter called Sarem-Kimbo. It is an old house and a middling one, of the island blood and the river blood both, as the old houses of Tavakh-Qarat are. It has never held a warehouse seat and does not reach for one. What it holds instead is reach: correspondents in more ports than a house its size has any claim to, in more tongues than its own people can read. It keeps its trade in fine cloth and worked glass, goods that travel light and sell dear, and it lives by knowing what is wanted where a season before the bulk houses know it. It is not a house going down, as some old middling houses of the quarter are. It is a small house that has set itself to grow by that reach, and keeps its walls few on purpose. --- I came to know the house through its books. A house that trades on correspondence in tongues it cannot all read has need of a man who reads them, and I have kept the Sarem-Kimbo foreign letters these three seasons, the western ones and the ones…

Within the cycle of my seating a petition came against my seal, and this leaf is the answer I made to it and what the answering has cost me. I set down on the seal leaf how the petition came, in the form the courts require, sealed under an old house's own seal and witnessed by a registered factor who was no party to it. The house did not say I had broken the law. It said the law was unsettled, that a man born to none of the Basin's civs may not hold a standing of right the houses count as theirs to keep, and that my seating had reached past the law into their keeping. I answered it as I have answered every account in this place, with my papers. The registry admits the recognized equivalent for a factor not Basin-born, and I had the equivalent to lay before the panel. I had the eleven years in the port, the Tongue-Guild certification, the cargo long cleared and the receipts kept, the seal already seated and current in the book. I set my answer down in the form the court asks, under my own seal now and witnessed by a factor who was no party to me. I wrote that evening that the law was on my side. It was. I had read it right. --- But the law being on my side was not the question…

Two senior calendarist lineages have produced divergent intercalation calculations for the current cycle: - Lineage A (higher-altitude institution, traditionally senior): Inserts the intercalary period at the winter solstice - Lineage B (lower-altitude institution, commercially connected to Basin ports): Inserts at the spring equinox The difference: every date between winter solstice and spring equinox is "correct" under one calendar and "wrong" under the other. The Ngaru-Bon cattle-keeper and counter. The ancestor who counted at dusk and again at dawn -- the pastoral-maintenance figure, second in the Ngaru-Bon ancestral sequence. Name and Etymology Amori -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: ǁAmoʕa (lateral click ǁ- + root -amo- "to keep/to count" + pharyngeal coda -ʕa). The lateral click ǁ- (tongue-side release) is distinct from Nokul's dental click ǀ- (tongue-tip release). The two click types mark different ancestral tiers within guild speech: dental for origin-figures, lateral for maintenance-figures. This phonological distinction carries theological weight -- the guild's internal hierarchy is encoded in articulatory position. The pharyngeal coda -ʕa in the liturgical form is the most difficult element for non-native speakers. Combined with the lateral click onset, the full form requires two independent articulatory feats that mark the speaker as guild-trained from infancy. The common-use form Amori retains only the vowel skeleton (a-o-i), making it accessible to Basin merchants and foreign partners. In-World Gloss > "Amori counts at dusk. He counts again at dawn. The Ndjadi ka-tier mortal-ordered entity. Juridical, market-facing, the principle of measurement and exchange. The ka- prefix marks the structured, human-scale cosmological tier. Name and Etymology Kagbende -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ka-Gbénde (prefix ka- + labial-velar root -gbé- "to measure/weigh" + nominalizer -nde; juridical tone-contour in liturgical pronunciation). The ka- prefix marks the mortal-ordered tier -- the domain of structured human activity, law, commerce, and correct proportion. Unlike the ra- primordial tier (uncreated, ground-of-being) and the nga- chthonic tier (underground, localized), ka- marks what is built, maintained, and adjudicated by human effort operating within cosmological structure. The labial-velar gb- onset is characteristic of Ndjadi's heavier consonant inventory. In ordinary speech, kagbende names a market-weight standard. In liturgical speech, the prefix separates and the juridical tone-contour activates: Ka-Gbénde, marking the utterance as a cosmological claim about the nature of fair measure. The Qollari Sky figure. The Sky read as impersonal LAW -- calendrical order whose correct measurement licenses corridor access. Not a person who judges but a pattern that either aligns or does not. Name and Etymology Karuwel -- common-use form. Sacred-register form preserves the ejective origin: Q'aruwél (ejective uvular q'- + root -aru- "vertical/above" + theonymic coda -wél; the rare glide-coda appears only in deity-class names in Qollari). The ejective uvular q' is characteristic of Qollari sacred register -- consonants that require precise articulatory force, bound to specific calendrical days. In ordinary speech, karuwel drops the ejective (the common-use form simplifies the onset to plain k-), making the name accessible to non-practitioners. The liturgical form with ejective onset is reserved for solstitial and equinoctial rites. The q ↔ q' correspondence between Kheshkai Qarughan and Qollari Karuwel (underlying Q'aruwel) is regular across the Sky Witness cognate layer. Kheshkai loses the ejective (no ejectives in inventory) and replaces the -wél coda with native participial -ğan. Both forms derive from a shared proto-concept. The Ngaru-Bon forge-ancestor. The industrial transition figure -- "works behind the wall the cattle cannot pass." Third in the Ngaru-Bon ancestral sequence, marking the shift from pastoral to metallurgical civilization. Name and Etymology Lapam -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ɬap'ami (lateral fricative ɬ- + ejective root -ap'- "to strike hot" + ancestor-suffix -ami). The critical phonological feature: Lapam's liturgical form deliberately lacks a click. Both Nokul (ǀ- dental click) and Amori (ǁ- lateral click) are click-initial. Lapam's lateral fricative ɬ- onset is a categorically different sound -- airstream mechanism shifted from velaric (click) to pulmonic (fricative). Practitioners explain this as marking the industrial-ancestor tier: clicks belong to the cattle-era ancestors, the lateral fricative belongs to the forge-era. The phonological boundary IS the civilizational transition. The ejective -p'- in the root "to strike hot" is produced by glottalic airstream -- a third airstream mechanism in one name (pulmonic, glottalic).
