The Oravan dyadic figure. Two aspects, not two gods. The ocean and the hearth are the same hand. Name and Etymology Maawara -- base mawara "salt-mother-water" with sacred vowel-length on root. Two aspect-epithets: - Maawara Taasi (ocean aspect) -- taasi "long salt" - Maawara Apii (hearth aspect) -- apii "inner flame"; never reduplicated (reduplication would demote to household-familiar status) The sacred vowel-length (maa- rather than ma-) is the register-mark. In ordinary speech, mawara means simply "salt-water." The lengthened form enters the sacred register of Oravan artisan-priests. This is an innovative feature, not inherited -- the Qalībin's counter-argument against cognacy with Ndjadi Ramwen rests partly on this point. In-World Gloss > "She who salts the bowl and lights the bowl. Same hand." This is the foundational liturgical phrase, spoken at every workshop initiation. It encodes the dual-aspect doctrine: salt (ocean) and fire (hearth/volcanic) are not opposites balanced against each other but the same creative-destructive force expressed in two media. Islands are born from fire and salt simultaneously; fleets are destroyed by the same combination. Theological…

The Ndjadi nga-tier chthonic entity. River-bends, underground waters, the places where flow forgets its direction. The nga- prefix marks the localized, earthbound, subterranean cosmological tier. Name and Etymology Ngandim -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Nga-Ndímba (prefix nga- + prenasalized root -ndím- "to coil/river-bend" + class marker -ba; breathy medial vowel in liturgical pronunciation). The nga- prefix marks the chthonic tier -- underground, localized, site-specific. Where ra- (Ramwen) names the uncreated source and ka- (Kagbende) names the mortal-ordered structure, nga- names what has sunk below, coiled back, or become bound to a specific place. The prefix is the same one used for localized spirits (nga-beli) in everyday Ndjadi, which creates a deliberate taxonomic ambiguity: is Ngandim a deity or the largest spirit? Scribal colleges disagree. The prenasalized cluster nd- plus the breathy medial in liturgical form make this the most phonologically marked of the three tier-figures in sacred-register speech. Ordinary pronunciation (ngandim) drops the breathy quality and the class suffix, collapsing the liturgical complexity into a manageable proper noun.…

The Ngaru-Bon first-ancestor. Cattle-origin figure -- "struck the first hollow" that cattle answered. The founding act of Ngaru-Bon civilization is an acoustic event: a hollow struck, an animal responding before a person could. Name and Etymology Nokul -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: ǀNoɬa (dental click ǀ- + root -noɬ- "to stretch a skin/to hollow" + class marker -a; the click IS the name in liturgical speech). The radical simplification from ǀNoɬa to Nokul demonstrates the sacred-register concept perfectly: the liturgical form requires a dental click and lateral fricative that non-Ngaru-Bon speakers cannot produce. The common-use form strips these to accessible consonants (n-, -k-, -l), making the name speakable across the continent. Ngaru-Bon practitioners consider the common form a convenience, not the real name -- "you say Nokul; we say what he is." The dental click ǀ- in the liturgical form is the most significant phoneme. Clicks enter Ngaru-Bon infants through parental speech from birth; the acquisition window closes in early childhood. An adult learner can approximate but never achieve the articulatory precision required for sacred-register use. This is not…

The Oravan Fire-House figure. The fire at the center of the house, the roof-beam junction, the domestic hearth. Not Maawara's hearth-aspect -- a separate, older entity. Name and Etymology Pulino -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Pulinaa (puli "pillar-wood" + agentive -na + sacred length -aa). The sacred length -aa marks the register boundary. In ordinary speech, pulino names the central roof-beam junction of a traditional Oravan house. The lengthened liturgical form Pulinaa enters artisan-priest speech only during construction rites and hearth-lighting. Reduplication is forbidden. Where Oravan sacred register typically intensifies through reduplication (e.g., tama tama → taa-ma taa-ma), Pulino resists this pattern. Workshop-lineages explain this differently -- some say reduplication would "spread the fire beyond the house" (catastrophe), others that Pulino is too old for the reduplication system (pre-Water-Covenant claim). The prohibition itself is universal across all workshop-lineages even where the explanation diverges. In-World Gloss > "Pulino stands where the four roof-beams meet. Do not set the pot on her." This phrase is spoken during hearth-lighting ceremonies.…

The Kheshkai Sky figure. The ONE named high entity in Kheshkai theology. Not a god who blesses or curses -- a presence that notes. The Sky as impersonal WILL read through shamanistic interpretation. Name and Etymology Qarughan -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Qaruğan (back-harmony root qar- "that-which-watches-from-above" + -uğ- abstract-elevation suffix + participial -an; uvular q + velar-fricative ğ in liturgical pronunciation). The back-harmony vowel pattern (a-o-a) is characteristic of Kheshkai sacred speech. The language's vowel-harmony system -- where an oath in perfect harmony binds and a broken-harmony oath is a non-oath -- makes the phonological form itself load-bearing. Qarughan's name is, in this sense, already a correctly-formed utterance: the harmonious back-vowel chain enacts the binding it names. In ordinary steppe speech, qarughan serves as an impersonal construction: "it is noted," "it is watched." The participial -an ending gives it the quality of ongoing observation rather than completed act. The sky is always noting. For Kheshkai speakers, this is not metaphor -- it is a literal description of how the Sky works. In-World Gloss > "Qarughan does not…

The Qollari Ancestor-Stone figure. Mountain-facing, genealogical. The ancestor who became stone, whose back is every road. Reflects Qollari's membership in the Ancestor-Stone complex alongside their Sky-Mandate membership. Name and Etymology Qullpar -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Qhullpar (aspirated uvular qh- + root -ull- "set-in-place/weighted" + agentive -par; geminate -ll- + stop cluster tolerated only for ancestor-class names in Qollari phonotactics). The aspirated uvular qh- distinguishes ancestor-class names from sky-class names (which use ejective q'-). This phonological distinction IS a theological one: ejective onset = sky-tier, aspirated onset = stone-tier. The common-use form Qullpar neutralizes the aspiration, making the name accessible outside liturgical contexts. The geminate -ll- plus stop cluster (-llp-) is phonotactically heavy -- permitted only in ancestor-class proper nouns. Ordinary Qollari words avoid this combination. The weight of the consonant cluster is (practitioners say) iconic: the name is heavy because the ancestor is heavy. Stone names sound like stone. In-World Gloss > "Qullpar's face is turned into the mountain. His back is every…

The Ndjadi ra-tier primordial entity. Not a person in the Oravan sense -- a grammaticalized cosmological position. The ra- prefix IS the theological claim. Name and Etymology Ramwen -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ra-Mwéne (prefix ra- + prenasalized root -mwén- "to open/source" + class marker -e; high-tone penult in liturgical pronunciation). The ra- prefix marks the primordial cosmological tier in Ndjadi grammatical theology. Three tiers exist: - ra- -- primordial, uncreated, ground-of-being - ka- -- mortal-ordered, structured, juridical - nga- -- chthonic, underground, localized Ramwen occupies the highest tier. In ordinary Ndjadi speech, ramwen functions as a proper noun without active prefix analysis. In liturgical speech, the prefix is stressed and separated: Ra-Mwéne, foregrounding the cosmological claim. Scribal-priests who use the wrong tier-prefix for this figure are not making a grammar error -- they are making a theological error with (practitioners say) cosmological consequences. In-World Gloss > "Ra-Mwéne opens her mouth at the delta; her teeth are the sandbars." This liturgical phrase is spoken during delta-mouth rites at the seasonal flood's arrival.…

Irrah ancestor figure. Explicitly NOT a deity -- classified as ancestor by Qalībin, keeping Irrah's structural rule: no named high deity. The Great Sealer, who stamps the tomb-brick. The highest-ranked named figure in Irrah, and still only an ancestor. Name and Etymology Tabbaq -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Ṭabbāʕ (√ṭ-b-ʕ "to stamp/to impress a seal" in intensive-agent pattern CaC₁C₁āC₂ → "the Great Stamper/Sealer"). The triconsonantal root system is characteristic of Irrah's Qalib sacred register. The intensive-agent pattern (CaC₁C₁āC₂) doubles the middle radical and lengthens the final vowel, marking the form as denoting someone who performs the action professionally and intensively -- not someone who once stamped, but "the one whose nature is stamping." The common-use form Tabbaq simplifies the emphatic ṭ- to plain t- and the pharyngeal coda -ʕ to plain -q (uvular stop substituted for the pharyngeal fricative -- a regular simplification in Basin trade speech). The full liturgical form requires the emphatic and pharyngeal articulations that mark trained Qalib speakers. The root √ṭ-b-ʕ belongs to the oath-binder profession's phonotactic subset. Only oath-binders…

Disposal: Desert burial in raised tower-tombs and cairns, strung into funerary avenues that link oases and cluster at permanent water sources. The Rite In the Irrah drylands the dead are buried in stone chambers raised above the sand, shaped from the same rock that holds the wells. A body is washed, wrapped, and placed in the chamber with its face turned toward the route its lineage traveled, and the chamber is sealed under a tower-tomb or a low cairn depending on wealth and rank. The tombs are not scattered. They line the caravan avenues that run between oases, so that a traveler moving from well to well passes through corridors of the dead. The densest tombs stand at the permanent water sources, where several avenues meet and where the living must still pause to drink. Mourning is brief at the grave but renewed at each caravan season, when offerings are left at the avenue tombs before a major journey. Afterlife and Ancestors Irrah belief holds that the dead remain connected to the Five Waters, especially the hidden Tenth Water that once moved in their bodies. In the Five-Waters necropolis cult, the ancestors buried along an avenue are understood to keep the route open and the…

Disposal: Barrow burial under a raised earthen mound on the open steppe, accompanied by sacrificed horses, portable grave-goods, and, for the highest elite, a buried retinue. The Rite A Kheshkai death on the steppe interrupts the seasonal movement of the clan. The body is prepared, dressed in its best wool and gold, and placed in a wooden chamber dug into a chosen rise while kin drive horses and cattle to the site. Horses are sacrificed at the barrow's edge, their bones arranged so that the dead may ride, and the chamber is sealed beneath a mound of turf and stone that will stand long after the tents have moved on. The funeral lasts until the mound is complete, sometimes many days for a great khan, and ends with a feast and the swearing of oaths at the barrow's foot. For common clanspeople the mound is smaller, the goods fewer, and the rites shorter, but the shape is the same: a fixed mark made by a mobile people. Afterlife and Ancestors Kheshkai belief holds that the sky receives the worthy dead. The barrow is not a grave in the lowland sense but a launching place: the dead lord lies with his horses, his weapons, and his people, ready to enter the sky-order that Qarughan…

Disposal: Secondary processing in a charnel structure, followed by interment in or beneath a communal earthwork mound on the floodplain. The Rite When an Ndjadi householder dies, the body is first laid in a charnel house near the lineage compound while kin gather and the scribes begin the mourning record. After a period that may last from several weeks to a full season, the remains are gathered, sometimes bundled with selected bones of earlier dead from the same house, and placed within or beneath the lineage mound. The mound itself is not a single grave but a layered monument: each new burial adds earth, and the height and width of a mound record the accumulated deaths and labor of a kin-group. Mourning continues through planting and harvest rites, when the dead are addressed as part of the river-order that governs the delta. Afterlife and Ancestors Ndjadi belief holds that the dead do not leave the river-order. They sink into the same earth the river renews each flood, and from that earth they continue to anchor their kin-group in the cosmic grammar of the Water-Covenant. The mound is understood as a vertical charnel-house, with older dead deeper and newer dead higher, each…

Disposal: Two registers governed by plateau scarcity: excarnation and sky-exposure for most, and rock-hewn burial inside a sacred monumental complex for the elite. The Rite On the high plateau wood is too scarce to burn a body and the ground is too hard to dig graves for everyone, so the dead of ordinary households are carried to an exposed stone platform and laid out for the air and the birds. The flesh is removed from the world in the natural order of height, and the bones are gathered afterward for placement in a cairn or a niche. For kings, great smith-lords, and the founders of guild-lines, the body is instead carried into the rock-church complex and interred in a hewn chamber within the consecrated stone. The difference is not only rank but access to metal: the elite burial requires tools, labor, and guild authorization that common households cannot command. Mourning lasts until the commemorative feast is held, sometimes a year after death, when the land-grant that funds it is publicly confirmed. Afterlife and Ancestors Ngaru-Bon belief holds that the ancestor is literally in the worked material. For the sky-exposed dead, the bones return to the stone of the plateau; for…

Disposal: Collective burial in a shared lineage tomb, with secondary treatment of bones and a maritime strand in which the dead are sent toward the sea. The Rite When an Oravan householder dies, the body is first laid on a stone shelf in the lineage tomb while kin bring oil, wine, and the first fruits appropriate to the season. After the flesh has gone, the bones are gathered, and selected skulls and long bones are arranged in clay chests or niches along the tomb walls. The tomb itself is reused across generations, sometimes for centuries, so that a single chamber holds the dead of a whole lineage. For those who die at sea, the body is committed to the water from a boat, and a small clay token bearing the lineage mark is placed in the tomb instead. Mourning is marked by recurring gatherings at the tomb, not by a single funeral, and the largest gatherings coincide with the calmer sailing seasons when many kin are ashore. Afterlife and Ancestors Oravan belief holds that the dead remain present in the lineage tomb and that the sea carries what must travel. The Fire-House cult fuses volcanic fire with oceanic water, so that death is understood as a passage from the hearth into the…

Each of the six civilizations does something different with its dead, and each does it for reasons that cannot be settled. This layer documents disposal, mourning, the funerary economy, and who officiates, across all six. It does not settle whether the dead persist. That question is held open on purpose. The Undecidable Dead The reality of the afterlife is permanently undecidable in Veydria, exactly as the sacred registers are (see and ADR-0026). No funerary practice confirms that the dead hear, own, or answer, and none confirms that they are simply gone. Every per-civ file therefore carries two readings that the data layer never adjudicates: - a practitioner's reading, in which the dead persist and must be served, kept, or consulted, and the rite does real work; - a skeptic's reading, in which the practice is doing inheritance, succession, social memory, and legitimacy work, materially and without remainder. This is the four-layer ambiguity of (Design Rail 2, no confirmed deities; Rail 7, ambiguity preserved) extended to mortality. The practitioner's reading is carried by the believers in the file; the skeptic's reading is carried by the naturalists every Veydrian tradition…

Disposal: Highland cold desiccation, wrapping, and curation; the dead lineage-head remains a present social person rather than an interred memory. The Rite The Qollari highlands do not favor decay. Cold, dry air above the terraced valleys draws moisture from a corpse faster than burial would hide it, so the body is cleaned, desiccated, wrapped in dyed cloth, and seated in a dry niche within the lineage house or a small ancestral chamber. The wrapping is not a farewell but a preparation: the dead continue to sit at council, to receive offerings, and to be addressed on matters of land and succession. Mourning lasts through one full agricultural cycle, during which the household suspends major decisions until the preserved head has been formally consulted. A younger heir may be invested with office before the cycle ends, but the property itself remains spoken of as belonging to the seated dead. Afterlife and Ancestors Qollari belief holds that the dead do not depart. A preserved lineage-head is tended as one who still hears, still owns, and still answers through the intermediaries who keep him. This is the Ancestor-Stone principle made literal in flesh: the ancestor is a fixed…

The Aethelian Basin has no calendar. This is not an absence. It is an architecture. Where other civilizations declare time — the Qollari priesthood through khipu intercalation, the Oravan priestess-queen through solstice consecration, the Irrah scholar through isnād-certified star-reading — the Basin receives time. Four ports host six foreign calendars and compose from their overlap a commercial rhythm that no single civilization authored and none can unilaterally amend. The Basin's temporal authority is procedural, not declarative. It does not ask which calendar is correct. It asks which contract was sealed with the seven-stroke Filer's Hand before witnesses who remained for the full cadence. The Composite Year The Basin does not count years. It counts rotations. A Basin "year" is the complete circuit of the Triple-Seal Arbitration Court through four port zones — Tavakh-Qarat, Ki-Mbuhari, Halani-Tamu, Dzong-Tamu — each hosted at the season when that port's ecological and administrative conditions are most stable. The Court packs its seals, its witness-rosters, and its senior arbitrators' personal familiarity with each port's variant of the Filer's Hand, and moves. A…

A loose fraternity of skeptical scholars concentrated in Aethelian port cities. Not an institution in the strict sense -- no hierarchy, no initiation, no buildings. A network of people who share a specific intellectual position: the sacred registers work, but calling their effects "divine" is a category error. Tamah bint Sarqaf The founder-figure. Her treatise On the Breath of Stones (c. 80 years before the playable present) argues: 1. Ghilan are observable ecological entities -- marsh-lights, cave pressure-anomalies, canyon acoustic echoes -- without moral stance toward humans 2. Sacred-register magic produces real, costly, ambiguous effects explicable as learned acoustic-psychological engineering 3. Therefore, calling these phenomena "divine" is a category error Tamah does not deny the sacred register works. She denies its theological interpretation. This is closer to Xenophanes and Carvaka than to modern atheism. She is not saying "there are no gods." She is saying "what you call gods are natural phenomena that we happen to interact with through trained phonological performance." Tamah herself was, per surviving accounts, personally vindictive and professionally corrupt. Her…

The Irrah year is not declared. It is certified. Twelve months indexed to Azmarāʔ star-readings exist in parallel across the oasis-courts, each computation independently derived, each valid if its scholar's isnād-chain is unbroken. There is no single calendar. There are many calendars, and their agreement is institutionally normal. This distributed architecture is the deep inversion of Qollari. Where Qollari has one declared system whose schism is catastrophic because everyone is on it, Irrah has many certified systems whose divergence is the default state. A caravan-master who departs on the date certified by one Azmarāʔ scholar and arrives at a Basin port where another scholar's computation prevails does not experience a crisis. He experiences the ordinary texture of Irrah time. The Azmarāʔ Star-Readings as Year Anchor The year's master rhythm is solar-astronomical, computed from star-positions observed at each oasis-court venue. The Azmarāʔ sub-register — the Qalībin path-finders who own the glottalic and uvural phonological monopoly — transmits the computation methodology through isnād-chains that connect every certifying scholar back through named teachers to the…

The Kheshkai do not have a calendar. This is not an absence. It is a doctrine. "Basin calendars are paper and paper does not know the grass." The Oral-Memory Council's senior speaker delivered this ruling six master-shaman transmission cycles ago, in response to a Khazadari clerk who proposed that the Council's pasture-rotation hearings be transcribed into Basin contract notation. The ruling stands. The Council has refused every subsequent proposal for written codification — from Tongue-Guild basin-port translators, from Ndjadi scribal reformers, from Qollari khipu-record keepers who argued that the Three-Year Skyward required a shared temporal notation. This file documents the refusal. It is not a calendar in the Qollari or Ndjadi sense. It is an account of how a civilization keeps time without keeping records. The Oral-Memory Council The Aman-Sanah Zövlöl is the only authoritative record of Kheshkai time. Its membership is not fixed. Any clan elder who has witnessed three pasture-rotation hearings may speak. Any master-shaman who has completed a transmission cycle may challenge a ruling. The Council convenes at the autumn festival circuit, at the spring thaw campaign…

Legitimize but cannot constrain. Their confederation-consensus structure means when a khan wins, the argument ends; when he loses, shamans switch sides. They set up no permanent institutions. They travel with caravans, witness on the move, collect fees, vanish. How They Work Sky-shamans diagnose Qarughan's will retroactively. They do not predict outcomes -- they interpret them after the fact. A khan wins a battle; the shaman confirms the sky approved. A khan's horse dies on the morning of a raid; the shaman advises retreat. The diagnosis is always post-hoc, which makes it unfalsifiable and structurally honest: the shaman never promises what the sky will do, only reads what it meant. The shaman is identified by "hearing-gift" -- often individuals with perfect pitch or exceptional sensitivity to harmonic patterns. Training is master-to-apprentice on horseback, oral-only, with no scribal tradition. Every generation re-negotiates orthodoxy because there is no text to anchor it. A shaman's authority is personal and contingent, not institutional. Vowel-Harmony as Binding Grammar Kheshkai magic uses vowel-harmony as a binding grammar: an oath in perfect harmony binds; a broken-harmony…

The Ndjadi year is not a circle. It is a pulse — a single annual flood that rises, crests, recedes, and leaves the land either sown or hungry. There is no spring, no summer, no autumn, no winter. There is only the flood, the recession, the growing, and the hungry gap. The calendar is hydrology, not astronomy. The Flood as Year Anchor The year begins when the Floodwatch Augmented Bureaucracy publishes the flood-window prediction. This is not a celebration. It is a ruling. The prediction classifies the coming year as "ordinary," "heavy," or "low" flood, and that classification determines the levy schedule, the harvest-guarantee underwriting terms, and the volume of prefix-notarization the Court of the Three Mouths will process. The prediction is based on gauge-readings from a network of upstream stations whose data is compiled by the Floodwatch and ratified at the River-Lord House Assembly convened the week after publication. The Assembly elects a rotating speaker; the Floodwatch does not vote. The classification is technically determined and not subject to commercial override — though three upstream irrigation districts have disputed the "ordinary" designation for the current…

The people who certify correct speech. Since correct speech IS prayer, the scribes who control certification hold a functional veto over any public act that requires liturgical authorization. They are notaries, priests, and cosmological regulators in one institution. The Grammatical Mechanism Ndjadi sacred grammar maps a three-tier cosmological order onto every noun through prefixes: - ra- -- primordial tier (the oldest, most fundamental things: the delta itself, the original water, the foundational concepts) - ka- -- mortal-ordered tier (human institutions, tools, settlements, everything made by living people) - nga- -- chthonic tier (underground, ancestral, spirit-level entities) A misapplied prefix is not a grammar error. It is a cosmological miscategorization with consequences. The canonical teaching-case parallels the Vedic indrashatru accent disaster: a word intended to mean one thing means its opposite when the accent (or in Ndjadi's case, the prefix) falls wrong. Calling a primordial entity by the chthonic prefix doesn't merely insult it -- it reclassifies it, and the reclassification persists. This is the strongest Veydria-specific invention in the whole religion…

The Ngaru-Bon year has two scales. The short scale — what merchants and farmers use — is a solar year of twelve months, anchored to the msasa red leaf-flush and the cool-dry-winter smelting-season opening. The long scale — what matters — is counted in ancestor-smith tier promotions: Nokul, Amori, Lapam. A generation is not a span of time. It is a name that may refer to one mortal, a sequence of inheritors, or a fiction the Outside-Forge Network maintains for institutional continuity. Neither the Inner Council nor outsiders can determine which without disrupting the institutional position. The Smelting Season as Year Anchor The year's most important transition is not the sowing, though the msasa's red leaf-flush signals it. The year's most important transition is the opening of the cool-dry-winter smelting season, when the bloomeries relight and iron is made. This is when the continent's steel supply is determined. The Inner Council's consecration schedule gates the year's production. Each bloomery operation must be preceded by a reconsecration rite whose timing is set by the Council's ritual bell, click-register access, and forge-temple grain allocation. A bloom that fires…

Legitimize by constraint. The guild controls both ritual and military production. Their Investiture-Controversy-style interdict is a forge-strike -- refusing to produce weapons or reconsecrate tools. Great Zimbabwe's dzimbahwe logic: rainmaker kings depend on ancestor-sanctioned regalia that the guild makes. The Guild Structure The ancestor-smith guild is patrilineal and hereditary. Membership is by birth into a guild family, apprenticeship beginning in infancy. The guild is not a priesthood -- smiths are craftspeople whose craft happens to be sacred. The distinction matters: they do not preach, do not maintain temples, do not perform public rituals. They forge, and the forging IS the ritual. The guild controls: - Weapon production. Every blade, spearhead, and piece of armor on the plateau passes through guild forges. Unforged metal is not weaponry -- it is raw material. - Tool reconsecration. Agricultural and mining tools must be periodically reconsecrated through forge-chanting. A tool whose consecration has lapsed is ritually inert -- farmers and miners believe it works less well, and in a world where the ambiguity devices prevent certainty, they may be right. - Regalia…

The Oravan year is not computed. It is performed. The priestess-queen's body at the solstice Tavamala Consecration is the only instrument capable of opening the sailing year, and her physical absence — whether by death, dispute, or cyclone — closes it. There are no archivists, no knot-records, no star-tables. There is only the ocean-salt register on her left hand and the hearth-fire register on her right, and the declaration she makes when both are present. This makes the Oravan calendar the most fragile on the continent. A succession crisis is never merely political. It is a calendrical suspension during which convoys cannot sail insured, the Harbor Covenant's wave-tithe receipt-book cannot be stamped, and the Three-Cove Concord's parallel pricing circulars gain commercial force precisely because the official calendar has stopped. The Monsoon as Year Anchor The year's master rhythm is bimodal: the wet northwest monsoon brings convective rain and breadfruit fruiting through the lunar months the islanders call the "water quarter"; the drier southeast trade season opens the clove-nutmeg harvest and the canoe-voyaging window. Between them lie the cyclone shoulders — the transition…

The priestess-queen IS the dual aspect of Sea-and-Fire in her body. The palace doesn't need divine sanction; it is the divine manifest in office. Every succession dispute is simultaneously a theological one. This is the civ most vulnerable to schism-as-civil-war. The Fusion Model Oravan palace-priestesses operate on the Fifth Dalai Lama's Ganden Phodrang model (1642): spiritual and temporal authority collapse into one office. The priestess-queen does not rule by divine right -- she rules because the office IS the goddess in institutional form. When an Oravan priestess taxes a harbor, the tax IS the liturgy. There is no church-state separation because the distinction does not exist. The palace functions as the largest artisan-workshop. Artisan-priests work under the priestess-queen's authority, combining craft-production with sacred-register invocation. Every significant craft act is a ritual act. Every ritual act is an economic act. Workshop Pluralism No single Oravan priesthood controls all sacred practice. Each island's dominant workshop-lineages hold their own pronunciation traditions for the reduplication-based sacred register and routinely accuse each other of "sloppy…

The Irrah water-scholar order. A quietist institution whose doctrinal restraint is precisely what makes it the richest and most geographically pervasive religious body on the continent. The Quietist Creed "Water does not serve one house." The foundational principle is structural, not merely pious. The Qalībin holds that the Five Waters -- surface, underground, sky, dew, and the Tenth Water (bodily/hidden) -- are cosmological categories that exist prior to civilization and cannot be owned, directed, or enlisted by any political authority. A water-scholar who places the order's resources at the service of a specific house, faction, or war has misunderstood the nature of water itself. This is a Veydrian analog of the Suwarian tradition (al-Hajj Salim Suwari's quietist precepts among the Soninke/Jakhanke/Juula/Dyula merchant-clerical diaspora) combined with the Sanusiyya zawiya network (Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi's 146 lodges by c. 1900). The Qalībin is a scholarly order like the rabbinate or ulama, not a hierarchy with a capital. There is no Qalībin caliph. A vertical hierarchy that legitimizes and constrains in one move. Trade-corridor access IS calendrical access. The calendar-priesthood functions like the Delphic Oracle as inter-polis arbitrator: opacity is power. The Calendar as Genealogy The Qollari calendar is not merely an astronomical instrument. It is a genealogical record. Dead lineages become fixed points in the sky -- stars, constellations, eclipse-recurrence positions. The calendar's accuracy is simultaneously scientific achievement and ancestor-honoring. Correcting the calendar means revising the genealogical record. This is what makes calendar-reform scandals politically explosive. When rival calendar-keeper lineages dispute an intercalation (whether to add a corrective day to prevent drift), they are simultaneously disputing whose ancestors occupy which celestial positions. An intercalation error is both an astronomical mistake and an insult to specific dead lineages. Ejective-Calendrical Magic Qollari magic is calendrical: ejective consonants bind to specific days in a ritual calendar. Uvulars are reserved for solstitial rites. A specialist produces consonants the population can also produce -- the real monopoly…

Veydrian religion is four overlapping traditions resting on a shared pre-civilizational substrate, not six parallel belief systems. No central authority governs any tradition. No deity is confirmed to exist. No civilization maps cleanly to one religion. The political logic follows phonology: magic is culture-locked and untranslatable, so every question about divine power routes through training pipelines, pronunciation authority, and cross-register jurisdiction. Oravan monsoon-reversal pilgrimage. Every Aethelian port with an Oravan trade-quarter sends ships home to the First Caldera -- a seawater-filled volcanic crater that is literally the dyad's cult-site. The ritual calendar IS the sailing calendar. Route and Timing The circuit follows the biannual monsoon reversal. Outbound: northeast monsoon carries ships from Aethelian ports toward the archipelago. Return: southwest monsoon brings them back. The timing is non-negotiable -- miss the monsoon window and you wait six months or risk open-ocean sailing without wind-support. This means the pilgrimage is structurally identical to the trade cycle. Every merchant vessel making the monsoon crossing is potentially a pilgrim vessel. Every pilgrim vessel carries cargo. The distinction between commerce and devotion does not exist in Oravan practice -- the wave-tithe paid to port priestesshoods is simultaneously a religious insurance premium and a commercial fee. The Wave-Tithe Economy Oravan palace-priestesshoods at each port skim a wave-tithe on blessed cargo. The mechanism: - Ships departing under priestess-blessing pay the tithe (typically a percentage of cargo value) - Blessed ships carry…

The Aethelian's main religious-and-trade axis: Ndjadi habal-copyists undertake a "correction pilgrimage" to Irrah pyramid-necropolises to collate their sacred prefixes against pre-reform attestations. The route strings through Aethelian entrepot copy-houses, crosses Irrah caravan lanes under Qalībin path-finder protection, and returns with necropolis-blessed amulet-bound copies. Route and Timing A slow dry-season caravan. The route: 1. Departure: Ndjadi delta copy-houses (habal scribes assemble correction-lists) 2. Aethelian transit: Through Basin entrepot cities, stopping at each city's copy-house to collate local variants 3. Desert crossing: Into Irrah territory under Qalībin path-finder escort (the only legally recognized escorts through ghilan-inhabited territory) 4. Necropolis terminus: Irrah pyramid-necropolises where pre-reform inscription attestations are preserved in tomb-brick stamps 5. Return: Same route, carrying necropolis-blessed corrected copies The timing is seasonal (dry-season caravans only) and annual (one major pilgrimage cycle per year, with smaller correction-missions between). A triennial Kheshkai-Qollari cycle tied to a sky-calendar conjunction both civilizations half-share. Sky-shamans drive sacrificial horse herds into cloud-forest passes for a joint ritual at the Breath-of-Cloud sanctuary -- the one fixed window each three years when the Qollari corridor is guaranteed open to Kheshkai caravans. Timing and Mechanism The triennial cycle is determined by a sky-calendar conjunction that both the Kheshkai and Qollari recognize independently: - Kheshkai reckoning: Shamanic interpretation of a specific star-cluster position (observed from open steppe) - Qollari reckoning: Calendrical computation from khipu-records (calculated in mountain observatories) Both arrive at the same three-year window by different methods -- the convergence is the theological content. Kheshkai shamans call this "the Sky noting twice." Qollari calendarists call it "the calendar confirming itself." The Breath-of-Cloud Sanctuary A high-altitude site at the Kheshkai-Qollari border where cloud forest meets steppe. The only permanent cross-civ sacred site in Veydria. A charismatic shaman -- Tegu Bokh (PROPOSAL) -- preaching that there is ONE sky and therefore ONE correct liturgy, and the confederation's polyvocal practice is degeneration. This ignites only under ecological trigger (a bad-grass decade, a horse-plague read as divine judgment on shamanistic disunity). Status: LATENT in the playable present. Activates under ecological pressure. The Argument Tegu Bokh's position: The Sky is one. Correct liturgy is one. The confederation's tradition of multiple shamanic interpretations (each generation renegotiating orthodoxy, each master transmitting their own variant) is not pluralism but degradation. The bad-grass years, the horse-plague, the military setbacks -- these are the Sky's response to liturgical chaos. Unity of practice will restore alignment. Traditional shamanic response: The Sky notes differently at different times. Multiple interpretations are not disagreement but attentiveness to the Sky's changing position. A single liturgy would freeze observation into dogma. The bad-grass years are weather, not judgment. Habal copy-service scribes producing vernacular-glossed sacred-prefix editions. The scribal-cosmological priesthood condemns this as "if nga- is explained, it ceases to do its cosmological work." Pamphlet circulation bypasses senior interpretive authority. Status: SIMMERING in the playable present. The Innovation Traditional habal (sacred copies) are written in full liturgical notation with tier-prefixes, tonal contours, and class-markers. Only tribunal-certified scribes can read them correctly. The vernacular-habal movement produces editions with interlinear glosses: the sacred text on top, a vernacular (non-sacred register) explanation underneath. The innovation is technological, not theological: it changes who can access the content without changing the content itself. But the scribal priesthood recognizes that access IS the power: - If anyone can read the gloss, the decade-long training pipeline becomes "merely" phonological drill - If the cosmological tier-system is explained rather than performed, the explanation replaces the performance - If pamphlet-masters produce authoritative-seeming glosses, they become alternative interpretive authorities without tribunal…

The quietist creed has drifted over two generations into a full naturalist reading: the Five Waters are hydrological categories, not sacred persons; the water-scholar's job is empirical hydrology dressed in ritual register. The splinter faction -- the Unnamed-Water school (qalib al-ma' al-majhul) -- argues this openly. Status: ACTIVE in the playable present. The Argument Unnamed-Water position: The Five Waters are observational categories. Surface water flows downhill. Underground water follows aquifer geology. Sky water falls as rain. Dew condenses on cold surfaces. The Tenth Water is bodily moisture. These are facts of hydrology. Calling them "sacred" adds nothing that careful measurement does not already provide. The Qalib register works because it trains practitioners in precise articulatory control, which produces focused attention and disciplined observation -- not because the phonemes carry cosmological weight. Orthodox position: The Five Waters are cosmological structure. Hydrology is how the structure manifests, not what the structure IS. Stripping the cosmological reading leaves "mere measurement" -- which anyone with eyes can do, destroying the basis for the…

Summary Kheshkai shamans use vowel-harmony as a binding grammar: an oath in perfect harmony binds; a broken-harmony oath is a non-oath, hearable-but-ineffectual. The system is oral-only (no scribal class), master-to-apprentice on horseback, and identified by "hearing-gift" (often perfect-pitch individuals). Each generation renegotiates orthodoxy. For phonological detail, see (sacredregisterphonology.Varkosh). Political Function Who controls the training pipeline: Individual master-shamans, each with 1-3 apprentices. No institutional structure, no college, no guild. Selection is by "hearing-gift" -- the master identifies a child (typically ~8-12) who can detect harmony-violations that ordinary speakers miss. The gift is often correlated with what linguists would call perfect pitch. Who adjudicates correct pronunciation: The confederation's shamans collectively, through consensus that shifts with each generation. There is no written standard, no canonical recording, no reference pronunciation. When a senior shaman dies, their specific harmonic tradition dies with them unless an apprentice has perfectly internalized it. This makes Kheshkai sacred-register knowledge the most…

Summary Mixed-heritage individuals are rare, politically freighted, and irreplaceable. A child of an Irrah caravan-mother and an Oravan dockworker raised in the Basin might acquire pharyngeals AND vowel-length natively. They can articulate phrases across registers; they cannot legitimate them, because they lack isnad and initiation. They are security concerns for multiple institutions and hired by everyone. The Acquisition Problem Sacred registers are phonologically gated -- each requires articulatory skills best acquired in childhood. The standard model assumes monocultural upbringing: one register per person, acquired through one training pipeline, legitimated by one institutional chain. Mixed-heritage individuals break this model by acquiring multiple phonological systems natively through exposure to multiple linguistic environments in early childhood. This is not supernatural -- it is the same process by which bilingual children acquire two languages' phonologies without accent in either. What they acquire: - Articulatory ability -- the physical capacity to produce sounds from multiple registers - Pattern recognition -- intuitive knowledge of which sounds belong to which…

Summary Ndjadi magic is the strongest Vedic analog in Veydria: speaking correctly IS prayer, a misapplied prefix is not a grammar error but a cosmological miscategorization with consequences. The three-tier prefix system (ra-/ka-/nga-) simultaneously classifies cosmological rank, determines liturgical validity, and gates institutional authority. For phonological detail, see (sacredregisterphonology.Wazahaki + grammaticalizedcosmology). Political Function Who controls the training pipeline: Scribal colleges (delta temple-colleges). Multiple colleges exist and cross-recognize credentials, but each maintains its own internal pedagogy. Entry requires childhood (age ~5), making adult conversion effectively impossible. Who adjudicates correct pronunciation: Senior scribes at each college. Cross-college disputes are rare because the prefix system is grammatically regular (unlike Oravan's competing phonetic traditions). When disputes arise, they concern contextual prefix-selection (which tier applies to a given referent), not pronunciation per se. What counts as a valid utterance: Three conditions: 1. Correct tier-prefix for the referent (ra- for primordial, ka- for mortal-ordered,…

Summary Ngaru-Bon practitioners hold that their click-and-lateral chants enter the iron at the forge. Clicks are the hardest cross-linguistic acquisition in the real world, which is why Ngaru-Bon must start training in infancy (parents deliberately use click-speech to infants) and why this register is the hardest in Veydria to fake or leak. The guild is simultaneously religious institution, labor union, and military chokehold. For phonological detail, see (sacredregisterphonology.Gyamsgra). Political Function Who controls the training pipeline: The ancestor-smith guild. Exclusively. There is no second institution, no competing school, no reformist alternative. The guild IS the training pipeline, and the training pipeline IS the guild. Who adjudicates correct pronunciation: Guild elders. Their judgment is final and unappealable. No external authority (not Irrah scholars, not Qollari calendarists, not any Basin institution) has standing to evaluate Ngaru-Bon click-pronunciation. Summary Oravan magic exploits vowel-length distinctions and reduplication patterns -- an artisan-priest's invocation distinguishes tama tama (ordinary doubling) from taa-ma taa-ma (ritually-lengthened, tone-governed). The register is tied to craft-acts: you cannot invoke without the associated labor, which is long and witnessed. For phonological detail, see (sacredregisterphonology.Tavamala). Political Function Who controls the training pipeline: Workshop-lineages. Each island's dominant workshops hold their own pronunciation traditions. There is no central academy, no standardizing body, no canonical text that arbitrates between competing traditions. Who adjudicates correct pronunciation: Each workshop-lineage adjudicates its own standard. Cross-workshop disputes are never formally resolved -- lineages routinely accuse each other of "sloppy length" (insufficient vowel-distinction) or "over-reduction" (applying ordinary-register rules to sacred forms). This is the Oravan equivalent of competing Vedic shakha schools, each maintaining their own recitation tradition. Summary Qalib is the most scholastically disciplined register in Veydria: triconsonantal roots, pharyngeals (h, '), emphatics (t, s, d), uvulars, with the three Qalībin professions each owning a subset of roots and articulatory patterns. Transmission via isnad-chain -- a Qalib-speaker without traceable chain is producing "mere Qalib-shaped noise" no matter how phonologically accurate. For phonological detail, see (sacredregisterphonology section -- complete). Political Function Who controls the training pipeline: The three Qalībin professions (oath-binders, weather-readers, path-finders), each operating independently within the Qalībin order's umbrella. No single profession controls the whole register -- each owns a phonotactic subset. Who adjudicates correct pronunciation: The isnad-chain system. A practitioner's authority is not proven by demonstration but by traceability -- "who taught you, who taught them, who taught them." A perfect pronunciation from an untraced chain is illegitimate. This is the Quranic ijaza/sanad model adapted to magical practice. What counts as a valid utterance: Three conditions: 1. Correct phonological production (profession-specific emphatics,…

Summary Qollari magic is calendrical: ejective consonants bind to specific days in a ritual calendar, uvulars are reserved for solstitial rites. The practitioner produces consonants the general population can also produce -- the real monopoly is over which utterances are licit when, enforced by a khipu-plus-calendar knot-record that only the calendarist hierarchy can read. For phonological detail, see (sacredregisterphonology.Willkaqallu). Political Function Who controls the training pipeline: The calendarist hierarchy. Vertical and centralized (relative to Veydria's other traditions), with seniority determined by altitude of home institution (higher = more senior). Training occurs at mountain-terrace colleges. Who adjudicates correct pronunciation: This is the wrong question for Qollari. The adjudication is not over pronunciation (most Qollari can produce ejectives) but over timing. A correctly-produced ejective on the wrong day is the error. Only calendarists with access to the khipu-records know which day is which in the ritual calendar -- the ordinary population knows the agricultural seasons but not the sacred intercalation. Summary Tavas-Kaj is the Aethelian Basin's trade pidgin -- structurally leveled to remove every marked phonological feature that constitutes a sacred register. No clicks, no pharyngeals, no ejectives, no vowel-harmony constraints, no length-distinctions, no cosmological prefixes. This is exactly why it is trade-useful and magically inert. Loanwords enter Tavas-Kaj stripped of precisely the features that made them sacred. Tavas-Kaj is not a sacred register. It is the anti-register -- the linguistic space where all sacred material becomes costume. Its inclusion in this directory is structural: understanding what Tavas-Kaj strips explains what each register's load-bearing features are. Structure Tavas-Kaj is a contact pidgin (not a creole -- no native speakers, learned as a second-language trade tool). Its structure: | Feature | Tavas-Kaj Rule | What This Strips | |---------|---------------|-----------------| | Consonants | Only plain stops, nasals, fricatives, liquids | Strips clicks (Ngaru-Bon), pharyngeals (Irrah), ejectives (Qollari) | | Vowels | 5-vowel system, no harmony constraint, no length distinction | Strips harmony-binding (Kheshkai), vowel-length (Oravan) | |…

A volcanic vent on the Aethelian Basin's southern rim where multiple civilizations independently developed ash-fall divinatory practices because the vent produces a real, observable, ambiguous atmospheric signal. Delphi's layered sanctity -- geographic inevitability draws multiple traditions, each interpreting through its own theology. Why Multiple Traditions Converge Here The vent is geologically active: periodic gas emissions, ash-plumes, mineral deposits, and temperature fluctuations produce observable, unpredictable, interpretation-demanding phenomena. Where the Ndjadi delta's five distributaries braid before the sea. A site of theological contestation without physical confrontation -- the dispute plays out entirely in manuscript-debate. The Two Readings Ndjadi reading: The five distributaries are the cosmological ra-/ka-/nga- triad plus two unnamed waters. The three-tier prefix system maps onto three of the five channels; the remaining two are "unnamed" -- either primordial (pre-prefix, older than the grammar) or fallen (once-named, now forgotten). The site's geography IS the cosmological structure made visible. Irrah reading: Qalībin scholars have begun reading the five distributaries as literally the Five Waters of Irrah in a different guise -- surface, underground, sky, dew, and Tenth Water mapped onto five visible channels. This is politically explosive because it implies either tradition is a regional adaptation of the other. Why It Matters The stakes are the legitimacy of every prefix-notarized cross-civ contract: - If the Irrah reading wins (Five Waters = universal, Ndjadi prefixes = local adaptation), then Ndjadi's claim to cosmological completeness collapses. Their prefix-system is a regional expression of a more…

A partly-submerged stepped platform at the Aethelian Basin's dead center. The most physically contested sacred site on the continent. Currently Oravan-garrisoned with Ndjadi time-sharing access. The Site A monumental stepped structure -- platforms descending into tidal water, the lowest courses permanently submerged, the upper courses exposed at low tide. The construction predates both Oravan and Ndjadi ethnogenesis. Neither civilization built it. Both claim it. The architecture is ambiguous by accident of geology: tidal submersion has eroded lower inscription layers while preserving upper ones, and periodic earthquakes have exposed, re-buried, and re-exposed different courses over centuries. The site is a palimpsest -- every generation's claims are literally carved over the previous generation's, and the tides selectively erase. The Name Dispute Even the name is contested: - Qhabal-Ur -- the Oravan name. The official register uses what appears to be the Ndjadi ka- prefix, re-analyzed as a glottalized qh- that Oravan phonology reads as a dual-aspect marker. Oravan linguists argue this is not a borrowed prefix but an indigenous glottalized uvular that merely resembles ka-. The…

Spirits are place-indexical (bound to specific wells, winds, ruins, seasons). Deities are portfolio-indexical (relating to cosmological domains or relational categories). A ghilan of a specific wadi is not a junior version of a deity, exactly as a Shinto rock-kami is not a junior Amaterasu. The lived religion of the trading class. Not a watered-down folk version of any high tradition. Not a separate belief system. It is where portable fragments from all six civilizations mix, recombine, and become something that works at the crossroads without belonging to anyone. What It Is The syncretic layer is the religion of people who live between traditions: merchants, sailors, dockworkers, translators, itinerant smiths, caravan guards. These people need functional religious tools -- oaths that hold across cultures, amulets that feel protective, formulas for safe passage -- without committing to any single tradition's full theological apparatus. The layer consists of: - Ghilan/djinn discourse -- Irrah-origin vocabulary for spirits, now universal merchant speech. A Ndjadi riverboat captain says "ghilan" for any uncanny presence, regardless of the Ndjadi nga-beli taxonomy. - Star-name pidgin -- Sky-Mandate navigational vocabulary stripped of theology, used by pilots everywhere. - Qalib oath-fragments -- Irrah path-finder root-words carved on ship prows and caravanserai lintels. Both Ngaru-Bon and Qollari treat ancestors-in-worked-stone as the civilization's political spine. The material differs -- Ngaru-Bon works metal, Qollari works terrace-stone -- but the principle is the same: ancestors are present in the material they shaped, and the material legitimizes the living through continuity of craft. Ngaru-Bon: Ancestors in Metal For Ngaru-Bon, the forge is where ancestors speak. Lapam -- "the striker" -- is the forge-ancestor who taught the first smith. The named-lineage ancestors (Nokul, Amori) are the cattle-keeper and counter who gave the culture its economic foundation. All three are ancestor-class figures, not deities -- they were people who became politically load-bearing after death. The ancestor-smith guild controls both ritual and military production. A forge-strike -- refusing to produce weapons or reconsecrate tools -- is the institutional lever. This parallels Investiture Controversy mechanics: the smiths don't command armies, but armies can't fight without their products. The Ngaru-Bon interdict on arms-shipments to a disputed Irrah faction is the trigger for the Metal Interdict Crisis. The ancestor is literally in the metal. Ngaru-Bon…

A local intensification on the Water-Covenant substrate, not a separate tradition family. The Fire-House fuses volcanic fire with the oceanic Water theology to produce something no other descendant of the Water-Covenant has: a dual-aspect divinity whose two media (salt water and volcanic fire) are treated as the same creative-destructive force. Why It's Not a Separate Family The Fire-House does not have its own substrate, its own proto-theology, or its own independent history. It is what happens when the Water-Covenant lands on volcanic islands. The fire was added to the water, not substituted for it. Oravan purification rites, tiered cosmogony, and the Tenth-Water-in-the-body concept are all Water-Covenant features. The fire -- the caldera, the eruption, the hearth -- is the local addition. This distinction matters for cross-civ analysis. When Ndjadi grammarians argue with Oravan priestesses about the Water-Covenant substrate, the fire element is not part of the dispute. The Ndjadi don't contest fire; they contest whether personalizing the Water is a valid development or a corruption. The fire is simply not their problem. Two civilizations -- Kheshkai and Qollari -- share a proto-concept of the Sky as an impersonal mandating order. Each moved in opposite interpretive directions. The shared substrate is NOT a proto-Sky god in the Tengri mold ("Central Asia with serial numbers filed off"). It is a concept: the sky orders, and the ordering can be read. The Substrate The Sky-Mandate substrate holds that the sky imposes order on the world below. This order is readable -- through weather, through star-positions, through seasonal cycles -- and the reading confers legitimacy. Whoever reads the sky correctly has the right to act. Unlike the Water-Covenant, the Sky-Mandate substrate did not leave behind a rich ritual vocabulary or a cosmological taxonomy. What it left is simpler and harder to fake: a shared conviction that the sky's order is impersonal, that reading it is a skill, and that the reading legitimizes action. The disagreement between Kheshkai and Qollari is over what "reading" means. Two Descendants, Opposite Metaphysics Kheshkai: The Sky as WILL Kheshkai reads the sky as a near-person. Qarughan -- "that-which-watches-from-above" -- does not bless and does not curse. He notes. The sky's favor…

Site-specific spirits that predate all named traditions. Rivers, passes, specific trees, particular wells, a named wind that blows in a specific wadi in a specific season. Every tradition has variably absorbed or suppressed them. They are the Veydrian equivalent of Shinto kami surviving under Buddhism, or ovoo cairns surviving under Central Asian Islam. What the Sub-Stratum Is These are not gods, not ancestors, not cosmological categories. They are place-entities. A spirit of a specific spring. A presence at a specific mountain pass. The thing that lives in a particular old tree. They have no portfolios, no priesthoods, no doctrines. They have addresses. The sub-stratum provides the ambient numinous texture of the world -- the Skyrim-style enchanted feeling -- without requiring any deity to be real. A traveler crosses a pass and feels watched. A well produces water that tastes different on certain days. A tree that has stood for centuries drops a branch the day a notable person dies nearby. Whether these are spirits, coincidences, or natural phenomena is never settled. The four ambiguity devices apply at this level too, but they hardly need to -- the sub-stratum is already…

The largest and most internally diverse tradition family on the continent. Three civilizations -- Oravan, Ndjadi, and Irrah -- descend from a shared proto-theology that held the cosmos is ordered by the movement and division of waters: surface, underground, sky, dew, and the hidden moisture in living bodies. Ngaru-Bon touches the edge through dew/river rites whose relationship to the main complex is actively debated. The Substrate The Water-Covenant has no founder, no revealed text, no covenant moment. It is recoverable only by inference, like the Vedic substrate or Proto-Indo-European dyeus. In-world scholars disagree about whether it was ever a "religion" or only a shared cosmological grammar. The absence of a founding narrative is deliberate: it prevents any descendant tradition from claiming priority through apostolic succession. What the substrate left behind: - A tiered water cosmology -- the idea that different waters (rain, river, well, dew, bodily moisture) occupy different cosmological registers with different sacred valence - Purification rites tied to water-contact (washing, drinking, immersion, sprinkling) with register-specific protocols - A Tenth Water concept --…

Signature withdrawal: the free-port never advanced an elder any honor for his years, so there is none to take back; standing here was always a man's credit and his usefulness, and the old keep exactly as much of it as they saved or can still earn, the propertied merchant honored as a name still good and watched as a risk about to fail, the spent porter swept along the day his strength gives out. The Honored Elder The Basin has barely an honored elder to speak of, and that absence is the point. The stateless port reads the gray head as it reads everything, by what it is worth this morning, and a man's years buy him no deference on their own account. There is no place where age as age is owed the last word, no feast where the old speak last, no cosmos that says the line must carry those who carried it. The nearest thing the port has to a venerated elder is the man whose name on a paper is still good, the old merchant or broker whose word still moves goods because his credit has not failed. He is heeded, but he is heeded as a live account and not as an elder, and the day the account closes the heeding ends. (The household texture of an old one's place at a Basin hearth belongs to…

Signature withdrawal: in the oasis market an elder's honor is held in proportion to what she still holds, her name securing credit and moving caravans while her judgment is read as sound, and withdrawn as it passes; the propertied house-head descends by the quiet erosion of her command, while the spent caravan-hand or bonded laborer is set aside the season his hands are no longer worth his keep. The Honored Elder The order's picture of the elder is the house-head or caravan-master whose name on a contract still moves goods, the gray head at the center of the courtyard whose word settles a dispute over a water-right or a route, whose guarantees are sought by younger partners because the market has learned to trust them. In the noble houses this head is often a matriarch, for Irrah's great houses are matrilineal and the accumulated authority of the line descends through her; in the towns it is more often a patriarch, but in both cases the standing is the same, a name that is still good. The oasis holds that the old who built the house are owed a place in it, that a caravan-master who has survived the sand has earned the right to be heard, and that to set such a person aside…

Signature withdrawal: on the steppe a matron's word is the order while she holds the herd-right that backs it, and when age forces the stock to her daughter the word does not pass with the herd but lingers by habit and respect, so the old matron is revered as the voice the camp still heeds and is, in the same fact, the authority her heir must rule around, an order outliving the stock it rested on; and because the steppe keeps no institution to retire a word or cushion a fall, the herder whose only leverage was his hands is dropped the season they fail, with nothing to soften it. The Honored Elder The order's picture of the elder is the matron whose word is the order, the gray head who holds the herd-right and the line that turns on it, the one who may speak last at the feast and whose judgment the camp seeks before it moves or makes a match. The steppe holds that age is owed this place, that the old who built the herd are carried by it in turn, and that a camp that will not heed its matron is a camp that has lost its way. The respect is real and is held by the old themselves, who expect it and mostly receive it while their word still moves the things of the camp. (The matron's…

Signature withdrawal: on the floodplain an elder's standing is held in the record while his river-share and office remain in his name, and the withdrawal comes at a stroke when the share is divided to his sons; the same scribal column that read him up into standing now reads his name down as his control passes, and the senior head who has not yet divided is revered as the compound's head and is, in the same fact, the dam behind which his grown sons wait. The Honored Elder The order's picture of the elder is the river-lord or compound-head whose name sits in the standing-column, a man provisioned through the flood season, consulted on the division of water and the marriages of his sons, his word carrying weight because the record recognizes him as the node through which the compound's river-share passes. The Ndjadi order is proud of this. It holds that the floodplain keeps its old by keeping them visible, that an elder whose name is properly entered is buffered by the same bureaucracy that buffers the dike and the harvest, and that to honor the gray head is to honor the record that makes the compound legible. The pride is largely true where the elder holds an undivided share,…

Signature withdrawal: on the plateau caste fixes a floor of honor that age cannot take, but the craft-command of the master-smith is held only while his eye reads the metal true and his hand makes the mark; as they fail he is moved toward an emeritus standing, his caste-rank intact and his command gone, while the low-caste worn-out laborer is simply dropped, and the refuge the institutions give some aged is itself caste-gated so that the unclean rank is barred even from that. The Honored Elder The order's picture of the elder is the master-smith whose name authorizes the guild's mark, the gray head at the forge whom apprentices defer to and buyers seek out, the man in whom the craft's memory has settled. The plateau holds that caste is a cosmic order, that the forge-family elder has earned, by birth and by work, a place no failing of the body can fully remove, and that to dishonor such a man is to dishonor the metal itself. The respect is real and is felt by the old, who expect their caste-rank to shelter them and who are mostly right: a master of a forge family will never be swept to the road like a bonded smelter, because the floor holds. But the floor is not the same as…

Signature withdrawal: in the volcanic archipelago the matriline's senior woman holds the alliance-memory and the navigation knowledge that bring the boats home, leverage that lives in her head and decays last, so her descent is the slowest in the set and she may hold standing until death; the houseless harbor-laborer or off-line elder, holding no memory the linked houses need, descends from a standing he barely had and is set aside when the work no longer wants him. The Honored Elder The order's picture of the elder is the matron of the mother's house, the priestess whose memory holds the linked villages together, the gray head who knows who owes whom a feast, which house helped which in the last bad year, and which stars bring the long boats back across the channel. Because Oravan is matrilineal and matriarchal, the senior woman is the natural center of this memory; the mother's house is the archive, and her word is the index. The archipelago holds that the line keeps its old because the old keep the line, that a matron who remembers is the keel of the linked houses, and that to set such a woman aside is to cut the memory that holds alliance together. The respect is real and…

Each of the seven peoples holds a picture of the honored elder: a gray head owed deference, a grandparent at the hearth, a line that keeps and feeds its old, a duty of the young to the aged. This sub-layer owns the asymmetric trajectory underneath that picture. Its subject is not what an elder's day looks like, nor the sickbed, nor the death-rite, but who keeps standing as they age and whose standing is withdrawn, slowly or at a stroke, as the leverage their honor rested on decays. Aging is the far gate of the lifespan, the complement to the front gate that owns; where childhood sorts a person in or out at the start, aging follows a standing held at the height and let down over a life. It is among the corpus's most overlap-heavy lived subjects and is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate the clinical body, the infirm and the dying and who can afford to stop working, which documents; the death and the rites and the ancestor-cult, which documents; gendered authority as a position of sex, the matriarch and the patriarch, which documents; or the elder's daily function, the memory-holder within the day, which documents. It also cedes inheritance…

Signature withdrawal: the imperial count keeps an elder's standing exactly as long as it keeps a use for him, and the two uses run opposite ways: the core lineage-head is honored more deeply the nearer he comes to becoming a seated ancestor, while the periphery levy-hand, still sound in body, is struck from the count the season his hands stop making his quota. The Honored Elder The order's picture of the elder is the gray head of a counted lineage, provisioned through the lean years, consulted on the terraces and the marriage-alliances, his judgment sought because his years are the lineage's memory of its land and its star-positions. The empire is proud of this. It holds that it keeps its old as it keeps its storehouses, that an elder of the order need not be cast out in his decline because the same count that buffers the household carries its aged, and that to honor the gray head is to honor the order itself, which is old. The pride is largely true at the core, where the elder of a deep lineage is the most provided-for person in it. (The rhythm of an old one's day, who tends him and the grandchildren about the hearth, belongs to ; this layer owns the standing the years confer…

Signature catastrophe: the grain-supply shock, the ship-borne plague, and the waterfront fire, met not as verdicts but as prices, in the one place that tells no cosmic story about its dead. The Signature Hazard as Experienced The Basin grows nothing. It is a clearing-house on a harbor, and it eats only what arrives by ship, so its catastrophes are the catastrophes of supply and of crowding. A distant drought it never feels directly arrives as a tripled grain price and an empty warehouse. A closed strait or a convoy lost arrives the same way. The plague arrives on a hull and runs through the lodging-houses packed along the quays. The fire arrives on a dry night in a timber waterfront built wall-to-wall, and runs until it reaches stone or water. None of these is read in the sky. They are read on the price-board at the exchange and in the bills of the underwriters, and the first sign of the coming disaster is not a low gauge or a thin pasture but a number climbing on a slate. Who Breaks First, Who Buffers Standing in the Basin is credit, and credit is the buffer. The registered merchant who has hedged his grain forward, insured his cargo, and kept his name good at the exchange…

Signature catastrophe: the drying of the underground foggara when the water-table drops, the prolonged drought that kills date-palms a generation took to raise, and the locust that strips a year's standing crop in a single day. The Signature Hazard as Experienced Irrah's calamities come in three forms, all of them ways the desert takes back the water the oasis borrowed. The foggara fails when the water-table drops and the underground channel no longer runs full, so the carefully timed water-turns grow shorter and the palms begin to yellow from the roots up. The drought is slower and crueler, a string of dry years that desiccates the fruit and then kills the palms themselves, which are not replanted in a single lifetime. The locust is sudden, a cloud that darkens the morning and leaves the garden stripped by evening, so that the crop that was meant to carry the village through winter becomes fodder for insects. The hydrology of the foggara and the ecology of the locust are documented in ; what the cultivator knows is the sound of the channel running thin and the silence of a garden after the swarm has passed. Who Breaks First, Who Buffers Water in an oasis is owned, and…

Signature catastrophe: the dzud, the killing winter, in which a dry summer leaves the grass too thin and a following ice-glaze seals the pasture, so the herds starve standing in the cold and a generation's wealth is erased in one season. The Signature Hazard as Experienced The steppe has many hard winters, but a dzud is the one the herders speak of as a living thing that eats the herds. It begins in the summer, when the rain fails and the grass stands short and stemmy, so the animals go into the cold already thin. Then the first heavy snow falls and a thaw freezes over it, locking the pasture under a shell of ice that hooves cannot break. The horses and sheep and cattle stand at the same ground where they have grazed all summer and starve there, because the food is beneath them and they cannot reach it. The mechanics of ice-crust, parasite bloom, and the pneumonia that follows are documented in ; what the herder knows is the sound of animals pawing uselessly, the silence that spreads through a camp when the weak ones stop, and the moment a man realizes he is watching his wealth walk toward death. Who Breaks First, Who Buffers The large camp breaks last. It has saved hay from…

Signature catastrophe: the inundation that fails or comes wrong, and the multi-year drought behind it, which converts a whole tier of free-farming households into dependents of the grain-lords. The Signature Hazard as Experienced The plain lives by one event a year. The river rises, spreads across the black soil, and falls back, and the wet ground takes the seed. When it does not come, or comes thin, or comes late and drowns the sprouted millet, the year is lost before it begins. (The hydrology and the disease that rides the bad water are documented in .) A single failed inundation is hunger that the stores and the patrons can absorb. The catastrophe is the second failed year, and then the third, when the held grain is gone and the price of a sack has climbed past what a season's labor can buy. The farmer reads the coming disaster early, in the height of the water against the old marks on the landing-stones, and can do nothing about it but watch the line stay low. Who Breaks First, Who Buffers The grain-lords and the river-merchants do not break. They hold the storehouses and the canoes, and a drought is the season their grain is worth the most and the desperate are cheapest to…

Signature catastrophe: the glacial-lake outburst flood that empties a moraine-dammed lake down a valley in an hour, the avalanche that buries a hamlet or a mine-adit, and the killing cold-snap that takes the unsheltered on the high plateau. The Signature Hazard as Experienced Ngaru-Bon's catastrophes come down from the ice and the rock above the settlements. The glacial-lake outburst flood begins with a roar that is heard before it is seen, as the wall of water and stone tears through the valley, taking bridges, terraces, and anyone who did not run high enough in time. The avalanche comes silent until it is almost on top of the hamlet or the mine mouth, burying the path and the people on it under tons of snow. The killing cold-snap is the quietest of the three; the temperature drops fast, and those with thin walls and little fuel are found stiff in the morning. The mechanics of outburst floods, snowpack, and hypothermia are documented in ; what the highlander knows is the sound of the valley filling with water, the absence of a path that was there yesterday, and the cold that enters a house when the fire goes out. Who Breaks First, Who Buffers The metallurgy economy runs on…

Signature catastrophe: the sudden cyclone and storm-surge that drowns a low coast and wrecks the season's boats, paired with the slow monsoon failure that strands the spice fleet and leaves a cash-crop archipelago without the grain it does not grow. The Signature Hazard as Experienced Oravan suffers two different catastrophes, one fast and one slow, and they punish different parts of the same fragile economy. The fast one comes off the sea in an afternoon: the wind rises, the water climbs above the stilts, and the surge carries boats up into the gardens and houses, so that a cove that was fishing at sunrise is a wreck by sunset. The slow one comes when the monsoon fails and the trade winds idle, leaving the spice fleet in harbor while the rice ships do not come, so that people who sell cloves and buy rice suddenly have neither crop nor cash. The mechanics of wind, surge, and the crop diseases that follow the wet are documented in ; what the islander knows is the sight of a boat he carved himself thrown against the shore, and the week when the price of rice doubles while the ships sit still. Who Breaks First, Who Buffers The rooted workshop-lineage, the one with land on a second…

Each of the seven peoples lives within reach of a signature calamity set by its land: the failed flood, the killing winter, the frost-cycle, the cyclone, the dried channel, the glacial flood, the grain-supply collapse. This sub-layer owns the cross-class lived experience of the acute shock and the memory, mourning, and meaning a people makes of it: who breaks first and who is buffered, how the comfortable middle is unmade, how the disaster is explained, and how it is remembered. It is the corpus's most overlap-heavy lived subject, bordering four owners at once, so it is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate the standing poverty of the poor in ordinary years (); the mechanics of the hazard ( and the biomes); the institutional crisis bodies that convene on a trigger (); the theology of the gods and divine justice (); or ordinary death-rites (). It references them and moves to the lived shock, the buffer, the unmade, the memory, and the gap between how the calamity is explained and who actually dies. The Frame Per ADR-0035 catastrophe takes the asymmetric frame of ADR-0027 (underclass) and ADR-0028 (warfare), not the shared-script frame of…

Signature catastrophe: the multi-year frost-and-drought of a failed cycle, and the sudden earthquake or debris-flow, met by a centralized state that stores against the bad year and feeds the loyal core first. The Signature Hazard as Experienced The high country lives at the calorie-ceiling, where a single hard frost on a wrong night can take a field at altitude, and where a failed rain-cycle can thin the maize and the tuber across whole terraced valleys for years at a time. Against this the state keeps storehouses, ranged along the roads and ridges, filled with maize and with freeze-dried tuber that keeps for years. So the slow catastrophe, the multi-year frost-and-drought, is the one the order is built to answer, and the question in a bad cycle is never only how thin the harvest is but whose storehouses are opened and in what order. The sudden catastrophe is the other kind: the earthquake that drops a terrace wall, or the debris-flow that comes off a saturated slope and buries a valley floor in an afternoon, faster than any granary can answer. Who Breaks First, Who Buffers The buffer here is not a household's own grain but the state's, and that changes who breaks. The imperial…

Signature recognition: the stateless free-port has no single cosmos to read a child as cherished or as cursed, so it reads him as a cost and a future asset. The abandoned newborn is received at the institution's wheel and entered in a ledger; recognition is a transaction, the contracted apprentice granted a path because someone has pledged for it, and the unclaimed child a matter not of belonging but of public order. This is the capstone, and the place where the Order's Account elsewhere is shown for the convention it is. The Cherished Child The Basin holds no common picture of the cherished child, because it holds no common cosmos to hold one in.
