A merchant house cherishes its heir as fiercely as any river-lord cherishes his, and the great houses rear their children long and well; but that is a private good a house buys for its own, not an ideal the free-port professes for every child. Where another people would say a child is owed a childhood and mean it as a duty, the Basin says a child is an expense now and a hand later, and arranges its institutions to manage both. The nearest thing to a shared account is the foundling house itself, a guild-funded charity that receives the…

Signature recognition: in the oasis drylands, the right to a protected childhood and a recognized passage is granted lavishly at the top of the market and denied flat at the bottom of the same one; the honored child's recognition is sponsored in proportion to the house that sponsors it, and the market-child's is purchased or it does not come. The Cherished Child The order's picture of childhood is a child whose passage is sponsored. In the propertied and oath-bound house, the child is a pledge of future alliance as much as a person to be reared; he is fostered outward to a house the parents wish to bind, and the foster-bond is witnessed and made kin, so that his standing is recognized twice over. The honored child is fed, guarded, and placed because his house can pay for the recognition, and the order holds that every child should be under such a house, claimed and witnessed into a place. (The texture of rearing in the tent and the courtyard belongs to ; the scholar-academy and the training of the scribe belong to ; the marriage-bar carried by milk-kinship and the descent rule belong to and . This layer owns the sponsoring of recognition, not the rearing, the school, or the…

Signature recognition: the moving camp grants almost no protected childhood as a separate, idle span; a child is productive from the time he can hold a rope, and the crossing into adult standing is not a rite the order confers but a competence the camp recognizes. Where there is no institution to confer a passage, the sorting runs nakedly: the trueborn of the line are recognized into the lineage and its herds, and the captured and the fostered-from-below are fed, worked, and never granted lineage-standing. The Cherished Child The steppe loves its children plainly and works them early, and sees no contradiction in it. A child is the line's continuation and its hands, wanted for both at once, and the order's picture of a good childhood is a child who is competent young: a girl who can milk and pitch the felt by the time she is waist-high, a boy who keeps his seat and minds the lambing flock not long after. There is no separate idle span the order holds a child is owed, and no notion that work delays a childhood, because work is how the camp makes a person. (The daily texture of that rearing, the felt tent, the games that are herding in miniature, the carved-bone toy flocks,…

Signature recognition: on the floodplain a child is only as much a child as the house that claims him and the record that names him; the pawned dependent's child, present in the same compound and set to its work from infancy, is labor before he is a child, and his crossing into adult standing is never notarized because there is no standing for it to confer. The Cherished Child The order's picture of childhood is a child read into a house. A child claimed by a father, entered in the lineage's reckoning, and given over to the long supervised rearing of the compound is, to the Ndjadi mind, a child in full: a name the house will carry, a future the house is investing in, a person the order is obliged to make. The reckoning is the love. A great house that names its child and provides for his rearing has done the first and largest of its duties to him, and the order holds that every child should be so claimed, that the fatherless should be taken into a kinsman's reckoning and the orphan absorbed into the compound rather than left outside a house. (The shape of that rearing, the inner court, the aunts and co-wives who pass the infant among them, the fostering of children between…

Signature recognition: the sorting is not earned or bought but fixed at birth by caste; the child born into a recognized rank is owed the rank's protected rearing and its assured passage into standing, and the low-caste and bonded child is born out, owed no protected span and no passage the order will confer. The Cherished Child The order's picture of childhood is a child born into his rank. In the recognized ranks, and above all in the smith-caste child consecrated into the forge-guild, the child is a gift to the order itself: honored where a lower order would shun the trade, set apart from birth as one who will keep the secrets of the forge. The rank is the house; the rank is the protection. A smith-caste child is claimed by the guild before he can walk, and the order holds that every child should be so claimed by the rank that made him, reared toward the standing that is already his. (The rhythm of rearing in the forge-house and the care of the caste infant belong to ; the guild training and the schooling of the plateau's institutions belong to ; the caste-law that fixes rank belongs to . This layer owns the caste-assigned recognition, not the rearing, the school, or the…

Signature recognition: in the volcanic archipelago, the mother's house is the unit of recognition; a child born into a matriline is reckoned its own and crossed into adult standing through the line's recognized passage, and the child with no matriline to claim her is outside the unit that confers recognition, present in the port-society but granted no line's protected span and no line's passage. The Cherished Child The order's picture of childhood is a child claimed by a mother's house. A child born into a matriline is reckoned its own from the first: reared across the linked houses of the line, fostered from island to island to bind the houses, and set on the passage that the line has always used to cross its young into adult standing. The mother's house is the unit of belonging; the matriline is the protection. A child with a house on the water is known wherever the line reaches, and the order holds that every child should be so claimed, that the foundling should be taken into a house's line and the off-line child absorbed rather than left outside a house. (The texture of rearing in the linked houses and the care of the island child belong to ; the priestess-workshop training…

Each of the seven peoples holds a picture of the cherished child and the passage owed to it: a span of protected rearing before the burdens of an adult, a name read into a house, a recognized crossing into adult standing that makes a person of the child. This sub-layer owns the asymmetric sorting underneath that picture. Its subject is not what a child's rearing looks like but who is granted a recognized childhood at all, and who is recoded out of it, worked from infancy, fostered as a status subordinate, pawned, sold, or processed as a foundling-unit. It is among the corpus's most overlap-heavy lived subjects and borders three owners at once, so it is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate the rearing texture (the rhythm of a child's day, who tends and fosters them, the rearing-by-rank), which documents; the learning-gate (the school, the curriculum, the consecrated threshold, the initiation-rite as an institution), which documents; or the marriage-passage (marriage as alliance, bridewealth, the conjugal instruction the rite carries), which and document. It also cedes a child's death and its rites (), the standing poverty of the poor and child…

Signature recognition: the imperial order reckons children as it reckons everything, outward from the center by the measure of how much it values them, and the child rendered to the order is taken from his own line's reckoning and entered into the center's, recoded from a child of a house into a thing the house has given up. The Cherished Child The order's picture of childhood is a child held in the order's regard. A child of a household inside the empire's count, named in the early naming that first makes him a person and entered in the knotted record that the order keeps of its people, is a child the order owes a protected rearing and an assured crossing into adult rank. The empire is proud of this. It holds that it provisions its children as it provisions its storehouses, that a child of the order need not starve in a lean year because the same stores that buffer the household feed its young, and that to be a child of the empire is to be counted, fed, and made. The pride is not empty at the core, where it is largely true. (The rhythm of that rearing and the early naming as a household event belong to ; the imperial schooling that trains the favored belongs to . This layer…

Daily life: A single street of stacked houses, townhouse, shop-house, and tenement room, where the same respectable ideal is measured floor by floor. The Household The Basin house is the stacked urban building, and here the gradient is vertical and visible in one street. The merchant's townhouse has a front-stage reception floor for guests and contracts, back-stage service rooms, a cellar of goods, and live-in servants who sleep in the attic or under the stairs. There are rooms for dining, rooms for accounting, and rooms the family never enters because they belong to the staff. The middling tradesman's house-and-shop has the family above the work: the counter and bench below, two or three rooms above, and perhaps a maid-of-all-work who sleeps in the kitchen. The shop window is the public face; the upper rooms are the private household. The wage-poor rent a single tenement room, sometimes shared by two families, with a curtain for the little privacy a divided room allows. There is no cellar, no attic, no kitchen beyond a brazier and a shared hearth. Domestic service is everywhere, a large share of poor women work inside richer households, so that the same young woman who sleeps…

Daily life: A courtyard-house behind the oasis wall, where water-turns, seclusion, and the caravan calendar divide the same honorable ideal between those who can keep it and those who cannot. The Household The Irrah house is an earthen courtyard-house behind the oasis wall. The walled oasis quarter packs modest homes and fortified merchant residences into one enclosure, so the cross-class gradient is visible street by street within a single wall. A merchant house has a court, a guest hall where men receive caravan partners, and a women's quarters set apart from both: the secluded wife moves between inner rooms unseen by trade guests. A private cistern and a separate kitchen allow the household to function without women entering the public lane. A middling date-grower's house has the same plan reduced: a small court, one or two rooms, and a corner where the women may withdraw when strangers come. The well-queue is shared, and the courtyard opens onto the lane, but the principle of separation is still honored. The khammes sharecropper has a room or two opening onto a lane, no inner court, and a place at the shared well-queue rather than a private cistern. There is nowhere for a…

Daily life: A tent household paced by the herd and the season, where a good winter can make a camp and a dzud can unmake one in a single season. The Household The Kheshkai house is the tent: a single round dwelling of felt and lattice, gender-zoned inside: one side for the men, their weapons, and the gear of the herd, the other for the women, the hearth, and the stored dairy. It holds the family and often three generations, sleeping with their feet toward the central fire. The rich do not live in a bigger tent so much as in more of them: a wealthy camp is a cluster of tents: the main household, the married sons, the store-tent for felt and dried meat, the guest tent that stands empty but ready. A wealthy household can receive a visiting camp without crowding its own sleepers. A middling household has one sound tent and perhaps a small second shelter for the young couple or the old. The felt is patched but warm, the lattices are sound, and the camp can move when the pasture demands. The poor zhataq has a worn single tent, patched past warmth, or none at all and must shelter with a patron. They sleep where they are allowed, and their household is whatever roof they can find. The…

Daily life: A graded compound measured by the people it holds, from the river-lord's crowded courtyard to the one-hut household that can barely hold its own. The Household The Ndjadi house is a graded compound: an outer gate, an entrance hall where men receive guests and conduct trade, and an inner court of kitchens, sleeping places, and women's and children's space restricted to close kin. A great river-lord's compound is multigenerational and crowded with kin, pawned dependents, craft-clients lodged on-site, and the servants who grind grain and haul water from the river. The entrance hall is where deals are made and dependents wait; the inner court is where the lord's wives and children live, shielded from public view. A middling trader's compound has the same sequence in miniature, a reception room, a walled inner court, a separate cooking shed, but the people inside are mostly his own family, one or two dependents, and perhaps a junior wife. The walls are lower and the gate is smaller, but the movement from outer to inner is the same. The poor have a hut and a shared yard: one room for sleeping, cooking, and storage, with a screen of woven grass for the little privacy a…

Daily life: A stacked stone house on the plateau, where the same dwelling form rises from the animal level to the shrine room, and where the Lower-Path line decides which floors a child may ever climb. The Household The Ngaru-Bon house is a stacked stone building: animals and stores on the ground floor, the family above, and a flat roof for drying grain, tanning hide, and working in the thin light. An elite Inner-Council smith house is tall and many-roomed, with a shrine room for offerings, quarters for retainers, a separate kitchen that does not share air with the living quarters, and a reception room where guests are served butter tea without seeing the domestic work. The house is a statement of estate and order. A middling smith or landholding household has the same shape smaller: one or two family rooms above the animals, a corner for the shrine, and a roof that serves as extra workspace. The rooms are fewer, but the movement upward from animals to people to the sacred is the same. Lower-Path Kinship households crowd a single floor or share the animals' level, sleeping on pallets in the same building where the elite keep their cattle below and themselves above. For them the…

Daily life: A timber longhouse over the water, where the blood-alliance turns every feast into a test of whether your house will feed others this season or be fed by them. The Household The Oravan house is a timber stilt house or longhouse built over or beside the water, often holding an extended household bound by the village blood-alliance. A prosperous trading lineage builds large: carved posts, a raised reception platform, separate hearths for the main family and dependents, and room enough for kin, bond-laborers, and the canoes pulled up underneath. The house is both warehouse and residence, with space to store spice, rice, and trade goods through the monsoon. A middling fishing-and-spice household has the same longhouse form in miniature: one hearth, a sleeping loft, a covered platform for mending nets, and a canoe or two drawn up on the pilings. It cannot host a whole village, but it can feed a few allied guests when the catch is good. The fishing-poor crowd a small house with a leaky boat, sleeping on the same planks where they dry fish and store nets. The longhouse is too small to hold a feast, and the blood-alliance knows it. Self-governance under the Harbor Covenant…

Each of the seven civilizations holds a picture of what an ordinary life well lived looks like: a proper house, a seemly meal, a child raised right, a festival rightly kept, and in each, the same picture is reached fully by some, gestured at by others, and missed entirely by the poorest. This sub-layer documents that ordinary texture across the whole social range: where people slept and who with, the shape of a day, what and when and with whom they ate, how children were reared and came of age, how the old were kept, and what people did for rest and play. It is the cross-class companion to , which documents the bottom stratum alone. Where the underclass files describe the floor, these describe the gradient: the same human activities refracted through rank, gender, and region. It does not restate marriage and inheritance law (), the food economy and famine (, the underclass files), or domesticate ecology (); it references them and moves to the lived texture they imply but never depict. The Shared-Script Frame Every per-civ file carries two readings, but the asymmetry between them is different from the underclass layer's. Poverty pits an elite ideology, told by the powerful to…

Daily life: A courtyard-compound, two daily meals, and a life paced by altitude and the ritual calendar: the same form scaled from the great ayllu house to the kinless waqcha room. The Household The Qollari house is a courtyard-compound of fieldstone and adobe, roofed in ichu grass that sheds the highland rain and insulates against the cold. An elite ayllu head holds several buildings around a paved court: a storehouse of cloth and dried tubers, quarters for yana retainers, a kitchen apart from the sleeping rooms, and a room set aside for receiving guests where no cooking ever happens. The courtyard itself is a workspace: women weave under the arcade, children grind grain, and visitors wait to be admitted. A middling herder-farmer household has the same shape in miniature: one or two rooms around a beaten-earth court, the family sleeping on raised platforms and a few animals brought in through the coldest months for shared warmth. Tools hang from the rafters, and the court doubles as pen and kitchen. The kinless waqcha dwells at the bottom of the same form: a single windowless room, one end for people and the other for a goat or a stored bundle of fodder, with no arcade, no…

The Order's Promise The Basin makes the thinnest promise about its surfaces of any people, and even it is not quite empty. The free-port has no sovereign to say what a body may wear and no single cult to vest it, so it does not claim that cloth shows the soul; what it claims, in the civic story the merchant houses tell, is that the port dresses a body by its industry, that a man who works and trades well comes to wear well, and that the good coat and the sound boots are the plain record of a life that earned them. The port is proud to be the one place a body off any river may arrive in rags and, by diligence and a little luck, come to wear the broadcloth of a solid factor; the almshouse and the confraternity are pointed to as proof that even the body the market has not dressed will be decently covered by the charity of the worthy. The clerks call it the fairest surface on the continent, because here a body wears what it has made and not what a tier or a caste allows. This is the promise the port makes about its surfaces, that the coat is the honest ledger of the industry behind it, and the factors who wear their broadcloth well make it in good faith. It is rendered here as the…

The Order's Promise Irrah tells itself that a body is read by whose house stands behind it, and the standing is honest because the cloth is vouched. In the noble line the matrilineal tent-holder wears the deep indigo of her mother's house, the house colors worked into her veil and the hem of her robe, and any eye in the oasis knows at a stride whose water-right and whose caravan-share pass through her. The accredited craftswoman of a house goes out with its seal on her warrant and its dye on her wrapper; the licensed master rides with the house colors at his shoulder and the chain of names that vouches for him close behind. The oasis is proud that its surface can be read so plainly, that a caravan-master coming in from the eastern corridor can tell a vouched body from an unvouched one before either speaks, and the pride is not empty: the house is real, the water-right is real, and the livery genuinely names whose credit stands behind the wearer. This is the promise the oasis makes about its surfaces, that the cloth shows the body for what the order has placed it, and the men and women who dress to their house in good faith make the promise with full hearts. It is rendered here…

The Order's Promise Kheshkai tells itself that a body's surface shows the standing it has gathered, and on the steppe the gathering is made portable. A mobile people cannot keep its wealth in walls and fields; it carries its herd on the person as worked silver, ornament, and the fine stuff of the tent, and the wearing is the honest display of what the camp has made. The great herd-owning matron goes to the camp-meet with the heavy silver of her line at her throat and her daughters' bridles bright with gathered rings; the renowned rider wears the worked belt and the arm-rings that say his raids have brought stock to the tent he serves. The steppe is proud that its surface can be read so plainly, that a stranger coming in from the settled margin can tell a prospering camp from a fallen one before either speaks, and the pride is not empty: the silver is genuinely worked, the herds are genuinely counted, and the camp's honor genuinely travels with its people. This is the promise the steppe makes about its surfaces, that the cloth and the silver show the body for what the camp has made it, and the men and women who dress to their gathered standing in good faith make the promise with…

The Order's Promise Ndjadi tells itself that a body is read as plainly as the flood-tiers, and the reading is honest because the cloth is true. A man wears the standing he has gathered: the dyed wrappers and the worked cap of a holder of people, the plain length of a hoe-farmer, the bare working cloth of a hand in a gang, each the visible truth of where the order has placed him. The river-country is proud that it can be read at a glance, that a stranger off the water knows a notary from a ferryman before either speaks, and the pride is not empty: the show of a great house, its wives in their good cloth and its children fed and decently covered, is a real accounting of the people that house holds and feeds. The reform voices call it a fair mirror, pointing to the certified hand who earned the right to a copyist's sober dress and wears it honestly. This is the promise the delta makes about its surfaces, that the cloth shows the body for what the order has made it, and the men who dress to their tier in good faith make the promise with full hearts. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and it is not the whole of what cloth does to a body. What the Body May Wear…

The Order's Promise Ngaru-Bon tells itself that a body's surface shows the state of the soul that carries it, and on the plateau the soul is reckoned in purity. The high body, the estate-lord and the monastic, is clean and quiet in good undyed wool and worked silver, and the cleanliness is held to be no vanity but the visible truth of a life the karma of past lives has made fit. The craft-castes wear the marks of their mystery, the master-smith in the forge-regalia and the worked iron only his line may set on its own body, and the order grants that these signs are earned in the keeping of a craft no neighbor can match. Each surface is held to be the body's own register, read off it the way the plateau reads the rank of a slope by the snow that lies on it: the pure show clean, the craft show their craft, the laboring show the plain covering of bodies whose work is rough and near the impure things. The monastic teachers call it a mercy that the eye can keep the order the doctrine requires, so that the clean need not learn by accident what a body is. This is the promise the plateau makes about its surfaces, that the look of a body is the plain face of its place in the purity of…

The Order's Promise Oravan tells itself that the open sea dresses its people freely and well, and the telling carries a real generosity. The archipelago is a place of many ports and many shades, where a body off any beach may be taken into a house and learn its craft, and where the fine barkcloth and the worked shell of a named house are the honest show of a craft the alliance trusts on open water. The order grants that a maker named by her mother's house wears the house's good cloth because she has earned the house's name, and holds that the sea, which carries every cloth and every body between the islands, makes the archipelago the least closed of all the peoples, a place where a hand from anywhere may rise to a house's beach. The keepers call it the gift of the water, that a body is known by the house that keeps it and not by the island it was born on, and that the open harbor lets a willing hand find a house to clothe it. This is the promise the archipelago makes about its surfaces, that the house cloth honors the named and the open sea has a place for the rest, and the houses that clothe their makers well make it in good faith. It is rendered here as the order's account of…

Each of the seven peoples holds a picture that a body is read truly by its surface: that the cloth, the ornament, and the keeping of the body show the place and the worth of the one who carries them. This sub-layer owns the asymmetric structure underneath that picture. Its subject is not the body a person is born with, nor the signs that say which people or guild a body belongs to, nor the type of the ideal man and woman, nor the maker's mark on the work of his hands, but the surface the order lets a body choose and the surface it makes a body wear: who may show what, and whose body wears a sign it did not choose. It builds the worn and marked layer on top of the inherited body that ADR-0015 fixed. It does not restate the phenotype and the identity-markers of belonging, which ADR-0015 owns; the ideal social type and the honor that polices conduct, which owns; the maker's mark on the product, which owns; the standing condition of the poor, which owns; staged costume, which owns; sacred vestment, which owns; the uniform of armed bodies, which owns; or any codified sumptuary statute, which owns. It references them and writes the chosen surface and the assigned mark on top. The…

The Order's Promise Qollari tells itself that the empire is a reckoning made visible, and the cloth that covers a body is the count's own statement of where that body stands in it. The fine mantle, the dyed wrap, the worked clasp that marks an attached specialist are not mere finery; they are the sun-favored state's allotment, given from the store to the body the cord-record has written into the reckoning. A robed specialist walks through the terrace market and the lane reads him as a hand the empire has chosen and keeps, a maker whose work the count names and whose cloth proclaims the naming. The highland is proud that its surface can be read so plainly, that a stranger coming up from the cloud-forest can tell the count's attached weaver from the levy-hand drafted to her loom before either speaks, and the pride is not empty: the cloth is genuinely fine, the attachment genuinely recorded, and the empire's tribute genuinely kept straight by the cord. The order's promise is that the body is honestly read by its cloth, that the mantle shows the place the count has made for it, and that the men and women who dress to their allotment in good faith make the promise with full hearts.…

Formal education: A stateless free-port where schooling is bought, the guild masterpiece is the gate, and the laundering is thinnest because the gate is called merit even though it is paid for, bonded, and inherited. The School The free-port has the most schools and the most kinds: the chartered guild that forms a craft by indenture, the fee-charging petty school that teaches a tradesman's child letters and figures, the grammar school for those who can pay more, and the informal hedge-school of a poor quarter. The tenement child learns at the work itself or not at all, and that belongs to the lived day and the underclass. Schooling here is a thing one buys. A father pays a schoolmaster to teach his child; a master takes an apprentice and charges a bond; a guild charters a craft and controls who may open a shop. What this means for the free-port is that the gate is nakedly commercial and therefore dressed most carefully as merit. The guild says the work speaks; the schoolmaster says any child who pays may learn; the city says talent rises. All three statements are true within their frame, and the frame is money. There is no sacred vow, no blood bar, no spirit-call to recode the…

Formal education: An oasis where learning is the memorization of the sacred text, the gate is a license granted master to student after a full recitation, and the unbroken chain of that granting launders a lineage's monopoly as the descent of correct prayer. The School The school is the recitation-house attached to the lineage compound and the larger town school where a master gathers students to learn the sacred text by heart. The elite and scholarly-lineage boy boards near his master or walks from a compound close by; the caravan-lineage boy learns enough letters for trade and route. The bonded and sharecropper child's schooling is the work itself, and that belongs to the lived day. Girls are taught within the household under seclusion, and the recitation-house is closed to them. What this means for the oasis is that schooling is deeply unequal and deeply sacred at once. The same text is memorized in every room, but the room decides what the memorizing means. A boy who learns the whole text and receives the license becomes a link in the chain; a boy who learns only letters becomes a clerk or a factor; a girl who learns from a kinsman behind a wall becomes a woman who can read…

Formal education: A steppe where there is no school, no building, no fixed course, and where the credential-function still exists in the spirit-chosen apprentice and the lineage name, so that reproduction runs naked and calls itself the natural order. The School There is none, and the absence is the content. The confederacy has no building, no class, no fixed term. The boy learns the herd from the herd, and that learning belongs to the lived day. But the structured training that has a threshold appears in two narrow channels: the spirit-chosen youth who is taken by an established shaman as a single apprentice, and the lineage whose name vouches for a man before he has done anything. The credential-function exists without the institution. This is not a lack to be lamented; it is the sharpest form of the rider, because with no schoolhouse to point to, the gate itself stands exposed. What this means for the steppe is that learning is not separated from life and then guarded by a door. A child learns to ride and to read the weather by doing it; that is daily life. The shaman's apprentice learns the spirit-roads by following his master across the grass; that is this domain, because…

Formal education: A river domain with two unlike schools: the freeborn copy-circle where correct sacred speech is certified hand to hand, and the praise-singer caste household where the spoken record is bred in the blood, each gate consecrated so that lineage reads as worthiness. The School There are two schools, and they are nothing alike. The freeborn scribal training sits in the river-town scholar's house and the copy-circle, where boys of clerical and trading lineages learn to read, to write the certified hand, and to guard correct speech. The school is a room, a circle of mats, and the master who presides; a boy boards near his master or walks from his father's compound, and the course runs for years. The praise-singer's school is the caste household itself. There is no building, the master is the parent or uncle, and the schoolroom is a lifetime of listening. A praise-singer child hears the genealogies before he can speak plainly and learns the names that bind houses while other children learn to hoe. What this means for the floodplain is that the freeborn child and the caste child are trained for opposite stations by opposite means, and neither can cross into the other's…

Formal education: A plateau where the only true school is the cloister, where a novice climbs through decades of doctrine to a graded degree won in open debate, and where the debate is called pure merit because the first gate, ordination, has already turned the Lower-Path away. The School The cloister-citadel is the only school the plateau has, and it is a school the way a forge is a fire: schoolroom, library, and the order that governs learning, all one body. A boy sent there does not attend; he enters, is lodged and fed by the order, and is formed by it for as long as the course runs, which is most of a life. There is no second school. A family that wants its son lettered has one door, and the door is the order's. What this means for the plateau is that learning and the sacred are not two things a child might pursue separately. To be schooled is to enter a consecrated house and submit to its discipline; there is no lay grammar-master, no fee-school in a market town, no tutor a merchant might hire to teach figures without vows. The smith-lineages train their own within the guild and the Lower-Path child is set to the ore (matters that belong to the guild and to the lived day,…

Formal education: An island alliance where the school is the court-temple compound, the curriculum is the sacred register that runs the records and the rites, and the gate is initiation into that register, dressed as ritual readiness so that trading lineage becomes worthiness. The School The school is the court-temple compound and the priestess-queen's household, where the children of trading and allied-village lineages are taken in to learn the sacred register, the records, and the etiquette of the alliance. The compound is at once a palace, a shrine, and a training ground; a child who enters lives inside it for years, fed by the alliance's stores and formed by its matrons and masters. There is no school open to the village at large. The fishing-poor child learns to bail and net young, and that learning belongs to the lived day. The artisan-priest is formed within the temple's own training pipeline rather than in a separate school. What this means for the alliance is that literacy and holy speech are trained in the same place and guarded by the same gate. A trading house does not hire a tutor to teach its child letters in private; letters are taught inside the compound, and…

Each of the seven civilizations holds the same conviction, that learning ennobles and the worthy may learn, and in each the door to real learning stands above the heads of most of the people. This sub-layer owns the structured course of training that has a threshold and an outcome-marker: the school as a site, the curriculum as what is taught and what is withheld, the consecrated gate that decides who is admitted, and the teachers who run it. It is, after food, the corpus's most overlap-heavy lived subject, so it is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate childhood-as-lived, apprenticeship as a child's day, or coming-of-age (); the priesthood, guild, or shaman body as a power institution and its monopoly (); the record medium as control (); or who is shut out of everything (). It references them and moves to the school, the curriculum, the gate, and the teacher those layers never depict. The Frame Per ADR-0033 every per-civ file carries the daily-life pair (ADR-0029) plus one rider. - The Normative Account is the civilization's shared ideal that learning lifts the learner, documented as a real social force and marked plainly as the ideal. It is…

Formal education: A highland domain where the state maintains a consecrated house of teaching for the sons of ruling lineages and a chosen-women's house for the daughters the sun favors, and where the gate is blood dressed as divine election, so that inheritance is read as readiness. The School The school is the house of teaching in the highland capital, endowed by the state and reserved for the sons of the lineages that rule. A boy enters around the threshold of youth and lives inside the house for a fixed course of years, lodged, fed, and formed by the state. Beside it stands the chosen-women's house, where girls taken from across the highlands are enclosed to be trained for the shrine, the loom, and the brewing of the sacred drink. These two houses are the only formal schools the highland has. There is no school for the commons; the ordinary child learns the field and the herd at home, and that learning belongs to the lived day, not to this gate. What this means for the highland is that schooling is not a service a family buys but a favor the state grants. A merchant with silver cannot purchase a place for his son; a village head cannot hire a tutor to teach the cord-records…

Food and cuisine: A port where most of the poor do not cook at all, the table is bought rather than grown, and a sacred calendar turns half the year into fish. The Kitchen and the Craft The Basin kitchen is a workshop, not a hearth. The baker's oven is a brick structure that bakes loaves for a neighborhood; the brewer's vat ferments small beer by the barrel; the curer's salting-shed preserves fish for the lean months. Most of the poor do not cook at home, because the tenement room has no hearth and no place for fuel. They buy ready food from the cook-shop, the street vendor, or the pie-woman at the corner. The merchant townhouse has a kitchen of its own, a hired cook, and a larder of imported goods. The tradesman's wife cooks above the shop on a small hearth, feeding the family between customers. The wage-poor buy a bowl of pottage, a piece of pie, or a loaf and a cup of small beer, and eat it where they stand or carry it to their room. The craft is the same city: bread, roast, pie, and broth; what differs is whether a house owns the means to make them. The cook-shop ordinary is a fixed-price cooked meal served at midday to anyone with the coin; the merchant cook roasts to a…

Food and cuisine: An oasis where water and fuel are too scarce to waste, the date is pressed for the road, and the table is governed less by what a house eats than by what it may not eat and when. The Kitchen and the Craft The oasis kitchen is built around scarcity of fuel and water, not abundance of food. Bread is the daily craft: a thin dough slapped onto the inner wall of a clay oven, or buried in hot sand and ash where there is no oven, and lifted out scorched and flat. The notable house keeps its own clay oven in the court; the lane shares one, and the poor bake in the sand of the threshold. The signature craft is the date-press. Ripe dates are pitted, pounded, and pressed into dense cakes that keep for a year and ride a caravan without spoiling; a well-made cake is worked with a little oil and sometimes ground grain until it holds a clean edge. Milk is soured in the skin overnight; grain is boiled to a porridge over a low fire of dung and brush, because wood is bought, not gathered. The elite court has a kitchen apart and hands to pound and press; the khammes household has one woman, one fire, and the dates she can reach, and her pressing is plainer and her oven is the…

Food and cuisine: A steppe kitchen of dairy and meat preservation, where the shared platter of boiled meat seats rank even as it feeds the camp. The Kitchen and the Craft The Kheshkai craft is preservation more than cooking. Milk is soured, churned, and dried to hard curd that keeps through a winter on the move. Meat is dried in the wind to fine shreds that can be carried in a bag and chewed for days. Fermented mare's milk is brewed for the season and stored in leather churns. Fresh meat, when it comes, is boiled in the one cauldron over the central hearth, not roasted, because fuel is scarce and the cauldron feeds many. The elite camp has several women to churn and dry, store-tents for the products, and churns enough to serve a feast. The middling household has one sound churn and one drying rack; the poor zhataq household has whatever it can carry and whatever a patron has lent. The same souring and drying are done everywhere; what differs is how much can be set aside before the next move. The kitchen is the tent itself. There is no room apart; the hearth is the center, the pots hang from the lattice, and the drying meat swings above the heads of sleepers. A wife's skill is…

Food and cuisine: A floodplain where the same stiff porridge unites the freeborn and divides them from the caste hand that may cook but may not share their pot. The Kitchen and the Craft The Ndjadi kitchen turns on the mortar and the boiling pot. Grain is pounded to flour by women at the mortar, a labor that fills hours of the day and sets the rhythm of the compound. The flour is boiled to a stiff porridge, turned out onto a platter, and covered with a sauce of leaf, dried fish, and oil. The surplus grain is brewed into a thick beer, sour and filling, that accompanies the feast. The elite compound has several women to pound and brew, a separate cooking shed, and enough pots to keep porridge and sauce apart until the moment of serving. The middling house has one woman and one large pot; the one-hut household has one woman, one smaller pot, and a mortar she shares with a neighbor. The craft is the same at every scale; what changes is how many hands can keep the pounding from becoming the whole day. A well-made porridge is smooth and holds its shape when the platter is tilted; a poorly made one is lumpy or too soft to carry the sauce. The beer is judged by its thickness and its…

Food and cuisine: A plateau kitchen built around barley roasted to a meal and kneaded with butter tea, where the monastery's hearth feeds merit and the Lower-Path hand may haul fuel but may not cook. The Kitchen and the Craft The staple Ngaru-Bon craft is roasting barley to a meal that needs no further cooking. The grain is parched in a dry pan over a dung fire until it is brown and fragrant, then ground fine and stored in a jar. To eat it, a person kneads the roasted barley meal with salted butter tea in a bowl until it forms a dough that can be taken by hand. The dough is the ordinary food of the plateau, eaten at dawn, at midday, and whenever work allows a pause. Butter and cheese are pressed from the herd in the warmer valleys and carried up to the high houses. Meat is dried or stewed for festival days. Fuel is the scarce thing: dung patties and scrub twigs are hoarded like grain, and the kitchen's heat is measured out according to the season. The elite house has a separate kitchen that does not share air with the living quarters and enough fuel to keep tea hot through the day. The Lower-Path household hoards a small basket of dung and counts each fire. The craft is in the…

Food and cuisine: An island kitchen where sago is leached by women's hands and whisked to a paste, and the same dish that mends a clan quarrel divides the sexes at the trough. The Kitchen and the Craft The signature Oravan craft is leaching sago. A felled palm is split, the pith is pounded to fiber, and the fiber is washed and squeezed in troughs of water until the starch settles to the bottom. The wet starch is dried into flour, a labor that takes days and turns one palm into the staple of a household. To eat it, the flour is whisked with hot water into a translucent paste that stiffens as it cools. Fish is smoked over the house fire or salted for the days when the catch is poor. The earth oven bakes the feast: a pit lined with heated stones, layered with sago and meat, and covered to steam. The trading house has several troughs and a raised drying platform; the poor longhouse has one trough and shares the labor among the women of the house. The craft is the same everywhere; what differs is how many palms and how many hands stand behind the meal. A well-leached sago is white and fine, without grit or fiber; a poorly leached batch tastes of bark and settles badly in the…

Each of the seven civilizations holds a picture of a proper table, and in each that table is set in full by some and only gestured at by others. But food is also the corpus's most-documented subject already, so this sub-layer is defined as much by what it does not cover as by what it does. It owns the meal as craft, emblem, rule, and trade: how raw becomes edible, the signature dish that marks a people, the taboo and the fast that govern who may eat what and when, and the labor and standing of those who make the food. It does not restate what is grown and traded (, ), what each class eats and with whom (), the poor's diet and famine food (), feast food (), or funerary offerings (); it references them and moves to the kitchen, the emblem, the rule, and the maker those layers never depict. The Frame Per ADR-0031 every per-civ file carries the daily-life pair (ADR-0029) plus one rider. - The Normative Account is the civilization's shared ideal of a proper table, documented as a real social force and marked plainly as the ideal. - The Lived Reality is canon: how the ideal was actually met, by capacity, and how its boundary was enforced. It is concrete (techniques, dishes, rules,…

Food and cuisine: A highland kitchen built around the stone-pit earth oven, where the feast that binds the ayllu is also the rite the kinless cannot host. The Kitchen and the Craft The signature Qollari craft is the stone-pit earth oven: a pit lined with fire-heated stones, the food laid on them, and the whole covered with earth and grass so that meat and tubers bake in their own steam. The elite compound digs a pit wide enough for a llama and a harvest of tubers; the middling farmstead digs a smaller pit for a joints worth of meat and a basket of potatoes; the waqcha roasts tubers in the ash of a scrub fire and rarely tastes meat baked in the earth. Preservation is the other half of the kitchen. Chuño, the freeze-dried tuber, is made by exposing frost-bitten potatoes to the cold night air and trampling out the water, then drying them until they keep for a year. Ch'arki, dried strips of meat, hangs in the storehouse and travels to the terrace. Chicha is brewed from sprouted grain chewed or malted by the household women, fermented in large jars, and skimmed until it is ready for feast or field-payment. The elite house has a kitchen apart, a storehouse, and hands to grind, pound,…

Gender and family: A stateless free-port that prescribes no family of its own, so the gender order runs on registry-standing and the purse, and the naturalization that is called the way of the world everywhere else here wears thin enough to see through. The Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman The Basin prescribes no ideal man or woman of its own. It is a port of many peoples, and each brings its own ideal in with its goods: the river-lord's patriarch, the island matron, the steppe rider, the oasis tent-holder all trade across the same quays and keep their own notions of what a man and a woman are for. What the port itself rewards is narrower and colder: the competent principal, the factor who keeps a clean ledger, honors a contract, and holds registry-standing. That figure is in principle sexless, for a person who can perform the filer's hand and secure standing trades on the same footing whatever their sex, and the port does not ask whose daughter or whose wife stands behind the seal. But the port's own merchant houses are not sexless, because they are made of families that came from somewhere. A Basin-born daughter is raised by her house's lights, and the great trading houses keep…

Gender and family: An oasis order where a noblewoman is her mother's line and a townsman's wife is her husband's roof, and each class calls its own arrangement honor. The Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman In the noble line, the proper Irrah woman is the tent-holder, the literate keeper of the caravan-right and the water-share that pass from mother to daughter. She is the one in whom the noble line settles, the mistress of the tent-qubba and the name that opens doors at the caravan council. The proper noble man is the sister's-son heir and the caravan-master, the one who rides for his mother's line and holds authority only through the women who anchor it. In the town below, the proper man is the head of the house, the one whose name covers wife and children; the proper woman is the wife-to-husband, the manager of his roof and the bearer of sons, whose honor is measured by how well she keeps within his walls. The two ideals live in the same oasis and read each other as failure. The townsfolk see the noblewoman who speaks to factors and rides to council as a woman outside proper seclusion, and they call her freedom license. The nobles see the townsman's wife hauling water in the lane…

Gender and family: A steppe order where the tent rests on the matron's word, the war-band rests on the man's name, and both are called the way the grass is. The Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman The proper Kheshkai woman is the matron of the tent and the line that holds it. She is the one in whom the herd-right and the camp-memory settle, the keeper of the felt-house and the kin who may speak last at the feast. Her virtue is steadiness: she knows which pastures answer to her mother's name, which alliances are owed what, and which daughter will carry the line after her. The proper man is the rider and the war-band leader, the one whose deeds travel on horseback and whose name is sung at the camp-meet. His virtue is skill in the saddle, luck in raid and herd, and the capacity to bring honor inward to the tent he serves. The order is told as the shape of the steppe itself. The woman is rooted like the hearth, the man is mobile like the wind, and a marriage is the meeting of root and motion in the tent. A girl is raised knowing she will one day be the matron; a boy is raised knowing he will ride for a matron's line, his own mother's or his wife's. There is no school, no court of women,…

Gender and family: A river-floodplain order where a man's standing is the size and good order of his compound, and the compound rests on a hierarchy of women, the senior wife over the junior, the mother over the daughters-in-law, ranked as plainly as the tiers of the flood. The Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman The proper Ndjadi man is a holder of people. His standing is the size and good order of his compound: wives, children, dependent kin, clients, and the bondsmen who work his fields, all held in their places and answering to him. A great man is not one who has much but one who holds many, and a household full of well-ordered dependents is the visible proof of a life lived rightly. The proper woman is the mother of his sons and, in time, the manager of his house's women. Her early worth is fertility, the sons who carry the patrilineal name and the daughters whose marriages bind other houses; her later worth is command, the seniority that lets her run the compound's inner life and rule the wives who came after her. The order is told as the shape of the river-country itself. The flood rises and falls in tiers, the land lies in ranked terraces from the water, and a great house…

Gender and family: A plateau order where one roof must hold many brothers, one wife must keep the peace among them, and the undivided plot is called proper husbandry of the household. The Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman The proper Ngaru-Bon man of the lower caste is the household-master, the eldest brother who holds the undivided plot and speaks for the brother-set. His standing is the roof that does not split: he inherits the house, the land, and the right to be called husband first, and a great household-master is one who keeps his brothers under one ridge. The proper woman is the wife-manager, the one wife who enters the brother-set and becomes the sole adult woman of the household, the keeper of its internal order and the distributor of its food, labor, and nights. Her virtue is not submission but stewardship: she must know how to give each brother his place without letting any one of them break the set. The order is told as the shape of the plateau itself. The land is scarce and the plot must not divide, so the brothers are the shoots of one root and the wife is the soil that holds them. A girl is raised knowing she may one day be wife to several men who are also brothers,…

Gender and family: An island order where the lineage settles in its women like the tide returns to the shore, and a man marries by leaving his mother's house to serve his wife's, honored for his making and never the voice of the house he feeds. The Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman The proper Oravan woman is the anchor of a line. She is the one in whom the workshop-lineage settles, the keeper of its craft and its standing, the still point that the canoes return to and the children are born into. Her virtue is not softness but steadiness: she holds the line's name through good seasons and bad, she remembers what each allied house is owed, and she does not let the mana she carries be spent or shamed. The proper man is the maker and the voyager who serves a line, the ship-binder whose hulls are sound and the navigator who brings the boats home. His virtue is skill and the wealth and renown that skill carries inward to a house. He is honored, sometimes greatly, but he is honored as a craftsman is honored, not as a foundation is honored. The order is told as the shape of the world. The mana runs in the female line the way water runs to the sea, and a man, the saying goes, goes where the…

Each of the seven civilizations holds an ideal of the proper family and the proper man and woman, and in each that ideal assigns a person their place by the sex they were born to. This sub-layer owns the lived gender order: the ideal man and woman as social types, marriage as a passage and an alliance, the honor and shame that police conduct before any court convenes, and the people the order has no slot for. It is the corpus's most overlap-heavy lived subject, bordering three owners at once, so it is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate the descent rule, marriage validity, divorce, inheritance, legal personhood, or the adultery sanction ( and ); the household as a physical space, the gendered division of domestic labor, childhood-as-lived, or coming-of-age (); or the gendered religious office as a power body (, ). It references them and moves to the type, the passage, the honor, and the no-slot case those layers never depict. The Frame Per ADR-0034 every per-civ file carries the daily-life pair (ADR-0029) plus one rider. - The Normative Account is the civilization's shared ideal of the proper family and the proper man and woman, documented…

Gender and family: A highland order where the cosmos itself is a pairing, the married adult is the complete one, and every honored exception is licensed by the same pair. The Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman The proper Qollari woman is the earth-mother half of the pair: rooted in the lineage-compound, keeper of the hearth and the loom, the one whose weaving and brewing bind the kin and whose children carry the line. Her domain is real and respected and fixed. The proper man is the sky-father half: the public, ascending figure who renders labor to the lineage, answers for the household at the terrace council, and moves between the compound and the higher rites. His domain is also real and also bounded, but it is the domain that faces outward. The two halves are said to make a single whole, and a life is incomplete until the pair is made. The order is told as the shape of the world. The sky and the earth are the first pair, and every proper household is their image. A girl is raised knowing she will one day be the earth half of a compound; a boy is raised knowing he must become the sky half or fail at adulthood itself. The teaching is not hidden behind a single institution; it is…

The Law's Promise The free-port makes the thinnest promise in the set and keeps it most exactly. It does not claim that justice is one, or that the oath binds all tongues alike, or that the law is no respecter of persons; it has no single cosmos to swear such a thing on. What it promises instead is a clean ledger and a fair price: that a wrong written into a sealed contract will be answered to the letter of the seal, that the forum which hears commercial wrongs is open to any body that can meet its terms, and that the terms are the same terms for everyone. A merchant whose factor is cheated, whose cargo is stolen against a sealed manifest, whose partner absconds, brings the wrong before the port's commercial forum and the wrong is answered, the seal enforced, the loss restored. This is real, and the houses that trade on it trade in good faith on the strength of it; a port that did not keep its seals would have no trade. The promise is that the door is open to all who can pay to come through it, and the port states the price without shame. It is rendered here as the port's account of itself, and the price is exactly the thing the account leaves out. Whose Wrong Is Heard A wrong…

The Law's Promise Irrah tells itself that its justice is the most truthful in the confederation, and the telling is not empty. A wrong properly vouched is properly answered: a body harmed is owed camels, a body killed is owed camels at the dead body's worth, and the worth is reckoned by the chain that vouches it. The forum is real and its parts are many, the Qalib oath-court and the caravan council, so that no single hand holds the whole of justice; and the Qalib seal is the spine of all of it, the sacred register in which a word becomes binding. The reform voices point to the bonded man who served out his years of the road, won his freedom, and was heard at the oath-court as a freedman plaintiff: proof, they say, that the chain is a ladder and not a wall, that a worthy body can win a link and the system will answer. This is the promise the oases make, and the bodies who bring their grievances in good faith make it with full hearts. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and it is not the whole of what happens to a wrong. Whose Wrong Is Heard A wrong reaches the Irrah forum only on the strength of a chain that will vouch it, and how strong a body's chain is was…

The Law's Promise The steppe makes its promise on the strength of the sworn word and the cleansing of a body that will take an oath in the open. There is no standing court that sits whether or not a wrong is brought, no register of crimes, no roll of officers; what there is, when a wrong is grave enough, is the gathering before the judge and the fire, where a man cleanses his word and swears it, and the camp holds the swearing binding. The promise is that a true wrong sworn truly will be answered, that the fire knows a false oath, and that no man, however many his horses, stands above the sworn word of an honest one. The camp believes this and lives by it, because a people that moves and scatters and gathers again cannot run on anything but the word, and a man who is known to have sworn falsely at the fire is a man no one will ride beside. It is a real justice and a hard one, and it is rendered here as the camp's account of itself. What the account does not say aloud is who can bring a wrong to the fire at all, and that is settled long before any oath is sworn, by the strength of the line a body stands in. Whose Wrong Is Heard A wrong is heard on the steppe if a body has the…

The Law's Promise Ndjadi tells itself that its justice is the most ordered in the delta, and the telling is not empty. A wrong properly brought is properly answered: a body harmed is owed grain, a body killed is owed grain at the dead man's worth, and the worth is reckoned, not guessed. The forum is real and its parts are many, so that no single hand holds the whole of justice; the river-court hears the material wrong, the women's council hears the wrong done to a woman or a child or a slave, and the gravest invisible wrong is laid before the ordeal, where the verdict is taken out of any man's mouth. The oath sealed in the sacred register is the spine of all of it, and the man who breaks a sealed oath has broken the one thing the delta holds above commerce. The reform voices go further and call the order meritocratic, pointing to the two bonded men who rose by river-canoe valor to carry a tier-prefix of their own: proof, they say, that the ladder is a ladder and not a wall, that the system answers worth and not only birth. This is the promise the delta makes, and the men who bring their grievances in good faith make it with full hearts. It is rendered here as the order's…

The Law's Promise The plateau holds that its justice is the most ordered under heaven because it is the most fitting: every body has its place in the great frame of castes, and the law answers each according to the place its birth assigns it, so that the high are held to the high duty and the low are spared the burdens they could not bear. A wrong is answered, on this telling, in the measure proper to the bodies it falls between. The monastery court reads the truth of a contested matter where mortal witness fails, and a master who harms his equal pays the full price of the harm, and the frame holds because each body keeps its station and the law keeps faith with the frame. The plateau believes this with real devotion; the high believe they carry a heavier duty for their rank, and many of the low believe the order is the shape of a just heaven and their own low place a thing earned in some former turning of the world. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and the measure proper to a body, the thing the account speaks of so easily, is exactly where the sorting lives. Whose Wrong Is Heard A wrong done to a Ngaru-Bon body is weighed by the caste of that body before…

The Law's Promise The archipelago holds that no wrong stands outside the balance, that every harm done shifts the weight between houses and must be set right so the weight comes level again, and that the gathered assembly exists to read the balance true and name what restores it. A body is not a lone thing before this justice; it is a face of its house, and when it is wronged the house is wronged, and the house carries the grievance to the assembly where the standing of the houses is weighed and the answer is set, a return given, a tapu laid, the balance squared. The promise is that the weight cannot simply be let lie, that a house that does a wrong will be made to restore it or will carry the shame of the unsquared balance, and that the assembly reads truly because the standing of every house depends on the reading being true. This is real and the houses live by it, and a wrong squared at the assembly is squared indeed. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself. What it rests on, and does not say, is that the justice is a justice of houses, and a body with no house behind it has nothing the balance is written to weigh. Whose Wrong Is Heard A wrong is heard in Oravan…

Each of the seven peoples holds a picture of one justice that binds all: that a wrong will be answered, that the oath is sacred, that the forum is no respecter of persons. This sub-layer owns the asymmetric structure underneath that picture. Its subject is not the court and its bodies, nor the evidentiary primitive each people runs on, nor the catalog of crimes, nor the repertoire of punishments, nor the written grid of who may testify, but what that machinery does to a body: whose wrong is heard and answered and whose is swallowed before it becomes a case, and whose body the law shields while it reaches another body only to discipline it. It builds the lived layer on top of the machinery that ADR-0018 gated and the family documents. It does not restate the court, the primitive, the catalog, the punitive repertoire, or the codified standing-and-witness grid, all of which owns; the recoding of capable labor into supply, which owns; the standing condition of the poor, which owns; the oath and the sacred register as a certification mechanism, which and own; enforcement and policing as institution, which owns; or the grievance dismissed because the wronged is a woman, which owns.…

The Law's Promise Qollari tells itself that the sun-favored state knows every body that matters, and the telling is not empty. A wrong brought by a counted body is reckoned: the registered mason, the cloister weaver, the attached specialist whose name sits in the cord-record, can carry a harm before the hundred-family officer and see it entered, measured, and answered. The khipu cord-record is the spine of this, the thing that writes a body into the count and writes the wrong against the body that did it, and a reading in the proper register seals what no memory alone could hold. The state promises that it will know a wrong when the wronged is known to it, that the specialist it has attached and provisioned will find the law at his back, and that the count keeps justice as it keeps tribute, straight and name by name. The promise is real for those whose names the count has chosen to keep, and they bring their grievances in good faith. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and it is not the whole of what happens to a wrong. Whose Wrong Is Heard Whether a wrong is heard is settled before it is spoken, by whether the count has attached the wronged body to a name the…

Signature migration: the clearing-house where every people's movement converges, a city built entirely of arrivals, where a person belongs not by birth or welcome but by the seals that vouch for him, and the uncertified of any origin is invisible. The Journey and the Arrival A person comes to the free-port the way a ship comes, from anywhere and for a reason of trade. The merchant arrives with goods and a letter from a house in his home city and is received at once into the strangers' business, given a berth and a clerk and a rate. The laborer arrives on the same deck with nothing but his hands and is received by no one, set loose on a waterfront that has work for him and no place for him. The bonded sold off a ship from the oasis or the islands arrives owned, changed from one owner's ledger to another's on the quay. And the child is born into the port to parents who came from two different peoples and a grandmother from a third, a native of the only city on the continent with no native stock. There is no gate-rite and no guest-law here, no sovereign's welcome and no shaman's oath; there is the harbor, the customs-slate, and the question every arrival is asked in the end, which…

Signature migration: the caravan city that every people crosses, where the free merchant passes through in a season and the debt-sold and the captive arrive to stay, kept in oasis households until their strongest years are spent. The Journey and the Arrival A person comes to the oasis belt in one of two ways, and the way decides almost everything that follows. The merchant arrives on his own beasts with his own goods, pays the gate, takes a room in the strangers' quarter, and is gone again before the wells turn over, one more transit in a city built for transit. The bonded arrives roped to a string of others, walked across the sand from a famine valley or a raided camp many wells away, sold once at the start of the road and again at its end, and set down in a household whose tongue he does not yet speak. The first crossing is measured in the price of water and the wear on a camel. The second is measured in the distance from everything the walker knew, and it is meant to be too far to walk back. The desert is the same desert to both, but the merchant carries the means to cross it and the bonded is carried across it as freight. Who Belongs, Who Is Absorbed, Who Is Moved Reception…

Signature migration: the absorbed incomer, the refugee who fled to the felt tents or the captive carried back from a raid, made fully of the people within a generation, so that the steppe leaves no diaspora behind it because everything it takes in it dissolves. The Journey and the Arrival Coming to the steppe is rarely a thing a person chooses on his own beasts. The settled refugee arrives at the felt tents driven by a worse fear behind him, a failed harvest or a lord's levy or a war in the lowlands, and he comes asking to be taken in. The captive arrives slung across a saddle, taken in a raid on a caravan or a border village, carried days from where he was seized so that the distance itself forbids return. Either way the arrival is the same in the end: a stranger set down among riders whose life he cannot yet live, who cannot mount or milk or strike a tent, and who is therefore nothing until he learns. The steppe does not house a guest in a quarter of his own as the oasis does; it folds him into a tent and waits for him to become a member of it. The journey ends not at a door but at the moment the newcomer is handed a task and expected to do it as one of the household. Who…

Signature migration: the floodplain bureaucracy receives the stranger by classifying him, assigning a cosmic rank that makes him legible to the ledger and invisible until it is done. The Journey and the Arrival The journey ends at the water-gate, where the river meets the walled town and every arrival must pass between the scribe's booth and the customs house. The foreigner who steps off the boat with goods to sell is not yet real to the delta; he is a body with cargo until a scribe assigns him the prefix that places him in the cosmic ledger and the tax roll. The same boat may carry a merchant with a letter from a known house, who is classified before his sandals touch the quay, and a deckhand from the upriver forests who will spend three days waiting on a bench before he learns whether he exists at all. The journey is therefore measured not only in leagues of brown water but in the number of seals a man can produce, the fee he can pay, and the face he presents to the scribe. Arrival is the moment the prefix is written; until then the stranger is economically invisible, able to sleep on the quay and eat what he brought, but unable to hire a boat, rent a room, or sign a contract…

Signature migration: the plateau's forge-town opens its trade to the stranger but keeps the forge sealed, while bonded miners and porters are drawn in from below to the work the guild families will not touch. The Journey and the Arrival The journey to the plateau ends at the trading town that clings to the edge of the heights, where the caravan road from the lowlands meets the stone paths that climb to the monastery and the forge. The foreign merchant arrives with pack animals and samples of metal, glad to find a market that pays well for goods the high country cannot easily produce. The labor migrant arrives with empty hands and a strong back, hoping to porter loads up the mountain for a season's wage. The bonded miner arrives roped to a string of others, walked from a lowland debt-court or a raid's aftermath (the war act that produced the raid belongs to and is not retold here) to the mouth of an adit where the air is cold and the rock is wet. All three stand in the same square, but the square is not the same place for each of them. The merchant sees an open town and a just price; the porter sees a steep path and a hard bed; the bonded sees the gate of a mine he did not…

Signature migration: the archipelago receives the sea-stranger through port-mixing, sea-marriage, and the daughter-house, because a maritime people cannot afford to refuse whoever the tide brings. The Journey and the Arrival The journey to the archipelago ends where the reef meets the beach and the outriggers are drawn up above the tide-line. The foreign captain arrives with a hold of trade goods and a letter from a house in a distant port, expecting to exchange iron and cloth for shell, spice, and fresh water. The in-married spouse arrives in the bridal canoe, sent from one island to another to seal an alliance between workshop-lineages, carrying a dowry of tools and a name that will be folded into the husband's house. The foreign deckhand arrives with a bundle and a willingness to haul line, having signed on at a foreign quay for a season's wage and a share of whatever the voyage brings. The boat-poor arrival comes with neither goods nor family, pushed by a bad season or a debt cleared by exile, hoping to be absorbed into the lowest rung of a workshop-lineage before the next monsoon. All four step onto the same sand, but the sand asks each a different question: what can you…

Each of the seven peoples has a signature way of receiving the stranger, set by its political economy and its basis of identity: the state that resettles whole communities by program, the bureaucracy that classifies the incomer before he may exist, the steppe that absorbs him totally, the guild that keeps him forever outside, the oasis that transits the merchant and keeps the bonded, the archipelago that cannot afford to refuse him, and the free-port that sells him a seal in place of a welcome. This sub-layer owns the cross-class lived experience of moving and the diaspora that movement makes: the journey, the arrival, what the crossing costs, the community a people of arrivals builds, the generational becoming, and who is moved as property. It is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate who can belong and the identity-theory of phenotype, assimilation, and gatekeeping (owned by ADR-0015); the standing poverty of the poor (); the acute environmental shock that drives flight (); the war act and captive-taking (); the trade mechanics (); pilgrimage theology (); or the travel-time routes (the geography spatial layer). It references them and moves to…

Signature migration: the highland empire moves whole communities by program, planting loyal colonists among loyal strangers and lifting restive ones away, feeding the resettled from the state granary last and watching them first. The Journey and the Arrival The journey begins with an order written in the capital's cord-house and carried down to the valley by a steward's runner. The household chosen for resettlement is given a count of days to gather its loom, its seed, and the bones of its dead, and then it marches up the road that switchbacks through the cold grasses to a basin it has never seen. Some go as loyal colonists, promised a terrace and a ration for their service to the crown; others go as the price of a valley's restiveness (the war act that produced it belongs to and is not retold here), so that the land they leave behind can be repopulated by those the state trusts. The climb is the first lesson. The lowlander who comes up gasps at the thin air and finds that the work he could do at home exhausts him after a morning here, while the highlander sent down to the warm valleys is told he has been honored with grain and soft air but walks the low roads like a man…

The family documents how Veydrians actually lived, as distinct from the structures that governed them. The law layer records what the slavery grades were and how manumission worked; the economy layer records what each civilization traded and what it could not do without. This family records the rest: what a person ate, where they slept, what a bad year did to them, and what small moves let one rise. It is the texture the structural layers imply but never depict. The Family Remit is orthogonal to the control layers, not a duplicate of them. It reads and and shows where they land on a body. A file here earns its place only by adding lived texture that the legal and economic documents never see. It does not restate stratification grids, slavery grades, or commodity tables; it references them and moves on. The Asymmetric Frame Where a Veydrian institution carries a contested meaning, this family does not always hold the two readings as co-equal. The religion layer holds the practitioner and skeptic accounts of death as equally true because the afterlife is genuinely undecidable (ADR-0026). Poverty is different. Per the realism discriminator (ADR-0018), the structural account of who…

The Order's Promise The free-port makes a thinner promise about its patrons than the kingdoms do, because it has no sovereign to dress the tie in fatherhood and no single cult to call it sacred. What the port says is that a man of standing on the waterfront, a broker who can vouch a stranger and carry his word across the lines that have no court to bind them, is a convenience the small trader could not do without, and that the convenience is fairly paid. The port is proud that a body with nothing but a cargo and a good name can find a broker to introduce it, stand surety for it, and open a door into a house that would otherwise never deal with it, and the broker who does this is reckoned a useful man and the trader he lifts speaks well of him. There is truth in it; the introduction was real, the deal was made, the small trader rose. This is the nearest the Basin comes to the kingdoms' promise of the protecting patron, that the broker's favor is a service honestly rendered and honestly bought, and the brokers who place a rising trader well make the claim without blushing. It is the port's account of itself, and it is thinner than it sounds. What Binds a Client A body comes under…

The Order's Promise The oasis tells itself that a great landholder is the keeper of the water and the shelter of those who drink it, and that the keeping is a trust as much as a possession. He maintains the channel that no single household could dig or clean alone, he carries the smallholder through the year the dates fail, and he takes the landless body into his following and gives it a turn of water it would not otherwise have, and in return the body gives its labor at the channel-mouth and its loyalty at the council, and the oasis calls this the right order of a dry country. A landholder is measured by the households that drink from his share, and a man who has kept a client family watered through three poor seasons is honored for it and the family calls him their protector. They do not lie; the water came, the dates were eaten, the children lived. This is the promise the ksar makes about its men of water, that the one who holds the channel holds it for the weak as well as himself and that the tie between the holder and the watered is a tie of guardianship answered by faith. The men who water their clients in a dry year make the promise in earnest. It is the order's account…

The Order's Promise The steppe tells itself that a wealthy camp-head is the sky's blessing made visible, and that the blessing is meant to be shared. When a hard winter ruins a man, the rich camp does not let him lie down; it gives him animals on saun, enough breeding stock that his household keeps milk through the summer and his name stays off the list of the zhataq.
