In return the borrower guards the animals, grazes them, and gives back the original stock at the agreed season, and the camp calls this the plain duty of the blessed toward the tested. The steppe is proud that a ruined man can find a door into a richer camp, that the lender is honored for the lending and the borrower is grateful for the lift, and that the bond between them is a kind of herding kinship, a camp-head acting as father to a man whose own fortune has failed. There is truth in it; the mare was real, the milk filled the bowl, the children grew. This is the promise the steppe makes about its wealthy camps, that the strong herd shelters the weak and the bond between the lender and the borrower is a bond of care answered by faith. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and the camp-heads who…

The Order's Promise The river-country tells itself that a great house is a roof a small body may shelter under, and that the sheltering is good on both sides. A holder of people keeps grain against the bad flood-year, stands the surety when a dependent is taken to the bureau, and redeems the pawn before the debt swallows the family whole; in return a man gives his loyalty, his paddle, his watch at the warehouse door, and the country calls this fair. The delta is proud of its strong houses and reckons a house great by the people it can feed, so that a river-lord with a hundred clients is honored for the hundred and the hundred name him father. A canoe-man who has weathered three droughts under one house will say the house carried him, and he is not lying, for it did. This is the promise the delta makes about its great men, that the strong arm is a kind arm and the bond between the holder and the held is a bond of care answered by faith. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and the men who feed their clients in good years make the promise with full hearts. It is not the whole of what the holding does to the held. What Binds a Client A body comes under a house…

The Order's Promise The plateau tells itself that a lord who holds dependents is also a lord who keeps them, and that the bond between them is a kind of household care. When a bound man needs to travel for seasonal work, his lord grants him mi-bogs, the human lease, an annual fee that buys the body physical mobility without severing the tie that holds it; when the traveler returns, the household is still his household and the lord is still his lord. The Lower-Path lines and the monastic houses speak of the lease as mercy, a way for a dependent to breathe without breaking the household, and they are honored for granting it. There is truth in it; the man walked, he earned a little salt, he came back. This is the promise the plateau makes about its lords and its monastic houses, that a bound body is still a body under protection, and that the lease is the proof: the lord could have held him fast, and instead lengthened the rope. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and the lords who grant the lease make the promise with full hearts. It is not the whole of what the lease does to the bound body. What Binds a Client A body comes under a lord when it needs a thing the…

The Order's Promise The archipelago tells itself that a house is a hull that must take on water to stay afloat, and that a house which absorbs the wrecked, the foreign, and the orphaned is a house the sea has made strong. A matron takes in a man whose own line has failed, gives him a place at her hearth, a share of the catch, and a name to sail under, and in return he gives his labor and his loyalty; the alliance calls this the way the islands stay whole, for the sea kills houses as easily as it makes them. The archipelago is proud that a body with no matriline can find a house to belong to, that the house which takes it in is honored for the taking, and that the bond between the absorbed and the absorber is a kind of kinship, a shelter answered by faith. There is truth in it; the place was real, the share fed him, the name kept him from being unanchored. This is the promise the islands make about their great houses, that the strong house shelters the weak and the bond between the one who gives a place and the one who takes it is a bond of care answered by service. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and the matrons who take in the off-line make the promise…

Each of the seven peoples holds a picture that the bond between a strong body and a weak one is a bond of care: that the patron shelters and the client serves, that a favor given freely earns a loyalty owed freely, and that the tie between them is a kind of kinship and a ladder the low may climb. This sub-layer owns the asymmetric structure underneath that picture. Its subject is not the poverty a body falls into, nor the trade it is named into, nor the kin it is born to, but the tie that binds one body to one patron by a favor it needed, could not refuse, and cannot leave. It is the final lived-experience layer of the campaign. It does not restate the standing condition of the poor or the debt designed never to clear, which owns; the maker's mark and the chain of names that recognizes a maker, which owns; real kinship, marriage, and household authority, which owns; or the codified bond-status, the pawnship contract, and the blood-price schedule as statute, which owns. It references them and writes the favor-bond on top. The Frame Per ADR-0043 patronage and clientage takes the asymmetric frame of ADR-0027 (underclass), ADR-0028 (warfare), ADR-0035 (catastrophe), ADR-0036…

The Order's Promise The highland tells itself that the mountain house is a single great household, and that the sovereign who sits at its head is the Huaccha Khoyaq, the lover of the poor. In the bad year it is the state's qollqa that opens, the state granary that pours out the grain a ruined household could not have saved, and the state terrace that takes the levied hand and feeds it before it works. A lord who attaches a yana to his compound gives the kinless man a roof, a ration, and a place in the labor roll; in return the man gives his service, and the country calls this the sacred pact by which extraction is repaid as security. The highland is proud that its storehouses prevent famine, that its lords are obliged to feed the mouths the mountain has ruined, and that a household which serves the state is a household the state carries. There is truth in it; the grain came, the children ate, the terrace stood. This is the promise the highland makes about its sovereign and its lords, that the strong mountain shelters the weak and the bond between the office and the dependent is a ladder any loyal hand may climb. It is rendered here as the order's account of itself, and the…

Performance and play: A stateless port where the guild procession, the licensed play, and the printed ballad turn the street into a market of spectacle. The Forms The Basin arts are the staged civic procession, the guild play, and the printed ballad. The procession is the city's public body: guilds, confraternities, and trading houses march in order, wearing their colors, carrying their signs, and displaying their place in the port's economy. The guild play is a scripted performance, often comic or moral, staged at the guild hall or in a hired yard. The printed ballad is the one mechanically reproduced art in the world. A single sheet can carry a song across the city in a day, and the ballad-printer sells the song as a commodity, the first performer who needs no stage. The merchant patronizes the full procession and the pageant; the tradesman joins his guild's march and watches the play from a good corner; the wage-poor buy the ballad sheet if they can read or hear it sung in a tavern. The same spectacle moves through every rank, but the capacity to commission it shrinks with each floor. Occasions and Performance The civic festival, the guild feast, and the market-day spectacle…

Performance and play: An oasis evening where the poem, the tale, and the contest honor the house, and the poor man's theater is the story he tells for coins. The Forms The Irrah arts are the poem, the evening song, and the told tale. The poem is the lineage's honor-instrument: a well-composed verse can praise a house, fix a genealogy, or shame a rival before the whole oasis. The elite lineage maintains a composed cycle of praise that is recited at weddings, funerals, and the arrival of great caravans. The middling household knows the shorter praise-verses and the standard tales; at the feast they join in the refrains and add a riddle or a proverb. The poor possess storytelling, already called the poor man's theater: he cannot sponsor the feast, but he can know the same poems and laugh at the same jokes. The same evening breeze carries the songs from the merchant's court to the khammes lane. What differs is whose name the song pronounces. Occasions and Performance The caravan's arrival and the seasonal festivals fill the cool of evening with performance. A notable lineage hosts the gathering in its guest hall or in the open court, providing dates, meat, and sweet tea; its poet…

Performance and play: A steppe gathering where the epic, the contest, and the host's hospitality carry a name across the camp-circle. The Forms The Kheshkai arts are the sung epic, the camp-meet contest, and the fireside tale. The epic is the only durable art in a culture that carries nothing it cannot pack; it travels in memory, not in goods. A great herd-owner may commission a long cycle that binds his lineage to the sky, the herd, and the founding camps; the same cycle is sung in humbler tents by anyone who has learned the verses. The middling household knows the shorter songs and the contest-chants that mark a meet. The poor zhataq has only the voice and the memory; he cannot commission, but he can still add a verse, correct a line, or carry the tale to the next fire. Here the elite own the feast and the bard's keep, not the art itself. The song belongs to whoever can remember it. Occasions and Performance The camp-meet is the stage on which Kheshkai rank is renewed. The host provides the feast, the prizes, and the fire around which the camps gather; his tent is the largest, his hospitality sets the scale, and his name is attached to the season. Marriages are arranged,…

Performance and play: A floodplain festival where the drum, the praise-song, and the dance make a house's name public, and the poor arrive only as guests. The Forms The Ndjadi arts are the drum, the praise-song, the dance, and the evening tale. The elite compound maintains its own drummer and its own praise-singer, whose verses bind the household's genealogy to the names of rivers, ancestors, and great deeds. The praise-song is not mere entertainment; it is a genealogical instrument that fixes where a house stands. A middling trader may hire a single drummer for a marriage or a naming day, and his household learns the simpler praise-verses that any compound of standing is expected to know. The poor possess the voice, the clap, the dance step, and the proverb; their art needs no instrument and no retained singer. The same drum rhythms move through every compound, but the great house owns the full cycle, while the one-hut household knows only the refrain. Occasions and Performance The seasonal festivals tied to flood and harvest draw the whole community to the riverbank or the market square. The big man sponsors the feast, the beer, the meat, and the music; his compound fills…

Performance and play: A plateau festival where the monastery stages theology, the lay contests run below the citadel, and the Lower-Path line runs through every performer. The Forms The great Ngaru-Bon arts are the masked spectacle and the painted icon. The masked dance is theology made visible: the figures who appear in the courtyard embody forces, virtues, and warnings, and their movements are read as doctrine acted out. The painted icon is the plateau's high visual art, produced in monastery workshops and in the studios of elite houses, its mineral colors fixed on cloth or wood. A great house may commission an icon for its shrine room and sponsor a masked dance at the festival; a middling smith household may pay for a small protective image and a single dancer's appearance at a family rite. The poor possess the chanted prayer, the watched spectacle, and the road-song; their art is the eye and the voice, not the brush or the mask. The same sacred figures move across every rank, but only some households can commission their making. Occasions and Performance The monastic festival-day gathers the plateau before the citadel. The monastery and the elite house sponsor the butter,…

Performance and play: A longhouse feast where the gong-and-drum ensemble and the shadow-and-mask play bind the blood-alliance, and the bird-fight vents its rivalries. The Forms The Oravan arts are the gong-and-drum ensemble and the shadow-and-mask play. The ensemble is the alliance's voice: a set of tuned gongs and drums played by ranked musicians, its rhythms announce the feast, accompany the dance, and mark the passage of the rites that bind villages. The shadow-and-mask play is ritual theater, performed behind a lit screen with carved figures and masked dancers, telling the stories of ancestors, alliances, and the sea. A great trading house sponsors the full ensemble and commissions a shadow play for a major alliance rite. A middling longhouse may field a smaller drum group and a single episode of the play at a village feast. The poor possess the dance step, the chorus, and the tale told by firelight; their art needs no gong and no carved screen. The same rhythms and stories move through every house, but the scale of their performance is measured by the rice and the alliance credit a house can command. Occasions and Performance The great leisure is the communal feast, which…

Each of the seven civilizations holds a picture of a life rightly graced: a feast honored with song, a name carried in praise, a festival kept, a contest honorably won. In each, that grace is commissioned in full by some, joined by others, and only received by the poorest, who hold instead the forms that need no capital: the voice, the footrace, the riddle, the known tale. This sub-layer documents what was actually sung, danced, told, made, played, and contested across the whole social range, and who made it and at what standing. It is the performance companion to , which owns festival as rest; this layer owns performance as content and the games and sport the corpus was otherwise silent on. It does not restate ritual chant and sacred iconography (), the sung epic as a record medium (), or the day off and who hosts it (); it references them and moves to the performance and play they imply but never depict. The Shared-Script and Licensed-Inversion Frame Per ADR-0030 every per-civ file carries the daily-life pair (ADR-0029) plus one rider. The ideal of a graced life is held across all classes, aspired to by the poor as much as staged by the rich; what divides people is the…

Performance and play: A highland feast where the host's cloth, song, and calendar processional measure ayllu standing, and the poor enter with voice and body alone. The Forms The highest Qollari art is cloth. A great house commissions a qompi hanging whose dyed wool and tight weave record lineage and calendar in a single surface; the same banner may hang in the reception room, be carried in the processional, and later be given to a shrine. The calendar processional is the public form of this art. At sowing, frost-watch, and harvest the image of the season is carried from shrine to courtyard, accompanied by the song the daily round already knows. The elite sponsor both the cloth and the singers; a middling household may contribute a lesser banner or a jar of chicha, and its women weave the simpler stripes that line the route. The poor possess the capital-free forms: the voice, the dance step, the known tale, and the riddle. Their performance needs no loom, no dyed wool, no storehouse of meat. Skill is everywhere; what differs is the medium that carries it. Occasions and Performance The feast is the stage on which rank is displayed. The sponsoring ayllu head sits under his own…

Signature sickness: in the free-port an illness carries no verdict, because the city has no single cosmos to read it as anything; it carries a price, and what the sick poor receive is decided not by what their suffering means but by what their bodies cost and what they can pay. The Affliction and the Sickbed The free-port's slow killer is the urban wasting, the consumption that ecology documents under the tenement's name (the mechanism is not retold here), and its sickbed is a rented pallet in a crowded room above a wharf or a dye-yard. The Basin is a city of arrivals packed into cheap rooms, and its signature illness is the one that breeds in exactly that, the long cough that thins a worker over a year or two of work he cannot stop doing until he can no longer do it at all. What is distinct about the Basin sickbed is not the disease, which the marshes and the ships and the crowding produce in their own ways elsewhere, but the absence over it of any story about why. In the forge-towns and the highlands a wasting is read as a verdict, a mark, a judgment, a thing the ancestors or the gods have done. In the free-port it is read as a fact of the ledger: a body that is failing, a…

Signature sickness: in the oasis drylands the sick-role is a good for sale, granted lavishly at the top of the market and denied flat at the bottom, and the same wasting is an honored debt in one chest and an unprofitable weakness in another. The Affliction and the Sickbed Irrah's signature illness is the slow stone chest of the wind-reader and the creeping blindness of trachoma, both documented by ecology as the occupational cost of reading sand at eye level and living in dust. Here the sickbed is a marker of price. In a deep house it is a curtained alcove with fresh linen, rosewater, and a servant to lift the patient; in a bonded dormitory it is a roll of felt in a corner where a man lies until his arms are worth more than his keep. The same wasting looks different depending on what the household can spend on it, and the first question asked at any sickbed is not what the man has but what he is owed. Who Is Permitted to Be Sick The propertied merchant and the oath-bound scholar are permitted illness as an extension of their contracts. Their sick-role is bought in advance through the wealth that summons the healer, the household that can release them, and the convalescent's…

Signature sickness: on the steppe an illness is measured against the season the camp must move, and the line a sick body falls on, whether it can ride when the herd does or cannot, decides almost everything that follows. The Affliction and the Sickbed The steppe sickbed is a place inside a thing that travels. A man laid up with the undulant fever or a hunter taken by the marmot-sickness (ecology documents both, and the mechanism is not retold here) lies on felt in a tent that will be struck and moved when the grass thins and the herd walks on. That fact sits over every illness on the steppe and makes the central question not what is wrong with him but will he be able to ride when we go. An illness that burns and breaks within a season is one the camp can wait out or carry through, a known passage with a known end. An illness that lingers, that leaves a man alive but unable to mount and hold a saddle for a day's drive, becomes something the steppe has no comfortable place for: a passenger in a way of life that has no room for passengers, a body the camp must either slow itself around or leave behind. Who Is Permitted to Be Sick The right to be ill on the steppe is the right to…

Signature sickness: on the floodplain an illness is only as real as the record that names it, and the chronic wasting of the paddy-laundress is never granted the sick-role because the work that makes her ill cannot stop. The Affliction and the Sickbed The Ndjadi signature is the chronic low-grade wasting of paddy and laundry labor: blood in the urine, the swollen belly, the fever that returns with the rains. Ecology documents these as the constant background of the floodplain, so ordinary that they are barely named as disease. The sickbed is not always a bed; it is a mat in the corner of the hut where a woman lies while the household decides whether what she has is an affliction that can be shown to the scribe or merely the ordinary cost of working in the water. Because the condition never announces itself with a single dramatic day, the household must argue, sometimes for years, over whether the sufferer is genuinely ill or simply slow. Who Is Permitted to Be Sick The titled, the lineage head, the man whose corvée can be deferred by a scribe's notation, is sick in full. His wasting is named, entered, and granted the rituals of rest: the household stops, the healer is called,…

Signature sickness: on the forge-plateau the long illness is not only a thing that happens to a chest but a thing that gets read, and the reading decides whether a man is tended as the work's honored casualty or cast out as a man the ancestors have marked. The Affliction and the Sickbed The plateau's signature illness is slow. The smelter wastes by the long cough ecology documents, taken over years rather than days, and that slowness is what makes the illness a social event rather than a private one. A fever burns and breaks; a wasting sits in a household for seasons, a man who can still talk and bless and eat but can no longer carry, a pair of hands subtracted from the work while a mouth stays at the bowl. The sickbed is a mat near the central hearth where the smoke is, set among the household that must decide, season by season, what the man on it now is. There is no moment of becoming sick that the plateau recognizes. There is only the gradual settling of a verdict, as the cough deepens and the household waits to learn whether the wasting will be called the furnace's honest cost or something the man earned. Who Is Permitted to Be Sick The right to be ill on the plateau runs…

Signature sickness: in the volcanic archipelago the terms of illness are set by the voyage, and a sailor who cannot pull is a cost the crew cannot carry, nursed if he may recover and put ashore when he may not. The Affliction and the Sickbed Oravan's signature illness is the body failing at sea: the leg-swelling and breathlessness of the rice-fed sailor, the sudden fever that breaks a crew's numbers, the sores that turn a man lame on a deck where every hand is counted. Ecology documents these as the constant cost of the spice trade, but what the sailor experiences is not epidemiology; it is the closing-in of a wooden hull, the distance from any land that might take him, and the knowledge that his shipmates cannot spare him. The sickbed on an archipelago ship is a swaying mat between cargo, and the sickbed on land is the hut a man returns to when the sea has finished with him. Who Is Permitted to Be Sick At sea, permission is set by the voyage. A sailor who may recover before the next leg is nursed, because a trained hand is worth more than the rice he eats while lying down. A sailor who cannot recover is put ashore at the next island, sometimes gently and sometimes with a coin…

Each of the seven peoples has a signature way of deciding what an illness means and what the sick are owed, set by its political economy and the reading its order gives an afflicted body: the empire that rations care outward from its center, the bureaucracy that grants no rest to a sickness it has not classified, the steppe that cannot carry the one who cannot move, the forge that reads a wasting as a verdict and shuns the marked, the oasis that sells the right to be sick as it sells everything else, the archipelago that sets the terms of illness by the sea, and the free-port that prices the sick body instead of judging it. This sub-layer owns the cross-class lived experience of being sick: the sickbed, the sick-role granted or denied, the nursing and its cost, the one who never recovers, and how the order's moral reading of affliction sorts the household. It is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate the medicine (what each disease is, the practitioners and their authority, the pharmacopeia, the quarantena, the divination that names a cause), all of which documents; the moment of death and its rites (); the standing poverty of the poor (); the…

Signature sickness: in the highland empire the right to stop and be nursed runs downhill from the imperial center, and the miner whose chest fails in the silver mountains is spent as the mine spent him, not tended as the center tends its own. The Affliction and the Sickbed The Qollari illness that shapes the household is the long chest-wasting of the mine and the quarry, the slow breathlessness that ecology documents among the men who drill the mine face and breathe its dust and fumes. In the core, the same affliction may visit a clerk or a minor official who has never seen a mine, and there it is a private matter of the hearth. In the periphery it is a public condition, a man's failing lungs becoming the household's central accounting problem: who will carry his quota, who will take his place at the waystation, whether the daughter set to nurse him can also grind the day's maize. The sickbed is a low pallet near the wall where the cold enters, and the sick man lies between the center that has forgotten him and the household that cannot afford him. Who Is Permitted to Be Sick Imperial households tied to the order by tribute, office, or kin to a waystation administrator are…

Underclass: Casual wage-laborers, dockworkers, bankrupt factors, and destitute in-migrants of the Outer Quarters in the grain-import free-port. Who the Poor Are The Basin has no internal slavery, so its poverty is urban and wage-based. Day-laborers on the quays, dockworkers hired by the load, bankrupt factors, and destitute in-migrants from upstream civilizations make up the poor. The bottom of the bottom lives in the Outer Quarters at Dzong-Tamu, the slum that already appears in canon. A person falls by injury, blacklist, failed speculation, or simply by arriving faster than work appears. Daily Life and Subsistence Bread, watered wine, onions, and salted fish are the ordinary diet, and it rides the grain price. In a dearth the poor shift to coarse grains and foraged starch from the lagoon margins. Housing is a cramped tenement room shared by several families or a pallet in a confraternity hall. They own the clothes they stand in, a knife, perhaps a barrow or a set of hooks for unloading. Scarcity and Famine The Basin grows nothing; it is a clearing-house economy entirely dependent on imported grain. A bad harvest upstream, a blockaded river, or a disrupted caravan route spikes…

Underclass: Oasis sharecroppers, servile herders, and transient caravan porters who live below the documented caste tiers and outside the monopoly of water. Who the Poor Are Below the Imajīn, Ḥarrāb, Ghūlām, and Qalībin tiers and outside the Azmarāʔ caste stand the khammes, the fifth-share sharecroppers of the date-palm oases, and the bonded herders who tend camels they do not own. Above them in precarity are the caravan porters and water-carriers who service the routes Irrah controls. Caste endogamy and the water-monopoly fix their station as firmly as chains, even where the law stops short of calling them slaves. Daily Life and Subsistence The oasis garden is three-tiered: date palms above, fruit trees below, and cereals in the understory. The khammes household does the clearing, the channeling, and the hand-pollination of the palms, then takes one-fifth of the harvest. The herder lives on pastoral millet and camel-milk. Famine-foods are wild desert grass-seed and roasted locust, eaten in the very plagues that cause the dearth. A khammes family owns a few pots, a mattock, and the right to sleep in a mud-brick room that belongs to the landholder. Scarcity and Famine…

Underclass: Herders who have lost their stock to winter kill or misfortune and fallen into dependence at the settled margins of the steppe. Who the Poor Are The zhataq, the ones who lie down, are herders with too few animals to migrate and live as Kheshkai should. A man with fewer than five horses is compromised; a household that loses its breeding stock to a dzud must settle at the edge of a town or attach to a richer camp. This is downward mobility, not caste. A zhataq may have been a prosperous herder two winters ago; birth means nothing when the herd is gone. Daily Life and Subsistence Dairy, curds, and airag are rationed or absent. The poor eat marmot and other small game, wild onion, and traded millet bought with odd jobs. A patched and under-insulated ger is colder than the portable homes of the mobile camps, because the poor cannot afford new felt and cannot follow the herds to better pasture. Prime horses are too valuable to eat; they belong to the lender or the patron. Scarcity and Famine The dzud, the winter herd-kill, is the great catastrophe. A single bad winter of ice-crust and cold can annihilate a family's biological capital and leave them with nothing. Distress…

Underclass: River-plain laborers and craft families bound by interest-only pawn-debt to river-lords and merchants in a wealth-in-people economy. Who the Poor Are Below the documented noun-class tiers are the pawned, the nyamakala craft-castes, and the mosque mendicants. The pawned are usually children or young adults given as interest on a grain debt; the nyamakala are smiths, leatherworkers, and lower jeli whose endogamous trades fix their standing; the mosque poor are those who have no patron and survive on alms. In a society that counts wealth in people, to have no dependents and no master is the most exposed condition. Daily Life and Subsistence The ordinary meal is millet or sorghum porridge with baobab leaf and dried fish from the river. During the brief fertile window after the inundation families hoe the heavy black soil from dawn to dusk. Mud-brick and thatch houses cluster near the water; in the cities the poorest sleep in the mosque courtyards or in the lee of river warehouses. They own little beyond a hoe, a cooking pot, and the debts their parents contracted. Scarcity and Famine Multi-year drought is the recurring catastrophe, and unlike the highland states Ndjadi…

Underclass: Ore-haulers, coal-burners, forge-tenders, and other bonded laborers whose blood-price is a fraction of the elite rate and whose work is fixed by ritual-pollution doctrine. Who the Poor Are The polyandrous-lower-caste, perhaps three households in five, perform the heavy labor of the plateau mines and estates. Ore-haulers carry ingots down mountain tracks; forge-tenders breathe coal smoke and beat metal for the Inner-Council smith elite; disposal workers handle the dead and the waste that ritual doctrine declares impure. Below them all are the landless rationed servants tied to an estate. Their stong, the blood-price, is set at a fortieth of the elite rate, which is itself a measure of how little standing the law grants them. Daily Life and Subsistence The daily ration is barley tsampa and butter tea, enough to work but not enough to thrive. Bonded miners sleep in stone barracks or lean-tos near the workings; forge-tenders live in segregated quarters at the edge of the smith precinct. When the lord's stores are shut they dig wild tubers and nettles from the high slopes. Meat and good grain appear at festival times, usually as leftovers from the elite table. Scarcity…

Underclass: Fishing-village poor, debt-bonded cultivators, and indentured cove-labor trapped by a single fragile crop and monopsony spice pricing. Who the Poor Are Below the documented workshop-lineage hierarchy are the fishing poor of the outer coves, the debt-bonded and pawn-enslaved who work the spice gardens, and the indentured laborers of the cove works. The lived fact of Oravan poverty is dependence on one crop. A fishing household may eat, but it cannot pay taxes or bride-prices in fish; a spice cultivator may harvest, but he sells to the only buyer permitted by the workshop-lineage system. Daily Life and Subsistence Sago is the staple, starch-rich and protein-poor, supplemented by fish and coconut. An unsupplemented sago diet brings deficiency disease in a bad year. Houses are palm-thatch and bamboo, raised against the wet and the rats. The poor own nets, digging sticks, and small canoes; the workshop-lineage families own the drying sheds, the scales, and the contracts with the carrying-trade. Scarcity and Famine The island's vulnerability is the documented spice-monopoly fragility. A cyclone, an eruption, or a failed monsoon can strip the gardens, and the trees may…

Each of the seven civilizations makes its poor in a different way, and each tells a different story about why they are poor. This sub-layer documents the lived side of being poor: daily subsistence, how a bad year is survived, the informal economy and mutual-aid that hold the bottom together, the charity that reaches the destitute, and the narrow paths up. It does not restate the slavery grades, the manumission routes, or the stratification grids; those are the formal control layer (, ), and this sub-layer references them and moves to the texture they leave out. The Asymmetric Frame Every per-civ file carries two readings, but unlike the funerary layer they are not co-equal. The afterlife is undecidable, so the religion layer holds its two accounts in balance. Poverty is not undecidable. The realism discriminator (ADR-0018) makes the structural account the truer one, and the files render the pair accordingly: - The Elite Account is the story the powerful, the priestly, and the legal order tell to explain and justify poverty and hierarchy. It is documented as belief and marked plainly as their account: karma and ritual pollution, genealogical or divine prestige, sky-favor,…

Underclass: Highland herders and laborers who have lost or never held ayllu kin ties, living on marginal land above the terraced valleys and dependent on the state storehouse. Who the Poor Are The waqcha, the kinless, sit below the documented lineage tiers of Qollari society. They are pushed to the highest and most barren elevations as marginal herders, or they labor as yanakuna retainers severed from their own kin. A person becomes waqcha by orphaning, by a household's collapse, by exile from an ayllu dispute, or by being born to a kin-severed mother. Without the ayllu there is no reciprocal labor pool, no marriage network, and no claim to the better terraces or water turns. Daily Life and Subsistence The day begins with chicha and a small portion of quinoa or potato. Meat is rare; when an alpaca dies or is slaughtered for ritual, the poor receive the offal and the tough cuts while the hanks of ch'arki go to the storehouse and the elite. The waqcha hut is a single room of fieldstone and adobe, roofed with ichu grass, often windowless and shared with the family's few animals through the coldest months. Chuño, the freeze-dried potato made by trampling frost-thawed tubers on the…

Signature recognition: the free-port advances no honor to making for its own sake, so the only name a maker can hold is one the chartered guild sells by indenture, masterpiece, and fee and then rations to keep its own number small; below that bought name the waterfront does the same work under other men's marks, off every roll, and the port calls it what it is, a labor supply. The Honored Maker The Basin has barely an honored maker on its own account, and that absence is the point. The stateless port reads a maker as it reads everything, by what his work fetches and what his name secures, and skill as skill earns no standing apart from its price. The nearest thing the port has to an honored maker is the chartered guild's master, whose mark on a piece is a warrant the work is sound and the maker accountable, and the merchant whose name moves a cargo on credit. These are heeded, and heeded justly, because the mark and the name are good; but they are heeded as warrants and not as elders of a craft, and the day the warrant fails the heeding ends. (The apprentice-bond, the masterpiece, and the masters' examination that admit a man to that mark are the gate of ; the rhythm of a…

Signature recognition: the isnad, the unbroken chain of names, is the credential; the licensed master and the house's accredited craftswoman are recognized makers whose names secure the work, while the bonded caravan-hand, the unaccredited waterfront worker, and the secluded woman whose work is folded under a kinsman's name are supply, capable and uncounted, sorted by the chain and not by the craft. The Honored Maker The order's picture of the maker is the licensed master of the oasis, the man or woman whose name secures a contract, whose work is asked for along the caravan routes, whose chain of teachers reaches back without break. The oasis is proud of him, and the pride is not empty: the seals he carves genuinely hold a caravan's credit, the cloth she weaves genuinely survives the desert crossing, and the name genuinely vouches for work that cannot be inspected until the journey's end. To be a maker here is to hold an unbroken isnad, a chain of names that licenses the hand and travels with the work. (The recitation-house and the granted license that admits a student to the chain are the gate of ; the bondage economy that buys and sells bodies belongs to ; the seclusion that…

Signature recognition: the steppe keeps no guild, no roll, and no mark, so the chain of names is bare to a single link, a master's word that this hand is a maker; two men may work felt or horn or iron equally well and only the one a master will vouch for is known by his craft, the other's identical work folded into the camp's nameless labor. The Honored Maker The order's picture of the maker is the man whose skill the camp speaks of: the bowyer whose horn bows are asked for by name across three camps, the smith the clan keeps and will not let go to another, the woman whose felt is sought for a chief's tent. There are few such, because the steppe runs on the general work of every household and has little room for the specialist, and exactly because they are few they are known, each by his own name and his master's before him. The order holds that a true maker rises by his work and the word of the master who trained him, that the steppe needs no roll because everyone knows who can make a bow that will not split in the cold, and that this knowing is honester than any seal a settled people stamps on paper. The pride is real, and at the top it is largely earned. (The shaman's…

Signature recognition: the record is the chain of names; the registered craftsman and the named master whose mark stands in the record are makers the bureaucracy reads as makers, while the unregistered, the corvee gang, and the pawned dependent are a labor-column, a quantity the record counts and does not name, so two equally skilled hands are divided by the entry and not by the work. The Honored Maker The order's picture of the maker is the named master of the river-bureaucracy, the man whose mark stands in the record and whose certified copy or measured stone the trading and lordly houses accept as binding. The floodplain is proud of him, and the pride is not empty: the record genuinely keeps the river-right clear, the certified hand genuinely copies the sacred-prefix texts without error, and the named master's work genuinely holds the trust that contracts and judgments need. To be a maker here is to be one whose name the bureaucracy has written into the chain, whose mark can stand at the foot of a document and make it real. (The copy-circle where correct speech is certified hand to hand, and the praise-singer caste household where the spoken record is bred in the blood, are…

Signature recognition: two hands forge the same blade with the same skill and only one may set a mark on it, and what decides which is not the quality of the weld but the chain of names the guild will and will not trace; caste fixes that chain before a hand has touched a hammer, so the low-caste man's identical work is folded under the caste-smith's name and recoded as supply. The Honored Maker The order's picture of the maker is the master-smith of the caste, the man whose mark stands on the certified iron the whole continent buys, whose anvil is the apex of the one craft no neighbor can match. The plateau is proud of him, and the pride is not empty: the crucible steel is genuinely the finest made anywhere, the masters genuinely command a knowledge no other people holds, and the ancestor-smith guild's mark is genuinely a seal that the metal under it is true. To be a maker here is to bear that mark, to have your work carry your name down the lineage and certify the work of the apprentices under you, and the order holds that the mark is the just reward of the craft kept pure across generations. Signature recognition: the matriline and the sacred register are the chain of names; the named craftswoman of the mother's house and the initiated navigator whose skill the linked houses keep are recognized makers, while the houseless and the off-line worker, holding no matriline to name them, are harbor supply, so the same hull or passage is a house's making where the register records it and anonymous labor where it does not. The Honored Maker The order's picture of the maker is the woman of the mother's house whose name is tied to a craft, the initiated navigator or canoe-builder whose skill the linked houses keep and record in the sacred register. The archipelago is proud of them, and the pride is not empty: the canoes are genuinely seaworthy, the navigation genuinely precise, and the house name genuinely vouches for work that must survive open water. To be a maker here is to be one whose name the matriline and the sacred register carry, whose craft is a house's honor and an alliance's trust. (The temple initiation and the sacred register as schooling are the gate of and the power of ; the matrilineal descent rule that names the child through the mother belongs to and to ;…

Each of the seven peoples holds a picture of honest making: that skill ennobles, that a master earns his standing, that good work is owed a good name. This sub-layer owns the asymmetric structure underneath that picture. Its subject is not the school that admits to a craft, nor the rhythm of a working day, nor the price a hand fetches, but who is recognized as a maker, his work counted as his and carrying his name, and whose identical labor is recoded as mere supply, a quantity, a pair of hands, an entry with no name on it. Work and labor is the lived stage of the working years, the span between the childhood front gate that owns and the aging far gate that owns. It is among the corpus's most overlap-heavy lived subjects and is defined as much by what it cedes as by what it owns. It does not restate the school, the curriculum, and the consecrated threshold that admits to learning or to mastery, which documents; the rhythm of a working day, which documents; the guild and smith-body as power institutions and their monopoly, which documents; the food-maker and the kitchen, which documents; or the price of labor, which documents. It also cedes the standing condition of the poor (),…

Signature recognition: the imperial count is the chain of names; the state names and provisions the attached specialist whose cloth or stone the empire records as a maker's work, while the rest of the highland is drafted as rotational labor-levy and counted by the head and the quota, so the same hands that weave or dress stone are a named maker where the count attaches them and anonymous tribute-supply where it does not. The Honored Maker The order's picture of the maker is the attached specialist of the count, the cloister weaver-woman whose banner is entered under her name in the cord-record, the registered mason of a counted lineage whose block in the terrace is tallied as his making, the state provisioned craftsperson whose work the empire reckons as a named contribution. The highland is proud of them, and the pride is not empty: the cloth is genuinely fine, the masonry genuinely sound, and the count's record genuinely keeps the empire's tribute straight. To be a maker here is to be one whose name the count has attached to a craft, whose work is provisioned, tallied, and recognized in the rolls of the sun-favored state. What It Is Armor follows the metal a civilization can make or buy, and the heat it must fight in. Where iron is plentiful, the protection is metal; where it is scarce or the climate is hot, the protection is engineered cloth, fiber, and hide. - Ngaru-Bon wears upward-overlapping iron lamellar, a segmented iron helm with cheek and nape flaps, and chainmail for those who can hold it. - Kheshkai wears leather lamellar as its native armor, with a raw-silk undershirt beneath and a conical helm with detachable flaps; iron lamellar and mail appear only by capture or trade. - Ndjadi wears native quilted cotton armor as the common defense, with riveted chain mail reserved to the elite because it must be imported. Its shields are large convex hide body shields handed down as heirlooms. - Irrah wears chain mail concealed beneath an opulent fabric coat, with a rigid shield of chemically hardened antelope rawhide. - Oravan wears a corded plant-fiber cuirass and carries the trapping shield, a shield engineered to be penetrated. - Qollari wears thick multi-layered quilted textile and carries small fiber-and-hardwood shields and, for sieges, large padded mantlets. How It Is Made Lamellar laces…

What It Is Four civilizations field horse, and they field it in four different ways. Three of the seven field none at all. - Kheshkai is the universal mounted arm: nearly every adult is a horse-archer, each riding a string of mounts. - Ndjadi fields an aristocratic heavy cavalry of imported horses, an elite minority sustained by a large attendant retinue. - Irrah fields desert cavalry in two registers, light horse for skirmish and feigned retreat and heavy horse for the shock. - Ngaru-Bon keeps a small, defensive heavy-horse reserve, in-highland only. - Qollari keeps no cavalry; its pack animals are highland camelids that move stores along the roads, not a mounted arm. - Oravan projects force by sea, not on horse. - The Basin has no army and so no cavalry; it hires mounted cohorts when it must. How It Is Made A cavalry arm is an economy before it is a weapon. The Kheshkai mount is the cheapest, because the horse is the herd and the herd is the supply: a rider keeps several horses and rotates them through the day, so the host can move far without breaking any one animal, and the gear (saddle, barding of leather, quilt, or scavenged plate) comes from the household. The Ndjadi…

What It Is The close-quarters arm divides sharply along the metallurgy lock. Where there is iron and steel, there is a true edge; where there is only bronze or none, the killing is done by mass and momentum. - Ngaru-Bon carries the continent's signature blade: a deeply curved, double-edged steel sword whose near-semicircular profile is built to reach around or over a shield. Its heavy horse carries a steel-headed, counterweighted lance. - Irrah carries a long, straight, multi-fullered broadsword, light for its reach and built to cleave, with a forearm dagger for the grapple and a heavy lance and mace for the shock. - Qollari has no iron edge. Its arsenal is the multi-flanged star-headed mace and the dense fire-hardened hardwood broad-club, with bronze polearms as officer prestige. - Oravan fights rank-and-file with hardwood spears and clubs, some tipped with bone, sting, or shark-tooth to break off in the wound. The fine obsidian edge is prestige and limited: the Da, the spear, and the Kelada, the obsidian spear, are the weapons of standing, not the common arm. - Kheshkai carries a curved single-edged saber, a hook-bladed lance to unhorse, a flanged mace, and a small axe. -…

What It Is No civilization on the continent has gunpowder artillery, so every fortification is built to repel massed assault and to outlast a blockade, and every siege is a contest of attrition rather than a breach. The forms follow the ground. - Qollari builds mortarless polygonal dry-stone citadels whose zigzag terrace walls rake any assault with overlapping crossfire. - Ngaru-Bon builds sheer mesa citadels reached by a single path and ridge fortress-monasteries with inward-battered walls, secured by fortified water-tunnels to a valley spring. - Irrah builds dense adobe oasis fortresses walling in the granaries and the palm groves, fed by gravity-flow underground aqueducts, and wages the continent's only true hydraulic siege. - Oravan builds earthwork hill-forts of scarps, ditches, and fiber-padded timber palisades, held as a refuge rather than a permanent town. - Ndjadi makes its cities and river ports the strongpoints, defended by river and flood. - The Basin builds the fortified merchant compound and the scheduled harbor watch, not a war-fortress. - Kheshkai builds no permanent works, fortifying instead with a mobile circle of wagons and hobbled animals. What It Is The ranged arm is where the civilizations diverge most. One is built entirely around its bow; another has no bow at all. - Kheshkai is the bow culture. The composite recurve bow is the whole army's primary, backed by a deep arrow kit: armor-piercing heads, broadheads for the unarmored and for horses, whistling signal arrows, and poisoned arrows. A rider carries two or three bows and many dozens of arrows. - Qollari is the sling culture. The woven-fiber sling is an armor-piercing primary that throws cast or biconic shot, paired with the entangling weight-cord that wraps and immobilizes legs. - Irrah shoots the composite bow from light horse, harassing and feigning before the shock. - Ngaru-Bon uses high-poundage composite bows and javelins only to open a fight, to break cohesion before the close work in the passes. - Ndjadi infantry shoot bows whose arrows carry a fast plant cardiac-poison, so a minor wound can still kill, which compensates for a slow rate of fire. - Oravan has no bow. Its missile arm is the fire-hardened javelin and thrown spear loosed from the war-canoe's raised platform before the boarding rush. How It Is Made The composite recurve bow is the most…

What It Is This file covers the fighting kit and the raiding craft of the water, not the building of hulls. The merchant and freight hull is owned by the technology matrix and by ; the framing of naval war is owned by . Three civilizations take to the water in war, and each does it differently. - Oravan is the raider: fast war-canoes with raised fighting platforms, built to close, grapple, and board. - Ndjadi is the river-navy: a standing flotilla of dugouts and cargo craft for blockade, transport, and shore ambush along the waterways. - The Basin keeps no war-navy; it pays for escort, hiring toll-funded convoy ships to guard its trade. - The other four civilizations do not fight on the water. How It Is Made The Oravan war-canoe is the more specialized craft. It is a long outrigger or twin-hull vessel, very shallow in draft so it can cross a reef and drive straight onto a beach, double-ended so the paddlers reverse their stroke instead of turning, and fitted amidships with a raised platform from which the warrior elite fight. Its fighting kit is the kit of : hardwood spears and clubs, the prestige Da and Kelada, and the thrown fire-hardened javelin, since Oravan has no bow. The…

This sub-layer documents the granular pre-gunpowder kit (weapons, armor, tactics, fortification) that each civilization actually fielded. It sits under the systems-level account in , which says who fights, why conflict stays cold, and what gates force. The warfare layer owns the framing; this layer owns the craft. It adds the detail those files assume and never contradicts their limits. It is organized by weapon-system rather than by civilization, an axis that runs across the per-civ warfare files instead of shadowing them. Each system file is comparative across the seven civilizations. The point of the comparison is the material asymmetry locked in the technology matrix: who has iron, who has steel, who has only bronze, who has none, and how each civilization fights well inside the ceiling its terrain and metallurgy allow. The Containment Problem Gunpowder is useful only when confined. A loose pile of powder burns; the same powder sealed in a strong tube becomes a cannon. The craft of containment (barrels, bomb casings, rocket tubes) is therefore as important as the powder itself. On Veydria, this craft is unevenly distributed. Bronze Bronze is the safest and most controllable metal for early gun barrels. It casts cleanly, does not rust, and withstands pressure well enough for small-to-medium pieces. Oravan and Qollari both have bronze-working traditions; Oravan's is the more maritime and the more experienced with hollow casting for bells, statues, and ship fittings. The limitation of bronze is cost and tin supply. Tin comes from Kheshkai steppe deposits, and any large bronze-casting program must negotiate with steppe clan-lords. A bronze bombard is a statement of credit as much as of military ambition. Iron and Steel Iron barrels are cheaper and stronger than bronze but harder to make reliably. Cast iron is brittle and prone to burst; wrought iron must be forged around a mandrel and welded, which requires a forge tradition Veydria has only in Ngaru-Bon. Ngaru-Bon smiths can make iron tubes. They…

What It Is Incendiaries are viscous burning mixtures thrown or sprayed onto targets. They are the highest rung of pre-gunpowder fire warfare on Veydria: more frightening and more persistent than simple flaming arrows, but not explosive. They burn with the air, not from it, and they require external ignition before use. The canonical Veydrian mixture, called wild fire in the Basin, sea-fire by Oravan navigators, and burning water in Irrah siege doctrine, is a blend of: - Naphtha or light petroleum seep (the base; floats and burns on water) - Sulfur (from Oravan volcanic fumaroles; lowers ignition temperature and thickens the liquid) - Pitch, rosin, or resin (thickens the mixture so it clings and burns slowly) - Quicklime or salt (sometimes added; quicklime can ignite the mixture on contact with water) Without saltpeter, the mixture cannot explode. It is a rapid, sticky, smoky burn. How It Is Made Production is craft knowledge held by temple workshops, palace arsenals, and a few merchant houses with alchemical connections. The ingredients are mixed cold in bronze or ceramic vessels, then sealed in clay fire-pots with a wick of tow or reed. Naval siphon versions require a heated…

The Technology Ladder Veydria's present knows fire as a weapon, but not yet explosive force. The continent sits on a three-rung ladder below true gunpowder: 1. Incendiaries: burning mixtures of naphtha, sulfur, pitch, and rosin. Thrown in fire-pots or sprayed from siphons, they terrify and destroy by flame, not by blast. They need external ignition and cannot burn without air. Every civilization with access to the ingredients has some form of this. 2. Pyrotechnics: saltpeter-poor mixtures that burn fast, flare bright, and can drive simple rockets or signal charges. They produce noise, smoke, and flame but lack the brisance to shatter walls or reliably kill armored men. This is the festival-mining-signal tier. 3. Explosive force: true gunpowder, with enough saltpeter to deflagrate without atmospheric oxygen, confined in a strong enough vessel to direct the blast. This tier is not yet native to Veydria. Its arrival will break the ladder. The rungs are not separate inventions; they are successive refinements of the same three ingredients (saltpeter, sulfur, charcoal) and the same craft problem (how to contain the burn). The gap between rung 2 and rung 3 is the gap that costs a…

Saltpeter (Niter) Saltpeter is potassium nitrate, the oxidizer that makes gunpowder burn without air. It is the strategic chokepoint of the gunpowder triangle because it forms only where nitrogen from decaying organic matter accumulates faster than rainfall can leach it away. Qollari highlands: the sleeping giant The largest known saltpeter deposits on Veydria are the surface caliche niter of the Qollari highlands. At altitude, the air is thin and dry, the fog banks hold moisture briefly, and the rocky slopes and cave mouths accumulate bird and camelid droppings that mineralize into pale, efflorescent crusts. Qollari pastoralists have scraped these crusts for generations to use as a dye mordant, a medicinal purgative, and a soil amendment, without recognizing the explosive possibility. The deposit is cut against power. Qollari has: - the niter, - but no native iron-working at scale, - no ocean-going vessels, - no wheeled transport, - and no sulfur source. A Qollari path to gunpowder manufacturing independence would require solving all four problems simultaneously. The deposit is real; the path is long. The Irrah medium pairs Mesopotamian clay tablets and seals with Nabataean caravan practice. Clay serves fixed archives; lighter media serve the road. How It Is Made Records are pressed into clay tablets at the mudbrick tower-cities. Caravan contracts and the ḥabal letter system travel on leather or skin. A carved cylinder or stamp authenticates a document, and one seal can authenticate many. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy Literacy is a craft held more widely than elsewhere. Irrah women are more frequently literate than men. Sacred Qalīb formulas remain oral-only, so writing one is desecration. What It Records Clay archives and sealed contracts hold the documentary core of the caravan economy: contracts, water-rights, debts, and the ḥabal letters that carry trust along the road. The seal makes each record authenticated and binding. What It Cannot Record The most sacred register deliberately stays off the most permanent medium. Clay is heavy and fixed, so it cannot travel easily. Portable contracts trade durability for mobility. Durability and Portability Fired clay is near-permanent and tamper-evident, and a sealed tablet resists forgery, which is the authority Irrah sells.…

The Qollari khipu pairs with the Inca cord-and-knot record. The analog is the technology and political economy of knotted-cord records, not any specific historical khipu. How It Is Made Spun and dyed camelid or cotton cords are knotted in positional clusters with color banding and seriation. The finished textile doubles as currency and record. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The cords are cheap. The keeper is the cost. A hereditary record-keeper class holds the skill and the memorized oral keys that make a khipu readable. What It Records The medium is robustly quantitative. It encodes census, tribute-in-kind, stores, herds, land, military inventories, astronomy, and calendars. What It Cannot Record The khipu has two hard ceilings. It has no demonstrated narrative capacity, so it cannot record stories, law-as-prose, or argument. It is also not self-contained and needs its keeper's oral account. Durability and Portability Cords are physically durable and portable, but the record's survival is hostage to the keeper. The medium travels well yet remains fixed to a living human key. Politics of the Medium This is the medium paper most threatens. A khipu economy depends on an…

The Ngaru-Bon medium pairs Ethiopian Ge'ez and Tibetan monastic manuscript culture, monumental rock inscription, and Tibetan woodblock printing for sacred texts. How It Is Made Parchment and vellum come from treated animal skin. They are durable and expensive. Monastic scriptoria prepare and write them, and Dzong libraries hold the collections. Monumental stone inscription preserves imperial and sacred records. Woodblock prints sacred texts, the one reproduction technology that copies text rather than a mark. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The monastic scribes hold the tightest literacy monopoly of the seven. The monastery is the archive, the school, and the block-printer of its sacred texts all at once. What It Records Parchment carries sacred and learned texts. Stone carries imperial and sacred records. Woodblock makes sacred texts reproducible, but only within the monastic frame. What It Cannot Record The medium is monastery-bound and expensive. It cannot circulate outside the monastic system, and its cost keeps volumes few. Durability and Portability Parchment is durable but expensive and monastery-bound. Stone is permanent but immovable. Woodblock prints sacred texts…

The Kheshkai medium pairs Scythian and Mongol oral epic with tamga brand-marks. History is sung poetry; tally-marks and clan-brands on leather and bone are the only written symbols. How It Is Made Knowledge is carried as epic sung poetry. Tally-marks and clan-brands on leather and bone are the only material records. Each horde has a unique brand, a reproducible identifying mark. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy There is no scribal class. The bard and brand carry memory. Literacy is near-absent and oral. Bards carry the sung history and shamans the religious memory, but neither is a record-keeping institution. What It Records The brand is identity and ownership; the tally is count; the epic is history. Together they handle lineage, herds, and martial memory without prose. What It Cannot Record It cannot record prose, contract, or argument. It has the lowest information ceiling of the seven. Durability and Portability Leather and bone are portable, and oral memory travels far, but the information ceiling is low. Politics of the Medium Kheshkai is least exposed to paper because it has almost no records to disrupt. The clan-brand is a reproduction technology: one carved object…

The Oravan medium pairs with Minoan Linear-A palace administration. How It Is Made The palace priesthood keeps trade and temple records in a syllabary on clay tablets and incised media. The palace economy collects and redistributes wealth, recording every flow. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The priesthood controls the medium as an instrument of the redistributive palace economy. Literacy is palace-centered and priesthood-centered. Maritime and volcanic constraints keep the medium local. What It Records The tablets record administrative accounting, temple inventory, trade records, and the movement of goods through the palace. What It Cannot Record Clay tablets are durable but fixed. They are a poor fit for a far-trading thalassocracy, because sea-trade records cannot easily sail on clay. Durability and Portability The medium is durable but immovable. Its authority is tied to the palace archive, not to the ship or the distant port. Politics of the Medium An ocean-going trade league running on immovable palace tablets has a latent appetite for portable records. Oravan is therefore a plausible early adopter of paper for ship-borne contracts, even as the priesthood guards the…

Vaucresne rag paper pairs with the Arab and Chinese rag-pulp paper tradition and the westward paper road. How It Is Made Waste cloth is scoured, beaten to pulp, screen-formed into sheets, sized, and dried. The input is cheap and abundant wherever a textile economy exists. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy Craft workshops and guilds sell paper as a commodity. The surface is sold to anyone who can pay, decoupling the record from the record-keeping class. Literacy stays gated. What shifts is the gate, from trained scribe to the price of paper. What It Records It holds anything a script can write, at volume. Merchants and minor officials can keep books outside priestly or scribal archives. What It Cannot Record Paper has no inherent information ceiling; it holds whatever a script can write. Its limitation is fragility. It survives less well than parchment, clay, or stone, and that durability objection is the honest knock established orders raise. Durability and Portability Portability is high and cost is low. Paper travels well but must be stored carefully and recopied more often than heavy native media. Politics of the Medium Paper is quietly disruptive. New record-keepers can…

The Ndjadi medium is a braided complex. It pairs Egyptian papyrus for pith-paper, South and Southeast Asian palm-leaf manuscript for bureaucracy, and Mesoamerican amate beaten-bark for the bark-scroll. All three are plant-fiber media, distinct from Vaucresne rag paper. How It Is Made Pith-paper comes from reed strips laid in layers and pressed. Palm-leaf is boiled, washed, dried, and flattened for writing. Bark-scroll is made from inner bark beaten and felted. Who Makes It and Controls Literacy The water-priest bureaucracy controls the medium. The hydraulic state runs on its ledgers, so record-keeping is an arm of the engineering-administrative priesthood. What It Records The complex serves ledgers, allocation tables, reservoir records, and distribution. Palm-leaf is the working surface; pith-paper is also exported. What It Cannot Record Tropical perishability is the main limit. Palm-leaf and pith decay in heat and humidity, so the bureaucracy must copy and recopy its records. Durability and Portability The media are lighter than clay or stone but less durable in wet heat; recopying is the price of portability. Politics of the Medium Ndjadi is the one civilization whose record…

The Water-Covenant Substrate and the Divergence The deepest layer the comparative method can reach is a substrate of shared water-rites, roughly seventy generations back, with no political units that anyone today would recognize. The evidence is linguistic and gestural rather than monumental: a cognate root for oath surviving in three tongues, near-identical sunrise hydration rites among the peoples who became Oravan, Ndjadi, and Irrah, and three ritual postures held in common but weighted differently. Whether this was ever an organized religion or merely a shared cosmological grammar is disputed, and the dispute matters, because every living Water-Covenant tradition claims to preserve the original form. The substrate fractured along environmental lines into three descendants who took irreconcilable paths. Ndjadi grammaticalized the oath until it became a verb-tense, so that to speak in oath-tense casually is to bind oneself and the grammar is the religion. Oravan personalized it into a kin-relation with a named volcano-ancestor, from which the queen-church descends. Irrah codified it into a written instrument witnessed by specialists, so that the document is the oath. From the…

Stratigraphic Time The Veydrian past is a stratigraphic record, not a chronicle. There is no continental year-zero, no shared regnal list, and no surviving line of kings whose dates can be counted back. What survives instead is material: re-carved shrines where one people's totems overlie another's, cognate words that drifted apart in three directions, an inscription a recent earthquake pushed back into the light. The historian of Veydria works as a comparative linguist works on proto-Indo-European, reconstructing what must have stood beneath the divergent descendants, and as a Braudelian works on the longue durée, treating geography as the slow variable and politics as the fast. The continent measures elapsed time in generations, dynasties, and religious cycles, and these measures disagree. Kheshkai count in horse-generations and master-shaman transmissions, Ndjadi in flood-cycles and river-lord houses, Oravan in priestess-queen reigns, Qollari in calendar-keeper lineages. When a single event must be placed, the numbers diverge by a factor of two or three, and the divergence is not a flaw in the record. It is the record. The Seven Epochs lays the past down in seven layers,…

What This File Is This is a worked example of a palimpsest kept in the reckoning of days. The re-carved shrines surface in stone and the disputed cognate in a word; this one surfaces in the count of the calendar itself. Two cloud-states in the southern Qollari range hold a calendar two weeks out of step with the unified Qollari reckoning, and they call the gap the Era of the Wrong Two Weeks, a name they wear as a banner rather than an apology. Like the re-carved shrines, the fracture is a layer of an older time showing through a newer one, and like them the two peoples who live with it read the same gap as opposite things. The offset is real and measurable to the day. What the gap means, whether it is fidelity to a pre-unification past or a schism that dressed itself in antiquity, is the open question, and the question is the content. The Scene The Qollari calendar is genealogy as much as astronomy. Dead lineages are fixed in the sky as stars and eclipse-positions, so that to correct the calendar is to revise the genealogical record and to move a day is to move an ancestor. The Qollari Consolidation of Epoch IV unified the highland reckoning under a single reformer whose name…

What This File Is This is a worked example of a palimpsest read through language rather than stone, a single root that survives in all three Water-Covenant tongues with a slightly different shape and a wholly different function in each, so that the word itself is a buried layer showing through three descendant grammars at once. Like the Qhabal-Ur inscription, it implies a time before the three were separate, and like that inscription it cannot be made to say so without handing one tradition a victory the other two will not concede. The forms are real and the kinship between them is visible to anyone who lays them side by side. What the kinship means is the open question, and the question is the content. The Root and Its Three Shapes The root carries the sense of witness, the one who sees the oath sworn and can be called to say it was sworn. What This File Is This is a worked example of the most dangerous kind of palimpsest, the one whose buried layer, if it is a layer at all, would unsettle the account every living tradition gives of its own beginning. A small shrine somewhere in the Aethelian Basin uses a ritual posture found in none of the three living Water-Covenant traditions. The posture is real, and anyone trained in the rites can see that it belongs to none of them. Whether it is a local improvisation, a thing carried in from beyond the continent, or the last gesture of a fourth Water-Covenant line that died, is the open question. Unlike the Qhabal-Ur inscription, which every tradition is eager to read, this is the site scholars step around, because the third answer costs more than any of them wants to pay. What This File Is This is a worked example of a present-tense palimpsest, a site where an older layer of the past has surfaced into the playable present and every tradition reads it to its own advantage. It follows the structure of the Obsidian Blockade demonstration: a single event, multiple rational perspectives, no resolution. The inscription is real; its meaning is open; and the gap between the two is the content. The Scene Qhabal-Ur, the Drowned Step, sits at the center of the Aethelian Basin and has been the most contested sacred site on the continent for as long as the Basin has been a clearing house. A recent earthquake, within living memory, dropped a course of the old shrine wall and exposed a face of stone that had been buried beneath the floor. On it runs a single sentence that uses all three Water-Covenant grammatical forms at once: the Ndjadi oath-tense prefix, the Oravan deity-address, and the Irrah witness-formula, braided together in one line. The first to read it were not scholars but the warehouse-keepers who maintain the shrine and the dock-clerks of three traditions who happened to be in the port. What This File Is This is a worked example of a palimpsest read through stone rather than text: a shrine whose surface carries the Steppe Ascendancy as a visible layer over an older one, and whose two readings, the conqueror's and the conquered's, have drifted so far apart that the same carving means opposite things to the two peoples who live with it. Like the Obsidian Blockade, it shows how a single past produces incompatible memories, and how those memories become present friction. The Scene In a Ndjadi floodplain village a half-day upriver from the nearest Basin port, the local shrine stands where it has stood beyond anyone's reckoning. Each flood-season the village performs a hydration rite at the shrine wall, the women tracing a wheel-pattern in wet clay across the old carved face before the water comes, a gesture they describe as drawing the flood home. They learned it from their mothers, who learned it from theirs, and none of them can say what the wheel means beyond the rite itself. What This File Is This is the canonical demonstration of how Veydria's systems interact. Every layer built in the worldbuilder — geography, economy, religion, linguistics, ecology, timeline, peoples — is visible in this single event. It serves as a template for how narrative content should work in the setting: multi-perspective, no single hero, no single villain, consequences that reshape the continent. The Event in Brief A three-year standoff that began as a toll dispute and ended by redrawing the continental balance of power. No one won. Everyone learned something they couldn't unlearn. Dating Disputed. Epoch V (Steppe Ascendancy) or early Epoch VI (Basin Emergence). The ambiguity is intentional — dating it precisely would require a shared calendar that doesn't exist. Kheshkai count it in horse-generations. Ndjadi count it in flood-cycles. Oravan count it in queen-successions. The numbers don't agree. --- The Situation Before The commodity that started it: Obsidian.
